Module 1: About Fit For Nuclear (F4N) and NucCol

1.1 What is Fit For Nuclear?

Fit For Nuclear (F4N) is a long-term business development programme that develops capability, capacity, and competitiveness in manufacturing and engineering companies who want to enter or grow in the nuclear sector. Originally developed by the Nuclear Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre (Nuclear AMRC) at the University of Sheffield over more than a decade, it is now delivered by Nuclear Collaboration Ltd (NucCol) – the successor organisation established by the Nuclear AMRC's own leadership team in 2024.

F4N is more than a checklist or assessment. It is a comprehensive, evidence-based sector development programme. It has been refined over more than a decade with support from top-tier nuclear clients and the UK Government. At its core, F4N develops the capability, capacity, and competitiveness of UK manufacturing businesses who want to enter or grow in the nuclear sector. It spans the full business lifecycle – from strategic leadership to shop-floor delivery – helping companies ensure they are not only technically competent, but culturally aligned with the safety, quality, and behavioural expectations of the sector.

What Makes F4N Different from Other Accreditations
F4N is a development tool – a structured journey to becoming 'match-fit' for nuclear – not a pass/fail accreditation. It covers the full business: strategy, people, processes, quality, supply chain – 'from strategy to torque wrench'. It includes a nuclear safety culture and sector-specific layer that no other general business improvement programme provides. It is not an alternative to ISO 9001 or ISO 19443 – it complements them, helping companies get their business ready to certify. It provides genuine ongoing support through the SCC relationship – not just an assessment result. 100% of surveyed F4N companies said they would recommend it to other manufacturers.

1.2 F4N vs ISO 19443 – Complementary, Not Competing

A common question from companies is whether they should pursue F4N or ISO 19443 certification. The answer is both – and they work in a specific sequence. F4N gets the business ready: it develops culture, capability, strategy, and operational maturity. ISO 19443 then proves it – it is the internationally recognised nuclear quality management standard that tier-1 clients and regulators require. Together, they make a company a credible, competitive, and compliant nuclear supply chain partner.

FeatureF4NISO 19443
Strategy & LeadershipFully embedded development programmeNot specifically addressed
Culture & PeopleCore focus – nuclear safety culture developedRequired but not deeply developed
Nuclear Safety AwarenessDeveloped through training and coachingRequired but self-managed
Quality SystemsAssessed and developedAudited and certified
Traceability & CFSIIncludedRequired
CertificationNo (status, not certification)Yes – internationally recognised
Support & ToolsProvided throughout journeySelf-managed

1.3 NucCol's Heritage and Proven Impact

  • Nuclear AMRC supply chain programmes: £3.57 billion in new contracts won, £161 million additional investment, 12,591 jobs created or safeguarded
  • F4N specifically: £2.1 billion new contracts won, 3,049 jobs created or safeguarded, £43 million additional investment
  • 100% of surveyed F4N companies would recommend the programme
  • 70% of F4N companies expect turnover to grow after engaging
  • Over 1,000 companies have taken the F4N self-assessment; 100+ currently hold Granted status

1.4 The Supply Chain Consultant (SCC) Role

As an F4N Supply Chain Consultant (SCC) or Senior Supply Chain Consultant (SSCC), you are the named point of contact for every company you support. You are not just an assessor – you are a mentor, coach, and trusted adviser throughout the entire programme lifecycle. The quality of the SCC relationship is one of the most important factors in whether a company successfully achieves granting.

ResponsibilityWhat This Means in Practice
Lead point of contactYou are the company's primary relationship with NucCol. They contact you first with questions, concerns, and updates.
Self-assessment reviewReview BE and NSS self-assessments. Identify over/under-scoring. Provide written feedback before the OSV.
OSV deliveryPlan and conduct the full-day On-Site Verification visit. Issue report within 14 working days.
Action plan supportHelp generate a prioritised, SMART action plan. Support execution. Ensure portal is kept up to date.
Pre-granting visitPhysical evidence verification before submitting granting recommendation. Confirm the 'Triple 85' criteria are met.
Granting recommendationSubmit formal recommendation to NucCol Granting Panel – your professional judgement is on the line.
Maintain & SustainConduct twice-yearly M&S reviews post-granting. Drive continuous improvement.
02

Module 2: The F4N Journey – All 8 Stages in Full

The F4N programme follows a structured, staged journey typically taking 12–18 months. Every stage has a check point before progression is possible. The entire journey is captured in the F4N online portal. As SCC, you are present and active at every stage.

Stage 1: Capability Questionnaire & Eligibility (Nuclear Capability Questionnaire – NCQ)

The NCQ is the mandatory pre-qualification step that all applicants must complete before progressing further in the programme. It gathers background information about the company including: business details (registration, ownership, website), financial performance (turnover, EBIT, exports), workforce size, capabilities and product types, safety, quality, delivery, and HR performance indicators, accreditations, and previous nuclear sector experience.

Why the NCQ is Critical
Assesses eligibility: companies must meet minimum criteria around size, turnover, UK manufacturing presence. Ensures appropriate support: helps NucCol understand how best to assist each company. Gatekeeping: prevents progression of companies not yet viable for nuclear supply chain development. Data-driven: auto-accept, auto-reject, or manual review decisions are made based on responses. Companies with no UK operations or extremely low turnover and no nuclear experience are auto-rejected. Collects data for Supply Chain Readiness Level (SCRL) modelling.

Stage 2: Online Self-Assessment – BE and NSS

Stage 2 is the online self-diagnostic assessment, which companies complete after passing the NCQ. The self-assessment is designed to benchmark current performance against nuclear sector expectations, identify gaps between current capabilities and nuclear industry standards, lay the foundation for a continuous improvement journey, and educate the company on the expectations of the nuclear sector.

The Business Excellence self-assessment covers the six core areas across 60 multiple-choice questions. The Nuclear Sector Specific assessment appears as a separate tab on the F4N portal (the Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) tab) and is introduced later in the journey – typically around 3–4 months before the expected granting date.

Important: How the Self-Assessment Works
Collaborative: not meant to be completed by one person – it requires input from across the business to ensure accuracy. Directors and senior managers must agree with the submission and participate in follow-up activity. Scoring: each answer carries a score (0, 2, 7, 10), and results generate a baseline performance profile. Evidence expectation: companies must demonstrate and provide evidence for their responses for pre-review prior to the OSV. SCC Review: before the OSV, the SCC reviews all responses and flags where scores appear inconsistently high or low.

Stage 3: On-Site Verification Assessment (OSV)

The OSV is a structured, full-day visit to verify the self-assessment claims against real evidence. It is not a pass/fail exam – it is a diagnostic that produces the action plan. The SCC spends the day examining all six BE categories, conducting a facility tour, meeting leadership and staff, reviewing documents, and providing initial feedback.

Why the OSV Matters

  • It ensures credibility and consistency of F4N scoring.
  • It builds trust in the process for both companies and industry buyers.
  • It acts as a benchmarking tool for continuous improvement.
  • It is the crucial gateway to the granting panel process further down the line.

Standard OSV Agenda

TimeActivity & Information Reviewed
09:00Meet & Introductions – meet over coffee, plan for the day. Directors and Senior Management.
09:30Strategy & Leadership – Vision, Values, Strategic Plan and deployment paperwork, Leadership and development. Directors and Senior Management.
10:15Tour of Manufacturing Facilities – walk through the manufacturing processes. Senior Management escort.
11:00Design & Project Management – PM system and status of projects. Technical Director.
11:45Process Excellence – Lean manufacturing strategy, VSM, improvement plans. Operations Director.
12:30Working Lunch & morning reflection.
13:00People Excellence – employee involvement, development and training. Senior Management/HR.
13:45QHSE – Health & Safety and Quality Management systems. Senior Management/H&S/Quality.
14:15Supply Chain – supply chain management system. Senior Management/Purchasing/Quality.
14:45Initial feedback & next steps – summary scoring and early action plan recommendations.
15:00Finish.

Following the OSV, a detailed written report is issued – verified scores, observations and evidence gaps, suggested improvements. This report forms the basis of the Action Plan (Stage 4) and ensures companies focus their improvement efforts on areas that truly matter in the nuclear supply chain.

Stage 4: Improvement Plan Generation & Execution

Based on OSV findings, the SCC works with the company to generate a prioritised action plan. Every action must be SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound). The company then executes the plan, with the SCC providing ongoing support, reviewing evidence of completed actions, and ensuring the portal is kept up to date. The SCC may visit again or hold calls to support progress, and helps ensure actions are meaningful and linked to real improvements.

Stage 5: Nuclear Sector Specific (NSS) Assessment

The Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) is typically introduced when a company is close to meeting the Triple 85 rule – approximately 3–4 months before the expected granting panel date. Introducing it too early can overwhelm the company, lead to vague or premature actions, and dilute strategic focus. The NSS assessment is completed by the company (self-scored 0, 2, 7, 10), with actions generated for gaps and linked to the overall action plan.

Why the NSS Assessment Matters
It ensures culture and behaviours are in line with the nuclear industry's expectations – not just technical systems. It is a strong indicator to clients and the Granting Panel that the company can operate reliably in high-integrity, regulated environments. It helps businesses embed nuclear-specific thinking into long-term strategy – not just pass an assessment. NSS scores are reviewed by the SCC with the same rigour as BE scores – the SCC must be able to challenge and justify every NSS score.

Stage 6: Pre-Granting Preparation & Evidence Demonstration

The pre-granting meeting is an in-depth review led by the SCC to ensure the company has genuinely achieved the required improvements, all F4N granting criteria are demonstrably met, and the SCC is confident and ready to recommend the company for granting.

The 'Triple 85' – Granting Eligibility Requirements

To be eligible for F4N granting, companies must achieve all three of the following:

RequirementDetail
85% overall scoreOverall Business Excellence score of 85% or above (adjustments made for non-design companies via the F4N Design Factor).
85% in Health & SafetyHealth & Safety subset score of 85% or above – reflecting the critical importance of QHSE in nuclear.
85% action plan completion85% of all actions in the improvement plan must be completed with evidence uploaded to the portal.
What Happens During the Pre-Granting Visit
Starts with a factory tour to confirm visible changes from the original OSV. Line-by-line review of the Action Plan – confirm evidence and scoring are consistent. Review of the Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) – assess alignment with nuclear culture. Review of ISO certificates, specifically ISO 9001, looking for Opportunities for Improvement (OFIs) and Non-Conformances with actions. Confirmation that evidence aligns with the scoring rationale. Confirmation of any nuclear-specific work won and target clients. SCC takes notes to build the case for panel recommendation. If concerns arise (weak evidence, misaligned scoring), the SCC may delay pre-granting and request further improvement before rescheduling.

Stage 7: NucCol Granting Panel

The Granting Panel is the final approval stage where the company's entire F4N journey is reviewed to determine if it is ready to be formally awarded Fit For Nuclear status. It is a formal, structured meeting involving senior members of the F4N team, NucCol programme leaders, and sometimes external representatives or sector specialists.

What Is Submitted to the Panel

  • A Business Excellence summary
  • Verified scores across all 60 self-assessment questions
  • Commentary on each section (strengths, gaps addressed)
  • A completed Action Plan, with evidence attached
  • A completed Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS)
  • Photographs, policies, ISO certificates, H&S documentation
  • A signed F4N Charter and Benefits Statement

Stage 8: F4N Granted Status & Maintain and Sustain

Once granted, the company receives their F4N Certificate and is listed on the Nuclear Supplier Database. They then move into the Maintain & Sustain (M&S) annual subscription (annual fee: £3,000). The SCC continues with twice-yearly review visits.

Maintain & Sustain Benefits
Retain F4N Granted Status: no reassessment required while the annual subscription is active. Nuclear Supplier Database: maintained prominent position, maximising exposure to Tier 1s and prime contractors. Twice-yearly SCC reviews: dedicated Supply Chain Consultant support for continuous improvement. Ongoing access: email and phone access to SCC for advice and guidance. Training modules: pre-recorded training modules and NucCol webinar access. Exclusive events: roundtables, networking events, and workshops with industry leaders. Note: without an active M&S subscription, F4N Granted status cannot be retained after the 1st year of granting.
03

Module 3: The F4N Scoring System

Every F4N question – whether Business Excellence or Nuclear Sector Specific – uses the same four-level scoring system. Understanding and applying this consistently and honestly is fundamental to the SCC role. Every score you award must be defensible to the Granting Panel.

ScoreWhat It Means – and What the SCC Must Look For
0 – NoneNo formal approach exists. Nothing is in place at all. Do not score 0 out of frustration – only when genuinely nothing exists.
2 – InformalSome activity takes place, but it is informal, inconsistent, or undocumented. Would fail if a key individual left. Score 2 when you see effort but no formal structure.
7 – FormalA formal, documented approach is in place and working. Evidence can be produced. May have minor gaps. THIS IS THE GRANTING READINESS THRESHOLD. Score 7 when you see a genuine, working system with evidence.
10 – Best PracticeBest practice fully embedded. Typically requires UKAS-accredited certification or demonstrably equivalent standard. Continuous improvement is driving the area forward. Score 10 only for genuine best practice – not just a strong 7.
Common SCC Scoring Mistakes
Accepting a 10 because the company has a policy. Policies alone score 2. Deployment and evidence of it working scores 7+. Scoring 7 because you feel sorry for the company. The Granting Panel will challenge every score. Be honest. Scoring 0 for design elements when the company is a pure service provider. If design is out of scope, scoring is adjusted – do not penalise them. Forgetting that 7 is the granting readiness threshold – not every element needs to be a 10 to achieve granting. Scoring based on what the company tells you, not what you actually see. Observational evidence is the most reliable. Not challenging over-inflated self-assessment scores. The self-assessment is the company's view – the OSV report is yours.

3.1 Common Scoring Traps by Category - What New SCCs Miss

Beyond the general scoring guidance, experience shows that certain elements in each category are consistently over or under-scored by companies and sometimes by new SCCs. The following category-by-category guide covers the most common traps.

Category - ElementCommon Trap and How to Handle It
Strategy: Mission, Vision and ValuesCompanies display MVV on walls and assume this scores 7. A 7 requires employees at all levels to understand and reference the values in their daily work. Ask an operator on the shop floor. If they cannot recall the values, the score is probably 2.
Strategy: CSIP / Leading ChangeA CSIP document that was written during the self-assessment and has no entries older than two months scores 2, not 7. The CSIP must be a live, active register of improvement projects with measurable outcomes.
Strategy: Visible SLT'We have an open door policy' is not evidence of visible SLT. Ask to see the Gemba walk schedule. If there is not one, ask when the MD last spent unscheduled time on the shop floor. Visible SLT requires documented, regular presence.
Design: FMEACompanies frequently claim to have FMEA but produce a blank template when asked. A live FMEA must show: the process or design being analysed, identified failure modes, severity/occurrence/detection ratings, and actions taken or planned.
People: SQEPThe most commonly over-scored element in the entire assessment. Having job descriptions and some training records is not SQEP. SQEP requires a defined list of safety-relevant roles, documented qualification and experience requirements for each, and verified evidence that the current post-holders meet those requirements.
Process: 5SA recently tidied shopfloor for the benefit of the visit is not 5S. Ask for the 5S audit records. When was the last audit? What scores were given? What improvement actions were raised? Without a sustained audit programme, 5S scores 2.
Process: SOPsSOPs stored in a folder that operators have not seen are worth 2, not 7. Ask an operator to show you the SOP for their task. Do they know where it is? Does the version on the floor match the controlled version in the system?
QHSE: Safety CultureA high near-miss reporting rate is positive, not concerning. Companies that report zero near misses in a month almost certainly have a reporting culture problem. Do not accept a low near-miss rate as evidence of good safety - probe the culture instead.
QHSE: CFSICompanies frequently have a CFSI procedure but have not trained their buying team or goods-in staff. Ask the person who raises purchase orders what CFSI means. Ask the person on the goods-in desk how they would identify a suspect item. If they cannot answer, the score is 2 regardless of what the procedure says.
QHSE: ISO CertificationsNon-UKAS accredited certifications are common. A certificate from an unaccredited body scores lower than one from a UKAS-accredited body. Always verify UKAS accreditation on the UKAS website (ukas.com) - do not take the certificate at face value.
Supply Chain: Supplier KPIsAn approved supplier list with no performance data against it scores 2. Supplier KPIs requires evidence that the company is actively measuring and managing their suppliers - not just a list of who they buy from.

1.5 What F4N Does NOT Cover - Scope Boundaries for the SCC

Understanding what is outside the scope of F4N is just as important as knowing what is inside it. New SCCs sometimes feel pressure to advise on matters that sit outside their remit, or to make commitments the programme cannot deliver. The following boundaries are important to understand from day one.

Out of ScopeWhat the SCC Should Do Instead
Legal or regulatory compliance adviceF4N assesses the presence of management systems and processes. It does not provide legal advice on employment law, environmental law, health and safety law, or nuclear regulation. If a company asks for legal interpretation, direct them to their legal advisers or the relevant regulator.
Technical engineering consultancyF4N assesses project management and design processes - it does not provide engineering design review, structural calculations, material specifications, or technical approval of products. If a company asks for technical engineering input, direct them to appropriate technical consultancies or NIA member organisations.
Certification or accreditationThe SCC cannot certify a company to ISO 9001, ISO 19443, or any other standard. F4N Granted status is not a substitute for formal certification. If a company believes F4N replaces ISO 9001, correct this misunderstanding clearly and early.
Procurement introductions or commercial brokeringThe SCC is not a sales agent or procurement broker. While F4N provides visibility through the Nuclear Supplier Database, the SCC should not promise specific introductions to customers or imply they can facilitate contracts. Signpost NucCol events and NIA activities instead.
Financial or investment adviceThe SCC cannot advise on funding, investment, grant applications, or financial planning. If a company asks about funding support for F4N-related investment, direct them to their regional growth hub, Innovate UK, or NucCol's commercial team.
Counselling or wellbeing supportIf an engagement reveals personal or organisational distress beyond normal business challenges, the SCC should handle this with care and empathy but recognise it is beyond their professional remit. Escalate serious welfare concerns to NucCol.

If in doubt about whether something is within your scope, the rule is simple: ask your NucCol engagement manager before you advise. Acting outside your remit does not serve the company well, and it exposes both you and NucCol to unnecessary risk.

Modules 4–9: Business Excellence Assessment – All 60 Questions in Full

The following six modules cover every one of the 60 Business Excellence questions in full. For each question you will find: the question title and introduction (what the SCC is looking for), all four scoring level descriptions (0/2/7/10), the key evidence to seek at the OSV, and a 'Why This Matters' section explaining why this question is relevant to nuclear supply chain readiness. These are drawn directly from the NucCol F4N question set.

Category: 1. Strategy & Leadership

The organisation has developed a vision of the future that is supported by clear values and a defined strategy that is deployed and fully integrated into daily business activities. The SLT sees the need for change and continuous development.

We are looking for a fully developed MVV – clearly defined, well-communicated, and embedded into the culture. The MVV statement should be available for discussion at verification.

0 – None
No defined mission, vision, or values.
2 – Informal
MVV exists but is poorly communicated or understood.
7 – Formal
MVV is well-defined and communicated, supporting alignment.
10 – Best Practice
MVV fully embedded, guiding strategy, culture, and behaviours.
Key Evidence: MVV statement published/distributed, shopfloor posters/screens, induction packs, employee survey awareness results, toolbox talks referencing MVV.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Without a clear Mission, Vision, and Values, an organisation has no north star. In nuclear, where decisions must be made under pressure and where culture drives safety outcomes, employees at every level need to know what the organisation stands for. A company that cannot articulate its MVV coherently is unlikely to have the cultural cohesion that tier-1 nuclear customers require. MVV is also the foundation from which all strategic objectives and deployment flows.

We are looking to identify whether the SLT has capability and experience to develop strategic objectives, and the extent of their involvement.

0 – None
No defined strategic objectives.
2 – Informal
Some objectives defined but lack clarity or measurable targets.
7 – Formal
Objectives are clear, measurable, and regularly reviewed.
10 – Best Practice
Objectives fully embedded, strong alignment to operations, performance, and CI.
Key Evidence: Board minutes, SMART objectives, departmental objectives linked to strategy, SLT competency records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Strategic objectives that are vague, unmeasured, or not reviewed are effectively decorative. In nuclear supply chain, customers will probe whether a company has direction and ambition – particularly around quality, capability development, and financial stability. The SLT's ability to develop and own meaningful strategic objectives signals the governance maturity nuclear prime contractors expect from their partners.

We are looking for a fully developed, forward-looking strategic plan including nuclear sector as a growth target and export potential. Plan must be available at verification.

0 – None
No formal strategic plan in place.
2 – Informal
A strategic plan exists but is incomplete or not consistently applied.
7 – Formal
A comprehensive plan is in place, communicated, and reviewed regularly.
10 – Best Practice
The plan is fully embedded, agile, and continuously improved with stakeholder input.
Key Evidence: Formal strategy document with nuclear sector target, export market identification, evidence of SLT involvement, plan review records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
A nuclear prime contractor or Tier 1 customer wants confidence that a supplier has a long-term future. A credible strategic plan – particularly one that identifies nuclear as an active growth target – signals that the company is investing in its capabilities, not just reacting to opportunities. Companies without a strategic plan are unpredictable supply chain partners.

We are looking for regular strategic reviews used to evaluate progress, manage risks, and adjust direction.

0 – None
No formal strategic reviews are conducted.
2 – Informal
Reviews are conducted irregularly or cover limited scope.
7 – Formal
Regular strategic reviews are conducted, covering key performance and risks.
10 – Best Practice
Reviews are fully embedded, data-driven, and trigger continuous improvement.
Key Evidence: Strategic review meeting minutes (last 12 months), frequency, attendees, evidence of strategy adjustment following reviews.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
A strategy that is never reviewed is not a living document – it is wishful thinking. Nuclear supply chains require suppliers who adapt to changing technical, regulatory, and commercial environments. Regular strategic reviews demonstrate governance maturity and the ability to course-correct. They also show the Granting Panel that the company's journey to nuclear readiness is deliberate, not accidental.

We are assessing how effectively strategy is deployed across functions and levels, with clear accountability.

0 – None
No clear process for deploying strategy.
2 – Informal
Deployment is informal or inconsistent across departments.
7 – Formal
Strategy is systematically deployed with clear accountability and communication.
10 – Best Practice
Strategy is fully embedded with alignment from enterprise to individual levels.
Key Evidence: Cascaded objectives at department/team/individual level, deployment process documentation, alignment evidence between strategy and shopfloor KPIs.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Strategy without deployment is aspiration. Nuclear customers need suppliers whose entire organisation – from board to shopfloor – is aligned to the same goals. Without a deployment process, strategic intent evaporates at the middle-management level and never reaches operators. Deployment is what turns a strategy document into actual business improvement.

We are looking at how clearly the organisation communicates its strategy and whether two-way feedback mechanisms are in place.

0 – None
No formal communication of strategy to stakeholders.
2 – Informal
Communication is limited or inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Strategy communicated clearly and regularly across stakeholder groups.
10 – Best Practice
Communication is fully embedded, two-way, and continuously improved.
Key Evidence: Town hall records, newsletters, visual management boards, employee survey awareness results, feedback mechanisms.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Employees who do not understand the strategy cannot contribute to it. In nuclear, where culture and behaviours must be aligned to safety and quality at every level, communication is not just a nice-to-have – it is a business risk. If operators on the shopfloor cannot explain what the company is trying to achieve, that company's culture is fragile. Two-way communication mechanisms also ensure the leadership team hears what is actually happening on the ground.

We want to understand how the organisation leads change initiatives (CSIP) aligned with strategic goals, with engaged SLT leadership.

0 – None
No formal change management process or leadership.
2 – Informal
Change managed ad-hoc with minimal leadership involvement.
7 – Formal
Change initiatives led systematically with leadership engagement.
10 – Best Practice
Change initiatives fully embedded, led by committed leadership, drive measurable improvements.
Key Evidence: CSIP document, Kaizen/Lean project register, SLT sponsorship, measurable CI outcomes, cross-functional involvement evidence.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
The CSIP (Continuous Sustainable Improvement Plan) is F4N's vehicle for structured, SLT-led improvement. In nuclear, the expectation is that quality, safety, and efficiency are continuously improving – not static. A company that only improves reactively (after failures or customer complaints) is high-risk. Companies with a proactive, leadership-owned improvement agenda demonstrate the culture that nuclear requires. The CSIP also provides the paper trail that shows the Granting Panel a genuine journey of improvement.

We are looking for clear SLT visibility in driving priorities, engaging with employees, and leading by example on the shopfloor.

0 – None
SLT largely invisible, minimal engagement with staff.
2 – Informal
SLT engages occasionally but inconsistently.
7 – Formal
SLT actively visible and engages regularly with staff on key priorities.
10 – Best Practice
SLT highly visible, regularly engaging all staff, driving strategic priorities.
Key Evidence: Gemba walk schedules, toolbox talk attendance by SLT, employee survey results referencing leadership visibility, SLT coaching records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Visible SLT is about more than leadership being seen – it is about the culture that visible leadership creates. When directors and senior managers are regularly present on the shopfloor, engaging with teams and leading by example, it reinforces the importance of quality, safety, and continuous improvement. Companies where SLT only appears for formal occasions typically have a disconnect between management intent and operational reality – a common cause of quality failures.

We are assessing whether leadership roles are clearly defined, communicated, and aligned with strategic goals.

0 – None
Leadership roles unclear or poorly communicated.
2 – Informal
Some leadership roles defined but communication inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Leadership roles well defined and communicated across the organisation.
10 – Best Practice
Leadership roles fully embedded, aligned with strategic objectives, regularly reviewed.
Key Evidence: Organisation chart, job descriptions for all leadership roles, RACI matrix, governance structure, delegation of authority policy.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Ambiguity in leadership accountability is a safety and quality risk. In nuclear, it is essential that everyone knows who is responsible for what – especially when things go wrong. Clearly defined leadership roles prevent gaps falling between individuals and ensure that nuclear customers can identify the right contacts for each aspect of business performance. They also underpin effective governance and succession planning.

We are looking to see how the organisation supports leadership development, structured programs, and succession planning.

0 – None
No leadership development or succession planning.
2 – Informal
Leadership development exists but lacks formal succession planning.
7 – Formal
Leadership development programs well structured with some succession planning.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive leadership development and succession planning fully embedded.
Key Evidence: ILM/NEBOSH/IOSH training records, PDPs for all leaders, succession planning matrix, skills gap analysis, coaching/mentoring records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Companies do not sustain excellence without investing in the leaders who deliver it. In nuclear, where the technical and cultural demands on leadership are exceptionally high, organisations that do not develop their leaders will find that capability erodes over time. Succession planning is particularly important – a company whose nuclear readiness depends entirely on one individual is a fragile supply chain partner. Leadership development also signals to the Granting Panel that the company has a sustainable future.

Category: 2. Design & Project Management

The organisation has a proactive approach to design/specification and project management. NOTE: If design is not in scope of the ISO 9001, the first 4 questions may score 0 and scoring will be adjusted accordingly.

How capable is the organisation in developing and specifying product or service design? Not all organisations have in-house design – this is acknowledged.

0 – None
No in-house design or specification capabilities.
2 – Informal
Basic design capability exists but lacks formal methods or consistency.
7 – Formal
The organisation has defined and generally applied design capability.
10 – Best Practice
Robust, well-documented design capability exists across relevant functions.
Key Evidence: CAD/CAE systems, engineering team structure, qualification records of design engineers, examples of design outputs.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
In nuclear, every component, system, and service must be designed to meet exacting standards. Companies without in-house design capability must still understand the specifications they are working to and be able to communicate intelligently with customers and designers. For those that do design, the capability must be demonstrably robust – nuclear clients will not accept poorly controlled design processes on safety-related items.

How effectively are design and specification systems established and used to manage inputs, outputs, and changes?

0 – None
No formal systems exist for managing design and specifications.
2 – Informal
Some systems in place but used inconsistently.
7 – Formal
Design systems are well-defined and generally followed.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive systems govern all design and specification activities.
Key Evidence: Drawing register, revision control system (PDM/PLM), ECR/ECN process, evidence of version control in practice.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Design systems are what prevent unauthorised changes, version confusion, and the introduction of non-compliant designs into production. In nuclear, a drawing issued at the wrong revision or a specification that has been superseded can result in non-conforming product reaching a safety-critical application. Robust design systems are a basic expectation of any nuclear supply chain participant.

How are design risks assessed using FMEA or equivalent risk assessment methods?

0 – None
No formal design risk assessment is conducted.
2 – Informal
Informal or occasional risk assessments are performed.
7 – Formal
Formal FMEA or equivalent processes are in place and regularly applied.
10 – Best Practice
FMEA fully embedded with proactive review and follow-up.
Key Evidence: Completed FMEA templates (DFMEA/PFMEA), cross-functional FMEA reviews, link between FMEA outputs and design changes.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) is one of the most important risk management tools available to a design engineer. It forces systematic thinking about what could go wrong, what the consequences would be, and what controls can prevent it. Nuclear clients and quality standards (including ISO 19443) expect FMEA to be embedded in design and process planning. Companies that only do informal risk assessments are exposing themselves and their customers to unidentified failure modes.

Does the organisation actively consider manufacturability during design, involving production teams at the design stage?

0 – None
No DFM consideration in the design process.
2 – Informal
Some informal DFM consideration, but no structured approach.
7 – Formal
DFM is part of the design process and applied to most new designs.
10 – Best Practice
DFM fully embedded with systematic cross-functional involvement at every design stage.
Key Evidence: DFM checklists, cross-functional design review records, examples of design changes resulting from DFM analysis.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
A design that is elegant but cannot be manufactured reliably is a quality risk. DFM ensures that production teams are involved in design decisions before they become expensive problems on the shopfloor. In nuclear, where process control and consistency are paramount, designs that are difficult to manufacture will generate non-conformances, rework, and potential safety implications. DFM is the bridge between engineering intent and operational reality.

How is design and specification change controlled to prevent unauthorised modification?

0 – None
No formal change control for design or specifications.
2 – Informal
Some change control exists but applied inconsistently.
7 – Formal
Formal change control processes in place and followed in most cases.
10 – Best Practice
Robust change control fully embedded with audit trails and clear approval authorities.
Key Evidence: Change control procedure, approval signature records, design change history/logs, controlled drawing register.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Unauthorised design changes are one of the leading causes of quality non-conformances in manufacturing. In nuclear, a change to a drawing or specification that bypasses the change control system can introduce non-compliant product into a safety-critical application. Robust change control – with documented approval, version history, and controlled distribution – is a fundamental expectation of nuclear quality management, explicitly required by ISO 19443.

How well does the organisation manage projects from the tender/bid stage through to delivery?

0 – None
No formal project management processes from tender onwards.
2 – Informal
Some PM practices exist but applied informally or inconsistently.
7 – Formal
Project management systematically applied from tender to delivery.
10 – Best Practice
PM fully embedded from tender, with consistent application and measurable outcomes.
Key Evidence: Tender review records, project initiation documents, evidence of PM methodology, resource planning at bid stage, project register.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Projects that are not formally managed from tender tend to run over time, over budget, and under-deliver on quality. In nuclear, where projects are typically high-value, long-duration, and involve complex customer requirements, informal project management is a commercial and reputational risk. A structured PM approach from tender ensures that customer requirements are understood, resourced, and tracked throughout delivery.

Are project scope, deliverables, objectives, and success criteria clearly defined at the outset of every project?

0 – None
Projects lack defined scope, objectives, or success criteria.
2 – Informal
Some projects have defined objectives but this is inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Project scope and objectives routinely defined and agreed with customers.
10 – Best Practice
Project definition fully embedded, customer sign-off and clear success metrics for every project.
Key Evidence: Project charters, scope documents, signed customer requirement records, acceptance criteria documentation.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Projects without clear scope and agreed success criteria are a recipe for customer disputes and delivery failures. In nuclear, customer expectations around technical performance, quality, delivery, and documentation are exceptionally high. Clear project definition at the outset – agreed and signed off with the customer – protects both parties and ensures everyone is aligned on what success looks like.

How are project plans, quality plans, and cost management integrated into the project management process?

0 – None
No integrated project planning, quality, or cost control.
2 – Informal
Some planning and cost control, but quality management absent or informal.
7 – Formal
Integrated project plans with quality and cost management for most projects.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated planning, quality, and cost control systems embedded across all projects.
Key Evidence: Gantt charts/project plans, quality plans, cost tracking reports, earned value reports, milestone review records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Cost overruns, missed quality milestones, and schedule slippage are all symptoms of poor integrated project control. Nuclear customers expect their suppliers to manage projects with the same rigour that they apply to their own operations. Integrated project plans – covering schedule, quality, and cost – demonstrate that the company is a reliable partner who can deliver what it promises.

How well are project risks, controls, and information security managed throughout the project lifecycle?

0 – None
No formal risk or information security management.
2 – Informal
Some risk assessments and security measures applied but inconsistently.
7 – Formal
Risks and controls actively managed; information security considered.
10 – Best Practice
Risks, controls, and information security fully embedded in project management.
Key Evidence: Project risk registers, RAID logs, information security policy, access control records, project control meeting minutes.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Project risk management is what prevents surprises. In nuclear, where surprises can have safety, regulatory, and reputational consequences far beyond the immediate project, systematic risk identification and mitigation is not optional. Information security is increasingly important too – nuclear projects involve sensitive commercial and technical information that must be protected throughout the supply chain.

How effectively does the organisation manage project closure and capture and share lessons learned?

0 – None
Projects closed informally, no formal review or lessons learned.
2 – Informal
Some projects have reviews but they are inconsistent or superficial.
7 – Formal
Project closure and reviews routinely conducted, capturing lessons learned.
10 – Best Practice
Project closure and reviews systematic, with lessons shared organisation-wide.
Key Evidence: Close-out reports, lessons learned register with recent entries, evidence of lessons applied to future projects.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Organisations that do not learn from completed projects are condemned to repeat the same mistakes. Lessons learned are how a company gets better at delivering complex projects over time. In nuclear, where continuous improvement is a cultural expectation, the absence of formal project reviews is a red flag. The Granting Panel will want to see that improvement is not just reactive to failures, but proactive and systematic.

Category: 3. People Excellence

Employees are seen as providing a competitive advantage. They have total involvement, are fully aware of the organisation's vision and goals, and their development is central to the strategic aims.

How well are employees aware of the organisation's mission, vision, values, and key goals at all levels?

0 – None
Employees unaware of the organisation's mission, vision, or goals.
2 – Informal
Some employees are aware but understanding is inconsistent across levels.
7 – Formal
Most employees understand the mission and goals and how their roles connect.
10 – Best Practice
Organisation-wide awareness of mission, vision, and goals embedded in culture.
Key Evidence: Employee survey results, induction records referencing MVV, toolbox talks with MVV content, MVV visible on shopfloor.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
An employee who does not understand what their organisation is trying to achieve cannot contribute to it effectively. In nuclear supply chain, this matters enormously – safety culture, quality standards, and continuous improvement all depend on people who are aligned to the organisation's purpose and values. A company where operators cannot articulate the MVV is a company where culture is thin and easily broken under pressure.

How effectively are individual employee objectives aligned with the organisation's strategy? Objectives should be SMART and regularly reviewed.

0 – None
Employees have no clear individual objectives or link to company goals.
2 – Informal
Some employees have objectives but alignment is patchy.
7 – Formal
Individual objectives routinely set and mostly aligned to strategy.
10 – Best Practice
Individual objectives fully aligned with the organisation's strategic plan.
Key Evidence: Sample appraisal forms (redacted), PDPs with SMART objectives, KPIs linked to strategic priorities, objectives review evidence.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
SMART objectives linked to strategy are how organisations turn strategic intent into individual accountability. In nuclear, where precise execution matters – every task, every time – employees who know what is expected of them and why perform consistently better than those who are simply told to 'do a good job'. Objectives also provide the basis for meaningful performance conversations and development planning.

How effectively does the organisation engage employees in its culture, initiatives, and improvements beyond their core tasks?

0 – None
No formal efforts to engage employees beyond their core tasks.
2 – Informal
Some engagement initiatives exist but sporadic or limited.
7 – Formal
Employees regularly engaged through initiatives and invited to contribute ideas.
10 – Best Practice
Employee engagement fully embedded with active participation in shaping improvements.
Key Evidence: CSIP/Kaizen participation records, suggestion scheme logs, CI project involvement, recognition scheme records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Engaged employees are safer, more productive, and more likely to raise concerns early. In nuclear, where near-miss reporting and a questioning attitude are cultural requirements, employee engagement is not a soft HR concept – it is a safety enabler. Companies where employees are disengaged tend to have weaker safety cultures, higher error rates, and lower near-miss reporting rates. The Granting Panel looks for evidence that employees are genuine contributors to improvement.

How effectively does the organisation monitor and support employee morale?

0 – None
No formal effort to assess or address employee morale.
2 – Informal
Some informal checks on morale but no consistent approach.
7 – Formal
Regular surveys or discussions monitor morale with some actions taken.
10 – Best Practice
Morale actively monitored and wellbeing programs embedded in culture.
Key Evidence: Employee survey results and trends, staff forum minutes, actions taken in response to surveys, staff turnover/retention data.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Low morale is a leading indicator of operational risk. Disengaged, unhappy employees make more errors, follow procedures less carefully, and are less likely to speak up when something is wrong. In nuclear, the consequences of such behaviours can be severe. Companies that actively monitor and respond to employee morale demonstrate a commitment to the people foundation that safety culture is built upon.

How well does the organisation support employee learning and development?

0 – None
No formal training or development opportunities provided.
2 – Informal
Some training offered but no structured development approach.
7 – Formal
Development plans and training available for most employees.
10 – Best Practice
A robust learning and development program embedded in operations.
Key Evidence: Training plan and course completion records, individual PDPs, appraisal records, qualification certificates, mentoring programme documentation.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Development is what creates and sustains competence. In nuclear, where technical and safety-critical skills must be current and verifiable, the absence of a structured development programme is a significant gap. Companies that invest in employee development retain talent, build capability, and signal to nuclear clients that they take their human capital seriously. Development is also closely linked to SQEP – the nuclear standard for competence.

How complete and accurate are the organisation's HR records? GDPR-compliant redacted records are acceptable.

0 – None
HR records incomplete, disorganised, or missing key details.
2 – Informal
Some HR records maintained but inconsistently updated.
7 – Formal
HR records well maintained and cover most key data points.
10 – Best Practice
HR records comprehensive, accurate, and regularly reviewed.
Key Evidence: Redacted HR records showing training history, promotions, succession plans, job descriptions with competency profiles.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
HR records are the documentary evidence that a company's people processes are real. In nuclear, where competence verification is a regulatory expectation, incomplete or poorly maintained HR records are a quality and compliance risk. If you cannot demonstrate that someone was trained, assessed, and qualified for their role, the training effectively did not happen for audit purposes. GDPR-compliant redacted records are perfectly acceptable – the point is having a verifiable system.

How effectively does the organisation ensure employees are Suitably Qualified and Experienced Personnel (SQEP) for their roles? Critical nuclear sector requirement.

0 – None
No process to verify qualifications or assess competence.
2 – Informal
Basic qualifications checked but no formal SQEP framework.
7 – Formal
SQEP requirements defined and most roles covered.
10 – Best Practice
A mature SQEP system in place with regular assessments and updates.
Key Evidence: Skills matrices (current vs required), SQEP records for all safety-relevant roles, gap analysis, structured competence assessments, CPD records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
SQEP (Suitably Qualified and Experienced Persons) is one of the most important concepts in nuclear supply chain. Nuclear operators, quality inspectors, welders, and engineers working on safety-related work must be able to demonstrate that they are qualified for what they are doing. A company without a SQEP framework cannot provide the assurance that tier-1 customers and regulators require. This is consistently one of the most common granting blockers – it must be addressed early in the F4N journey.

How does the organisation encourage employees to contribute ideas and suggestions for improvement?

0 – None
No formal process or encouragement for employee suggestions.
2 – Informal
Informal idea sharing exists but unstructured and inconsistent.
7 – Formal
A suggestion process exists and ideas are acted on occasionally.
10 – Best Practice
A robust idea management system embedded, with regular feedback and action.
Key Evidence: Suggestion scheme log with dates, implemented idea examples with measurable outcomes, recognition records, team meeting minutes showing ideas actioned.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
An ideas and suggestions scheme signals that a company values the intelligence of its workforce. In nuclear, where frontline operators often have the best insight into quality risks, process inefficiencies, and safety concerns, capturing and acting on employee ideas is not just a nice-to-have – it is a competitive and safety advantage. Companies where management makes all improvement decisions without employee input tend to have slower, less effective improvement programmes.

How effectively does the organisation plan and allocate human resources to meet its strategic objectives?

0 – None
No formal resource planning; work is reactive.
2 – Informal
Some resource planning exists but informal and inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Resources planned and allocated for most key activities.
10 – Best Practice
Resource planning fully integrated and regularly optimised.
Key Evidence: Workforce planning documentation aligned to strategic growth, recruitment plans, cross-training records, succession plan for critical roles.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Resource planning is what ensures a company can actually deliver its strategic ambitions. Winning nuclear contracts requires not just capability but capacity. Companies that grow reactively – hiring only when crises hit – struggle with quality and delivery when demand peaks. Proactive resource planning, linked to the strategic plan, demonstrates to nuclear customers that the company has thought through its capacity to deliver.

How well does the organisation promote health, welfare, and wellbeing? Goes beyond legal compliance.

0 – None
No formal health or wellbeing initiatives in place.
2 – Informal
Some programs exist but they are informal or occasional.
7 – Formal
Wellbeing programs established and accessed by many employees.
10 – Best Practice
Health, welfare, and wellbeing integral to organisational culture.
Key Evidence: Occupational health surveillance records, EAP communications, wellbeing initiatives (mental health, fitness, stress), health risk assessments.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
The health and wellbeing of employees is directly connected to operational performance. Fatigue, stress, and poor physical health increase error rates – a particular concern in safety-critical environments. Companies that invest in occupational health and wellbeing demonstrate a genuine duty of care that nuclear customers recognise and value. It is also a leading indicator of overall management quality: companies that look after their people tend to look after their products and processes too.

Category: 4. Process Excellence

The organisation sees the need for continuously improving their business operations. They have a formal strategy for process improvement across the organisation.

How clearly does the organisation define its product and service strategy aligned to its overall strategic direction?

0 – None
No defined strategy; decisions made reactively.
2 – Informal
Some strategies exist but not consistently applied.
7 – Formal
Product and service strategies in place and reviewed periodically.
10 – Best Practice
A robust, data-driven product and service strategy embedded across the organisation.
Key Evidence: CSIP strategy document, SLT-approved process improvement plan, investment plan for process upgrades, key efficiency targets.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
A company without a clear process improvement strategy is reacting to problems rather than preventing them. In nuclear supply chain, customers expect suppliers to be on a continuous improvement trajectory – always getting better on quality, delivery, and cost. The Products and Services Strategy element establishes whether the company has formalised this commitment and linked it to its overall strategic direction. It is the foundation of the entire Process Excellence category.

How effectively does the organisation manage value delivery and minimise waste? Lean thinking should be embedded.

0 – None
No focus on value delivery or waste reduction.
2 – Informal
Some efforts to reduce waste but inconsistent application.
7 – Formal
Value and waste reduction practices embedded in most processes.
10 – Best Practice
A culture of continuous value enhancement and waste elimination fully embedded.
Key Evidence: Value Stream Maps (VSM), TIMWOODS waste analysis, SMED records, CI project logs with productivity/cost saving metrics, Kaizen event records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Lean thinking – eliminating waste to improve flow and value – is the most powerful tool available to a manufacturer seeking to improve competitiveness. In nuclear, where customers expect high quality, reliable delivery, and competitive cost, waste in any form is a threat to supply chain viability. Value Stream Mapping (VSM) and TIMWOODS analysis are the tools that make waste visible. Companies without active Lean programmes are typically less competitive, less reliable, and generate more quality problems than those with embedded waste reduction cultures.

How does the organisation measure and monitor performance to drive improvement? KPIs must be visible and acted upon.

0 – None
No performance measurement system in place.
2 – Informal
Some metrics tracked but data incomplete or inconsistently used.
7 – Formal
Performance regularly measured and data used to support improvements.
10 – Best Practice
Performance measurement fully integrated and drives improvement across the organisation.
Key Evidence: KPI dashboards (shopfloor visual boards), OTIF/yield/downtime data, monthly reports, examples of KPI-triggered CI projects.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
You cannot improve what you do not measure. In nuclear supply chain, performance data – OTIF, first-pass yield, defect rates, downtime – is the language of accountability. Companies that make decisions based on gut feel rather than data are unpredictable. Nuclear customers expect real-time, accurate performance data, typically displayed on visual management boards that everyone in the organisation can read. KPIs that are only reviewed in monthly boardroom meetings are not driving operational improvement.

How well does the organisation train teams in process improvement and root cause analysis? Training must be applied in practice.

0 – None
No formal training; problem-solving is ad hoc.
2 – Informal
Limited or informal training, not consistent across teams.
7 – Formal
Teams regularly trained in structured problem-solving and root cause analysis.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive ongoing training ensures all staff skilled in process improvement and RCA.
Key Evidence: Training records for 5 Whys, 8D, PDCA, Fishbone, Six Sigma; real RCA examples applied; CI project logs.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Structured problem solving is the difference between fixing problems permanently and repeatedly addressing the same issues. In nuclear, where the same quality failure repeated twice signals a systemic management failure, root cause analysis (5 Whys, 8D, PDCA) is an expectation, not an option. Companies that train their staff in these tools but never apply them have wasted their money. Companies that genuinely embed structured problem solving get steadily better – which is precisely what nuclear customers require.

To what extent does the organisation apply 5S principles across all areas including offices?

0 – None
No use of 5S; work areas cluttered and disorganised.
2 – Informal
Some 5S elements used but inconsistently.
7 – Formal
5S practices widely used and teams take ownership of their areas.
10 – Best Practice
5S deeply embedded in culture; continuous audits sustain excellence.
Key Evidence: 5S implementation plans, 5S audit reports with scores and follow-up actions, visual management boards, before/after photos.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
5S is often misunderstood as a tidying exercise. It is not. It is a discipline that creates the stable, visible, controlled environment in which quality work can be done consistently. In nuclear, where traceability, controlled processes, and zero-tolerance for non-conformance are the standard, a disorganised workplace is a quality and safety risk. A well-implemented 5S programme demonstrates to visiting nuclear customers that the company can maintain standards – and it makes deviations from normal conditions immediately visible.

How consistently does the organisation use SOPs across key processes? SOPs should be live documents – followed, reviewed, and updated.

0 – None
No SOPs in place; processes vary by individual or team.
2 – Informal
Some SOPs exist but incomplete or inconsistently followed.
7 – Formal
SOPs cover most critical activities and are routinely followed.
10 – Best Practice
SOPs fully embedded; staff trained and CI applied to SOPs.
Key Evidence: SOP library for critical processes, SOP review records, evidence of use on shopfloor, updates following lessons learned.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
SOPs are the mechanism by which best practice is captured, communicated, and sustained. In nuclear, where process consistency is essential to product quality and safety, informally executed processes – 'everyone does it slightly differently' – are a significant risk. SOPs that are written but not followed are worse than useless – they create a false impression of control. Live, followed, regularly-reviewed SOPs are a basic expectation of any ISO 9001-certified supplier and are explicitly required by ISO 19443.

How well does the organisation plan and manage maintenance to ensure equipment availability and reliability?

0 – None
No planned maintenance; equipment repaired only when it fails.
2 – Informal
Some maintenance scheduled but inconsistent across equipment.
7 – Formal
Regular preventive maintenance scheduled and mostly adhered to.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive maintenance programme with preventive and predictive elements optimises performance.
Key Evidence: Maintenance schedules for critical equipment, PM logs and completion rates, machine downtime reports, TPM activity logs.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Equipment failure causes delivery delays, quality escapes, and safety incidents. In nuclear supply chain, where delivery promises must be kept and where field failures can have severe consequences, reactive-only maintenance is entirely unacceptable. Preventive maintenance programmes demonstrate that a company takes its obligations seriously and manages its risks proactively. TPM (Total Productive Maintenance) programmes, where operators take ownership of their equipment's health, are particularly valued as they embed a maintenance mindset across the workforce.

How effective is operational communication between teams and shifts?

0 – None
No formal operational communication processes.
2 – Informal
Some communication processes exist but informal or inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Effective communication processes in place and generally followed.
10 – Best Practice
Operational communication fully embedded with continuous improvement.
Key Evidence: Shift handover records, daily/weekly briefing notes, visual noticeboards, team meeting minutes.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Communication failures between shifts and teams are one of the leading causes of quality non-conformances and safety incidents in manufacturing. In nuclear, where handovers between shifts may involve safety-critical operations or ongoing inspections, poor communication can have serious consequences. Effective operational communication – structured shift handovers, visual management boards, regular team briefings – creates a culture of shared awareness and collective responsibility.

How effectively are in-process controls applied to ensure products and services consistently meet specifications first time?

0 – None
No formal in-process controls.
2 – Informal
Some in-process checks but applied inconsistently.
7 – Formal
In-process controls defined and generally applied.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive process control with SPC and CI driving right-first-time performance.
Key Evidence: Process control plans, in-process inspection records, SPC charts, right-first-time metrics, defect tracking data, calibration records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
In-process controls are what catch problems before they become escapes. Statistical Process Control (SPC), in-process inspection, and right-first-time metrics are the tools that make quality visible in real time. In nuclear, where traceability requirements mean that every non-conformance must be documented and dispositioned, catching problems at source is far preferable to finding them later. Companies with robust process control generate fewer NCRs, less rework, and better delivery performance.

How effectively does the organisation control products and specifications to prevent unauthorised deviations?

0 – None
No formal product or specification control.
2 – Informal
Some controls exist but inconsistently applied.
7 – Formal
Product and specification control processes defined and mostly followed.
10 – Best Practice
Fully embedded product and specification control with audit trails and zero-tolerance for unauthorised deviation.
Key Evidence: Job card/traveller system, controlled drawing register with revision history, specification change control procedure, inspection sign-off records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Specification and product control is the last line of defence before non-conforming product reaches the customer. In nuclear, where a component that does not meet its drawing requirements could end up in a safety-critical application, the consequences of inadequate specification control can be catastrophic. Job cards, travellers, controlled drawings, and sign-off at each inspection stage are the practical tools that make this control real. Companies with weak product and specification control are a liability in any nuclear supply chain.

Category: 5. QHSE

Quality, Health, Safety, and Environmental management. All standards must be formal, documented, and actively lived. UKAS-accredited certification is required for a score of 10.

Does the organisation have a formal QHSE policy and strategy, certified to relevant standards by UKAS accredited bodies?

0 – None
No formal QHSE policy or strategy in place.
2 – Informal
Basic QHSE policy exists but not aligned to strategy or formally certified.
7 – Formal
Formal QHSE policy and management systems in place, most certifications achieved.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive certified QHSE management systems (ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 45001 – all UKAS accredited) fully aligned to strategy.
Key Evidence: ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 45001 certificates (UKAS accredited), QHSE policy documents, QHSE strategic objectives linked to strategy.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
QHSE policy and strategy are the foundation of a company's commitment to quality, safety, and environmental responsibility. In nuclear, these are not just legal requirements – they are the baseline expectations of any tier-1 customer or prime contractor. UKAS-accredited certification to ISO 9001, ISO 14001, and ISO 45001 demonstrates that an independent, internationally recognised body has verified the management system against a rigorous standard. Non-UKAS certifications (e.g. from unaccredited bodies) score lower and should be flagged as requiring upgrade.

How visibly and actively is the SLT committed to QHSE? SLT must lead QHSE, not just approve it.

0 – None
No visible SLT commitment to QHSE.
2 – Informal
Some SLT involvement but inconsistent or reactive.
7 – Formal
Management consistently demonstrates active commitment to QHSE.
10 – Best Practice
Leadership actively champions QHSE, integrating it into decision-making and culture.
Key Evidence: SLT QHSE meeting minutes, evidence of SLT-led site tours and toolbox talks, safety briefing attendance records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Leadership commitment to QHSE is the single most powerful predictor of whether a QHSE management system actually works. Policies written and signed by people who are never seen on the shopfloor become meaningless to the workforce. In nuclear, where safety culture must be visible at every level, SLT engagement in QHSE is not bureaucratic box-ticking – it is the signal that safety and quality genuinely matter. The Granting Panel specifically looks for evidence of this visible commitment.

How effectively does the organisation set, monitor, and achieve QHSE objectives, targets, and goals?

0 – None
No QHSE objectives, targets, or goals established.
2 – Informal
Some objectives exist but poorly defined or inconsistently tracked.
7 – Formal
Clear QHSE objectives and measurable targets set and regularly reviewed.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive objectives and ambitious targets drive continual QHSE improvement and innovation.
Key Evidence: Documented QHSE objectives and KPIs, performance dashboards tracking H&S incidents/quality/OTIF, evidence of periodic review.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
QHSE objectives without measurable targets are aspirations, not commitments. In nuclear supply chain, customers want to see suppliers with meaningful, data-driven QHSE performance management – not just annual targets that are set and forgotten. KPIs for H&S incidents, near misses, audit findings, quality rejection rates, and environmental performance should be visible, reviewed regularly, and linked to improvement actions. This is the engine room of a genuinely improving QHSE management system.

To what extent is a proactive safety culture established? Safety must be owned by all employees.

0 – None
No established safety culture; safety seen as a compliance task only.
2 – Informal
Some safety practices exist but informal and inconsistently applied.
7 – Formal
A positive safety culture promoted with clear management support and employee involvement.
10 – Best Practice
Safety culture fully embedded with continuous improvement and shared accountability.
Key Evidence: Near miss/hazard reporting logs with trend data (high rate = healthy culture), toolbox talk records, employee-led safety activities.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
A proactive safety culture – where employees own safety rather than just comply with rules – is one of the defining expectations of the nuclear sector. This goes far beyond H&S compliance. It means near misses are reported enthusiastically (a high near-miss reporting rate is a positive indicator, not a problem), hazards are flagged by operators without waiting to be asked, and safety improvements are driven from the floor up as well as the top down. Companies that have achieved this level of cultural maturity are genuinely safer and more reliable nuclear supply chain partners.

How effectively does the organisation manage QHSE competence across all employees?

0 – None
No formal approach to identifying or managing QHSE competence.
2 – Informal
Some QHSE training provided but no systematic competence management.
7 – Formal
QHSE competence systematically assessed, developed, and maintained.
10 – Best Practice
QHSE competence fully embedded in organisational processes with continuous improvement.
Key Evidence: QHSE training records for all employees, competence matrix for roles with mandatory certifications (NEBOSH, IOSH), training effectiveness evaluation.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
QHSE competence is not just about having the right certificates on the wall – it is about ensuring every person who performs a task with a QHSE dimension is genuinely capable of doing it safely and correctly. In nuclear, where the consequences of a competence gap can be severe, the absence of a systematic QHSE competence management process is a significant risk. Mandatory certifications (NEBOSH, IOSH, COSHH), training records, and competence assessments demonstrate that the company takes this seriously.

How robust is the organisation's BCP and major incident planning? Plans must be documented, tested, and understood.

0 – None
No formal business continuity or major incident plans.
2 – Informal
Basic plans exist but incomplete, untested, or poorly communicated.
7 – Formal
BCP and incident plans documented, tested, and communicated across the organisation.
10 – Best Practice
BCP and incident management fully integrated into operations with continuous improvement.
Key Evidence: BCP document (ISO 22301 aligned), tabletop exercise reports, employee awareness evidence, plan update records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Nuclear supply chain disruptions – whether from a pandemic, a fire, a cyber attack, or a key person leaving – can have consequences far beyond the immediate incident. Tier-1 nuclear customers and prime contractors need confidence that their supply chain can continue to deliver even under adverse conditions. A robust, tested BCP demonstrates supply chain resilience. Companies without a BCP (or with one that has never been tested) are a single point of failure in the supply chain.

To what extent are quality plans developed, implemented, and aligned with ISO 9001 and ISO 19443?

0 – None
No formal quality plans in place.
2 – Informal
Basic quality plans exist but incomplete or inconsistently applied.
7 – Formal
Comprehensive quality plans developed, reviewed, and effectively implemented.
10 – Best Practice
Quality plans fully embedded, continuously improved, and benchmarked against best practices.
Key Evidence: Quality plan examples, process steps/inspection/testing/change control documents, approval process records, live quality plan on shopfloor.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Quality plans are the product-level expression of the QMS – they specify exactly how quality will be assured for a specific product, project, or contract. In nuclear, where customer technical specifications are exacting and where traceability of quality activities is expected, a quality plan that is not specific to the work being done is inadequate. ISO 19443 explicitly requires nuclear-specific quality planning. The SCC should expect to see live quality plans that are tailored to actual nuclear or safety-related work.

How effectively are HSE risks identified, documented, audited, and controlled, including use of Safe Systems of Work (SSOW)?

0 – None
No formal HSE risk management or documented controls.
2 – Informal
Basic HSE risk processes exist but informal or poorly maintained.
7 – Formal
HSE risks systematically assessed, documented, audited, and controlled with SSOW.
10 – Best Practice
HSE risk management fully embedded, data-driven, and continuously improved.
Key Evidence: Risk assessments and method statements (HSG65/ISO 45001), SSOW documents, internal audit schedule and reports, permit to work system.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
HSE risk management is how a company systematically identifies hazards, controls risks, and demonstrates it has done so to customers and regulators. In nuclear, where the Safe Systems of Work (SSOW) concept – documented, authorised procedures for high-risk tasks – is well established, companies without formal risk management processes are unacceptable supply chain partners. Internal audit programmes demonstrate that the system is working, not just documented.

How effectively are traceability, non-conforming product control, and CFSI managed? Non-negotiable for nuclear.

0 – None
No formal traceability, non-conformance, or CFSI processes.
2 – Informal
Basic processes exist but inconsistently applied or incomplete.
7 – Formal
Traceability, NCR management, and CFSI processes documented, implemented, and regularly reviewed.
10 – Best Practice
Full traceability, robust NCR control, and mature CFSI practices embedded and continuously improved.
Key Evidence: Material/product traceability records, NCR logs, quarantine procedures, CFSI control procedure, CFSI staff training records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Traceability, non-conformance control, and CFSI management are three of the most scrutinised areas in nuclear supply chain due diligence. Traceability enables every component in a nuclear facility to be traced back to its original material certificate and manufacturing records – essential when a safety-related failure investigation begins. Non-conformances must be captured, investigated, and closed, never ignored. CFSI (Counterfeit, Fraudulent and Suspect Items) entering a nuclear facility can have catastrophic consequences – the F4N CFSI requirement is based on hard lessons learned in the nuclear sector globally.

How effectively is CI embedded in the organisation, including lessons learned and corrective actions linked to QHSE?

0 – None
No formal CI or corrective action processes in place.
2 – Informal
Some CI activities occur but informal and reactive.
7 – Formal
CI is systematic with clear processes, assigned responsibilities, and regular reviews.
10 – Best Practice
CI fully embedded, data-driven, integrated with strong leadership commitment.
Key Evidence: CSIP register with QHSE-linked projects, CI strategy document, visual CI boards, audit finding follow-up records, corrective action logs.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Continuous improvement in QHSE means that the management system is not static – it gets better every year. Corrective actions are completed, not just raised. Lessons learned from audits, near misses, and incidents are shared and acted on. The CSIP (Continuous Sustainable Improvement Plan) includes QHSE improvement projects with measurable outcomes. Companies that treat their QHSE management system as a permanent fixture rather than a platform for improvement will find that standards erode over time – and nuclear customers will notice.

Category: 6. Supply Chain & Social Values

This section evaluates how the organisation collaborates with supply chain partners and delivers on its social value commitments. It is not just about who you work with – but how you work with them, and the wider impact you generate.

Are supply chain performance metrics defined, monitored, and used for CI – both internal and external supplier performance?

0 – None
No formal metrics or monitoring of supply chain performance.
2 – Informal
Basic metrics exist but limited in scope or not systematically used.
7 – Formal
Comprehensive metrics defined, tracked, and linked to improvement plans.
10 – Best Practice
Metrics fully embedded, driving supplier collaboration, innovation, and CI.
Key Evidence: Supplier scorecards and KPIs (OTIF, quality, lead time, cost), benchmarking reports, CI plans tied to supplier performance.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
