You cannot manage a supply chain you cannot see. Supply chain performance metrics – supplier OTIF, quality rejection rates, lead time performance, cost trends – make the supply chain visible and manageable. In nuclear, where supply chain failures can cascade into project delays with significant safety and commercial consequences, reactive supply chain management (only responding to problems when they occur) is unacceptable. Metrics drive accountability, early intervention, and continuous improvement.

How strong are relationships with suppliers? Is the relationship purely transactional, or genuinely strategic?

0 – None
No formal supplier relationship management or communication processes.
2 – Informal
Basic relationships exist but reactive and transactional.
7 – Formal
Strong relationships exist with regular communication, reviews, and joint improvement.
10 – Best Practice
Supplier relationships strategic, collaborative, focused on innovation and resilience.
Key Evidence: Supplier meeting agendas and minutes, regular review evidence, signed SLAs, communication logs demonstrating collaboration.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Purely transactional supplier relationships are fragile. They optimise for unit price at the expense of everything else – and in nuclear, where quality, reliability, and technical capability matter far more than price alone, transactional procurement is a strategic risk. Strategic supplier relationships – built on mutual understanding, joint improvement, and shared goals – create a resilient supply chain that performs consistently under pressure. Nuclear prime contractors will ask suppliers about their own supply chain management approach.

Are cost analysis practices supporting procurement decisions? Total Cost of Ownership thinking – not just unit price.

0 – None
No formal cost analysis conducted in procurement activities.
2 – Informal
Basic cost analysis done but lacks consistency or depth.
7 – Formal
Comprehensive cost analysis integrated into procurement processes.
10 – Best Practice
Cost analysis fully embedded, covering TCO, lifecycle, and CI with suppliers.
Key Evidence: Total cost analysis records, cost vs value reports, sensitivity analysis for alternative suppliers, procurement decision rationale.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) thinking is the difference between professional procurement and purchasing by price list. In nuclear, where the cost of a non-conformance, a delivery delay, or a quality escape is orders of magnitude greater than the cost saving from a cheaper supplier, TCO analysis is essential. Organisations that cannot distinguish between unit cost, total cost, and best value are making procurement decisions that expose them to preventable risks.

How effectively are supply chain risks identified, assessed, and managed? Continuity for safety-critical nuclear items is paramount.

0 – None
No formal supply chain risk management processes.
2 – Informal
Some risk identification and mitigation but not systematic or documented.
7 – Formal
Systematic risk management in place with documented assessments and mitigation plans.
10 – Best Practice
Risk management fully embedded, proactive, collaborative, using predictive tools.
Key Evidence: Approved supplier list with risk classification, supplier risk assessments, mitigation plans, dual-sourcing evidence for critical items.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Supply chain risk management is about ensuring that a company's supply chain cannot be disrupted in ways that threaten its ability to deliver to nuclear customers. Single-source suppliers for safety-critical items, suppliers with poor financial health, suppliers in geopolitically unstable regions – these are all risks that need to be identified, assessed, and mitigated. Nuclear prime contractors conduct supply chain risk assessments of their own suppliers and expect similar rigour further down the chain.

How advanced is digital transformation within the supply chain?

0 – None
No digital tools or systems used in supply chain management.
2 – Informal
Some digital tools used but processes remain largely manual.
7 – Formal
Digital tools integrated across supply chain processes, improving efficiency and data visibility.
10 – Best Practice
Digital transformation fully embedded, using predictive analytics, automation, and CI.
Key Evidence: ERP/MES system evidence, supplier portals, process automation evidence, analytics tools, IoT/digital twin examples.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Digital transformation in the supply chain – ERP systems, supplier portals, demand forecasting, analytics – is what enables a company to move from reactive to proactive supply chain management. In nuclear, where lead times for specialist materials and components can be very long, data-driven demand management is a commercial and operational necessity. Companies that still manage their supply chains primarily on spreadsheets and phone calls are structurally disadvantaged against those using modern digital tools.

How effectively does the organisation engage with and support its local community through social responsibility?

0 – None
No formal community engagement or social responsibility programs.
2 – Informal
Community engagement occurs ad-hoc with limited leadership involvement.
7 – Formal
Community engagement regularly carried out with leadership involvement.
10 – Best Practice
Community engagement a core part of strategy, driven by leadership, delivering measurable social value.
Key Evidence: Records of community projects/sponsorships, CSR initiatives, STEM ambassador activity, volunteer logs, impact assessment reports.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Community engagement reflects the character of an organisation and its social responsibility. In nuclear, which is a public-interest sector with a particular responsibility to host communities, suppliers who invest in their local communities – through STEM education, apprenticeships, volunteering, and charitable activities – align with the values of the sector's major clients. It also demonstrates an organisation that sees itself as part of a wider society, not just a commercial entity.

How well does the organisation ensure ethical sourcing, including prevention of child/forced labour?

0 – None
No formal ethical sourcing policies in place.
2 – Informal
Ethical sourcing practices exist but not fully formalised or monitored.
7 – Formal
Ethical sourcing well-established with regular monitoring and transparent supplier relationships.
10 – Best Practice
Ethical sourcing fully integrated into strategy with robust monitoring, reporting, and CI.
Key Evidence: Supplier Code of Conduct, Modern Slavery Act statement, supplier ethical audits, due diligence records, supply chain mapping.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Ethical sourcing – including Modern Slavery Act compliance, supplier due diligence, and fair labour practices throughout the supply chain – is a legal and reputational requirement for any company aspiring to supply into the nuclear sector. Nuclear prime contractors have sophisticated ethical sourcing programmes and expect their supply chains to match those expectations. A company that cannot demonstrate basic ethical sourcing discipline is a reputational risk to every customer it supplies.

How well does the organisation integrate environmental sustainability into its operations?

0 – None
No formal environmental sustainability strategy or practices.
2 – Informal
Some practices in place but not formally structured or integrated.
7 – Formal
Environmental sustainability practices well-established with measurable targets and regular reporting.
10 – Best Practice
Environmental sustainability fully embedded with a track record of measurable improvements and CI.
Key Evidence: ISO 14001 certificate or roadmap, environmental policy, energy/water/waste management records, environmental KPIs.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Environmental sustainability is increasingly important to nuclear sector customers, the UK Government, and the public. Nuclear energy is central to the UK's Net Zero strategy, and the sector expects its supply chain to take environmental responsibility seriously. ISO 14001 certification, measurable environmental KPIs, and a credible sustainability improvement programme are the visible signals of that commitment. Companies without any environmental management structure are increasingly difficult to justify as long-term supply chain partners.

How effectively does the organisation promote diversity and inclusion and a culture of respect?

0 – None
No formal diversity and inclusion initiatives.
2 – Informal
D&I initiatives exist but not fully embedded in culture.
7 – Formal
Well-established D&I practices supported by leadership and regularly monitored.
10 – Best Practice
D&I deeply embedded in culture, driving innovation and ensuring a fair and respectful workplace.
Key Evidence: D&I policy, recruitment/retention/promotion data by diversity metrics, unconscious bias training records, employee engagement surveys.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Diversity and inclusion are not just about fairness – they are about business performance. Diverse teams make better decisions, attract broader talent pools, and are more innovative. In nuclear, where the talent pipeline is a well-known challenge, companies with strong D&I practices are better positioned to recruit and retain the skills they need. Nuclear prime contractors increasingly require their suppliers to demonstrate D&I commitments as a condition of supply.

To what extent does the organisation comply with national and international labour standards?

0 – None
Does not comply with labour standards or has no documented policies.
2 – Informal
Some labour standards in place but insufficient evidence of systematic monitoring.
7 – Formal
Labour standards well-established and monitored regularly, with leadership commitment.
10 – Best Practice
Labour standards fully integrated, with continuous improvement in fair treatment and worker rights.
Key Evidence: Labour law compliance records, employment contracts ensuring fair wages, supplier labour audits, Modern Slavery Act/living wage policies.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Labour standards compliance – fair wages, safe working conditions, prohibition of child or forced labour – is the ethical floor of supply chain management. Modern Slavery Act obligations apply to any company with a turnover above £36 million, but the expectation of responsible labour practices extends throughout the supply chain regardless of size. Nuclear sector customers conduct supply chain audits that include labour standards, and companies that cannot demonstrate compliance are not acceptable supply chain partners.
05

Modules 10–11: Nuclear Sector Specific (NSS) Assessment – All Questions in Full

The Nuclear Sector Specific assessment is what distinguishes F4N from every other supplier development programme. These questions test whether a company genuinely understands and can operate within the nuclear sector's demanding environment. The NSS assessment is introduced approximately 3–4 months before the expected granting date – once the company is approaching the Triple 85 threshold on the Business Excellence side. Each question includes 'Why This Matters' context explaining the nuclear-specific significance of the topic.

NSS Section: Nuclear Industry Fundamentals

Understanding nuclear industry fundamentals is the cornerstone of operating safely and compliantly. This section evaluates whether the organisation grasps the foundational principles of nuclear operations. It is not just about knowing the rules – it is about embedding a culture that respects and acts on them.

Does the organisation understand and apply the fundamental principles of nuclear safety – specifically defence in depth, ALARP, and the Safety Case concept?

0 – None
We do not understand or apply these principles.
2 – Informal
Some understanding, but limited application of regulatory requirements.
7 – Formal
Clear understanding of regulatory framework, regularly implemented.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated understanding and adherence to regulatory framework.
Key Evidence: Staff training on ALARP, defence in depth and safety case; toolbox talks referencing nuclear safety principles; integration into risk assessments.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Defence in depth, ALARP, and the Safety Case are the three foundational concepts of nuclear safety that every person working in or supplying to the nuclear sector must understand. Defence in depth means never relying on a single safety barrier – every layer of protection matters, including the quality of components and services supplied. ALARP (As Low As Reasonably Practicable) sets the standard for how risks must be managed. The Safety Case is the documented argument for why a nuclear facility is safe – and every component, process, and service in the supply chain must be able to support it. Companies that cannot articulate these concepts cannot credibly operate in the nuclear sector.

Does the organisation understand the regulatory framework governing nuclear operations, including the role of ONR and relevant legislation?

0 – None
No awareness of regulatory requirements.
2 – Informal
Some understanding, but limited application.
7 – Formal
Clear understanding of regulatory framework, regularly implemented.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated understanding and adherence to regulatory framework.
Key Evidence: ONR awareness training records, compliance records with relevant legislation, understanding of nuclear licensing regime.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
The regulatory framework for nuclear in the UK is unique in its rigour. The Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) operates as the independent nuclear regulator with powers that go significantly beyond those of most industrial regulators. Understanding how ONR operates, what it expects, and how it relates to the companies that supply into nuclear facilities is essential context for any supply chain participant. Importantly, understanding the regulatory framework applies not just to direct licensees – it cascades through every tier of the supply chain.

Is the organisation aware of the key risks specific to the nuclear industry – radiological, operational, and environmental risks?

0 – None
No awareness or identification of nuclear-specific risks.
2 – Informal
Some recognition of risks, but lack of a structured approach.
7 – Formal
Solid recognition and management of most key nuclear risks.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive understanding and management of nuclear risks, with continuous monitoring.
Key Evidence: Nuclear risk awareness training records, risk assessments referencing nuclear-specific hazards, evidence of how risk awareness influences working practices.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Nuclear risks are qualitatively different from most industrial risks. Radiological contamination, criticality accidents, and waste management challenges are hazards that do not exist in most manufacturing environments. Companies entering the nuclear supply chain must understand these risks – not to be alarmed by them, but to ensure their own processes, materials, and behaviours do not inadvertently contribute to them. A company that has never considered radiological risk, for example, may unknowingly introduce contaminated materials into a controlled area.

Does the organisation have a strategy for engaging with stakeholders about nuclear safety and operations?

0 – None
No stakeholder engagement or communication strategy.
2 – Informal
Some engagement but limited in scope and effectiveness.
7 – Formal
Regular and structured engagement with key stakeholders on safety matters.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive, transparent, and proactive stakeholder engagement strategy in place.
Key Evidence: Stakeholder mapping, nuclear-specific communications plan, records of engagement with nuclear clients on safety matters.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
The nuclear sector operates in the public eye in a way that few other industries do. Public confidence in nuclear safety is hard-won and easily damaged. Stakeholder engagement – with local communities, national audiences, regulators, and political stakeholders – is part of the operating context for every nuclear facility. Suppliers who understand this context are more aligned with the culture and expectations of nuclear customers than those who see it as purely a technical business.

Is there a comprehensive understanding of nuclear safety culture within the organisation? This is distinct from general H&S.

0 – None
No awareness of nuclear safety culture principles.
2 – Informal
Some understanding of safety culture but application is inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Clear understanding and application of nuclear safety culture principles in most areas.
10 – Best Practice
Nuclear safety culture deeply integrated into all aspects of the organisation.
Key Evidence: Nuclear safety culture training records, cultural behaviours aligned with nuclear safety principles, use of nuclear industry resources.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Nuclear safety culture is a distinct concept that goes beyond compliance with health and safety regulations. It encompasses the attitudes, values, and behaviours of every person in the organisation – particularly around questioning, challenging, reporting, and learning. In the nuclear sector, safety culture is a formal assessment criterion and a regulatory expectation. The IAEA, ONR, and every major nuclear operator have published extensive guidance on what strong nuclear safety culture looks like and requires.

Does the organisation understand the key components of the nuclear sector – new build, decommissioning, defence, research – and the regulatory landscape?

0 – None
No understanding of nuclear sector or regulatory landscape.
2 – Informal
Some awareness of nuclear sector but limited understanding of regulations.
7 – Formal
Solid understanding of nuclear sector and regulations, with gaps in practical application.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive understanding of the nuclear sector and regulatory landscape.
Key Evidence: Evidence of staff at nuclear industry events/training, awareness of key programmes (HPC, SZC, SMRs), ONR regulatory guidance awareness.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
The nuclear sector is not monolithic. New build, decommissioning, defence nuclear, research, and SMRs each have different technical requirements, regulatory frameworks, commercial structures, and timelines. A company that understands this landscape can target its development efforts intelligently and have credible conversations with potential customers. A company that sees 'nuclear' as a single undifferentiated market is not yet ready to win work in it.

How well does the organisation understand core nuclear safety principles such as Defence in Depth, ALARP, the Safety Case, and the Graded Approach?

0 – None
No awareness of core nuclear safety principles.
2 – Informal
Some awareness but limited practical understanding.
7 – Formal
Strong understanding of safety principles but occasional gaps.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive understanding and application of safety principles.
Key Evidence: Formal training certificates, work instructions incorporating safety principles, examples of principles applied to actual work activities.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Defence in depth, ALARP, the Safety Case, and the Graded Approach are not abstract concepts – they have direct implications for how suppliers design products, manage quality, and interact with customers. The Graded Approach, in particular, is important: it means that controls are proportionate to the safety significance of the item or activity. A company that applies the same level of control to all activities regardless of safety significance is both inefficient and potentially non-compliant. Understanding the Graded Approach enables suppliers to direct their resources where they matter most.

Does the organisation understand the unique risks, public expectations, and societal responsibilities of the nuclear industry?

0 – None
No awareness of nuclear-specific risks or public concerns.
2 – Informal
Some awareness but limited appreciation of impact.
7 – Formal
Good understanding and consideration of nuclear-specific risks and expectations.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive integration of nuclear risks and societal responsibilities.
Key Evidence: Engagement with wider nuclear sector responsibilities (environmental, social, reputational), understanding of public perception.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
The nuclear sector carries a unique responsibility to the public and to future generations. The management of radioactive waste, the decommissioning of legacy facilities, and the long-term stewardship of nuclear materials are obligations that extend over timescales far beyond normal commercial horizons. Companies that understand and respect these responsibilities are more aligned with the values of nuclear customers than those who see nuclear work purely as a revenue opportunity.

NSS Section: Nuclear Safety Culture

A strong safety culture is non-negotiable in nuclear operations. This section explores the organisation's awareness, understanding, and application of the principles that underpin nuclear safety culture. It measures how well people and processes prioritise safety, even when no one is watching.

Does the organisation understand and actively apply the five principles of a strong nuclear safety culture?

0 – None
No awareness of safety culture principles.
2 – Informal
Some awareness but lacking practical implementation.
7 – Formal
Strong understanding of safety culture principles but gaps in organisational application.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive integration of safety culture principles throughout the organisation.
Key Evidence: Safety culture training records, documented principles displayed/communicated, evidence of cultural assessment, nuclear industry resources in use.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
The five principles of a strong nuclear safety culture – Leadership for Safety, Personal Accountability, Questioning Attitude, Just Culture, and Continuous Learning – are the behavioural framework by which nuclear organisations assess cultural health. They were developed from hard-won lessons in the global nuclear industry, including major accidents where cultural failures played a significant role. Companies new to nuclear will often have strong safety compliance programmes but weaker safety culture – the SCC's role is to help them understand the difference.

Does the organisation exhibit the leadership behaviours needed to support a strong safety culture? Leaders must model what they expect.

0 – None
No visible leadership or behaviours promoting safety culture.
2 – Informal
Some leadership visible but inconsistent behaviours.
7 – Formal
Strong leadership and behaviours but with occasional lapses.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive leadership demonstrating consistent, exemplary safety behaviours.
Key Evidence: Evidence of SLT conducting safety tours, leadership-led safety conversations, examples of leaders stopping work for safety concerns.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Leadership behaviour is the most powerful determinant of safety culture. When senior leaders demonstrate that safety is their highest priority – by their words, their actions, and how they allocate time and resources – the entire organisation tends to follow. When leaders cut corners, dismiss concerns, or are never seen on the shopfloor, the cultural message is clear: safety is secondary. In nuclear, this is not just a management philosophy – it is a regulatory expectation and an audit finding when it is absent.

Does the organisation learn from incidents and near misses? A high near miss reporting rate is a positive indicator.

0 – None
No formal process for learning from incidents and near misses.
2 – Informal
Some learning occurs but processes are informal or inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Learning is occurring but processes for action and improvement could be stronger.
10 – Best Practice
Continuous learning and improvement from incidents and near misses.
Key Evidence: Near miss reporting logs with trend data, incident investigation records with RCA, evidence of lessons learned communications.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Learning from incidents and near misses is how organisations get progressively safer over time. The critical insight in nuclear is that a high near-miss reporting rate is a positive indicator of a healthy safety culture – it means employees feel safe to report, and the organisation is catching problems before they escalate to actual incidents. Organisations with very few near misses are almost always under-reporting, not safer. The SCC must understand this counterintuitive principle and be able to explain it compellingly to client leadership teams.

Does the organisation foster a just culture and encourage transparent reporting of safety concerns without fear of blame?

0 – None
No just culture or reporting mechanisms in place.
2 – Informal
Some awareness but inconsistent reporting and limited just culture practices.
7 – Formal
Strong just culture but occasional reluctance to report safety concerns.
10 – Best Practice
Full integration of a just and reporting culture across the organisation.
Key Evidence: Just culture policy, near miss reporting rate trends, evidence of non-blame responses, staff survey results on confidence to report.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
A just culture – one in which employees feel genuinely safe to report concerns, near misses, and errors without fear of punishment – is the foundation of effective safety reporting. Without it, incident and near-miss reports are suppressed, problems become invisible, and the organisation cannot learn. In nuclear, the just culture principle is well established: the goal is to learn, not to blame. Companies transitioning from a blame culture to a just culture often find that near-miss reporting rates initially rise sharply – which is exactly the right outcome.

Does the organisation actively seek and implement CI in safety culture – proactively, not just after incidents?

0 – None
No focus on CI or ongoing safety culture development.
2 – Informal
Some improvement efforts exist but inconsistent or reactive.
7 – Formal
Continuous improvement initiatives in place but more integration needed.
10 – Best Practice
A culture of CI fully embedded and driving safety performance.
Key Evidence: Safety culture improvement plan, examples of proactive initiatives, measurement of safety culture over time (surveys, audits).
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Safety culture cannot be improved once and then left. It requires ongoing attention, measurement, and deliberate investment. The nuclear sector has learned that culture can drift towards complacency, particularly in the absence of significant incidents – sometimes called 'normalisation of deviance'. Companies must actively and continuously work to maintain and improve their safety culture, treating it with the same management rigour as any other operational metric.

NSS Section: Leadership and Governance for Nuclear

Strong governance and visible leadership are essential for setting the tone on nuclear safety. This section assesses whether the leadership team actively promotes and embodies nuclear safety values.

Does the leadership team clearly communicate and demonstrate nuclear safety expectations – beyond general H&S?

0 – None
No communication or visible commitment to nuclear safety from leadership.
2 – Informal
Some communication but not consistent or visible.
7 – Formal
Clear and consistent communication of nuclear safety expectations by leadership.
10 – Best Practice
Strong, visible leadership demonstrating nuclear safety as a core value.
Key Evidence: Nuclear safety-specific briefings by SLT, toolbox talks on nuclear safety culture led by leadership, nuclear safety objectives for all leaders.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Leadership commitment to nuclear safety must be visible, specific, and consistent – not just present in policy documents. There is a fundamental difference between a leader who signs a nuclear safety policy and one who personally conducts nuclear safety conversations on the shopfloor, challenges unsafe practices, and stops work when nuclear safety is at risk. Nuclear customers and the ONR look for the latter. A company whose leadership team cannot articulate nuclear safety expectations confidently does not have adequate nuclear safety governance.

Does the organisation have clear governance, oversight, and accountabilities for nuclear activities?

0 – None
No formal governance or unclear accountabilities.
2 – Informal
Some governance and oversight but roles and accountabilities need strengthening.
7 – Formal
Clear governance framework with defined roles and effective oversight.
10 – Best Practice
Strong governance and oversight system with accountability fully embedded.
Key Evidence: Nuclear governance structure document, defined roles for nuclear work, escalation procedures for nuclear safety issues.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Governance structures for nuclear activities must eliminate ambiguity about accountability. In a nuclear facility, ambiguity about who is responsible for a safety decision can lead to decisions being deferred, avoided, or made by people who lack the authority or competence to make them correctly. The same principle applies throughout the supply chain. Companies must be able to demonstrate that every nuclear-related decision has a clear owner, a defined escalation path, and appropriate oversight – and that these structures are documented, communicated, and followed.

Does the leadership demonstrate visible, nuclear-specific behaviours to reinforce safety and quality?

0 – None
Leadership rarely visible and shows no nuclear-specific behaviours.
2 – Informal
Some visible leadership but limited nuclear-specific focus.
7 – Formal
Regular visible leadership with clear nuclear-specific behaviours.
10 – Best Practice
Highly visible, respected leadership consistently modelling nuclear behaviours.
Key Evidence: Records of leadership nuclear safety walks, leadership involvement in nuclear-specific training, examples of questioning attitude demonstrated.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Leadership behaviours in nuclear are qualitatively different from standard management visibility. Nuclear-specific behaviours include actively seeking out and rewarding the reporting of concerns, demonstrating a questioning attitude about assumptions and risks, personally stopping or challenging work that appears unsafe, and being demonstrably knowledgeable about nuclear safety requirements. These behaviours cannot be faked for a verification visit – they must be embedded in how leaders operate day-to-day. The SCC should probe for examples of leaders actually exercising these behaviours, not just asserting that they do.

NSS Section: Quality and Compliance (ISO 19443)

Compliance in the nuclear sector is not just about ticking boxes – it is about demonstrating robust quality management, traceability, and continuous improvement aligned to ISO 19443.

Does the organisation understand the requirements of ISO 19443 and how they build upon ISO 9001?

0 – None
No awareness or understanding of ISO 19443 and relevant quality standards.
2 – Informal
Some awareness of ISO 19443 but understanding of application is limited.
7 – Formal
Good understanding of ISO 19443 and standards with some integration into practices.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive understanding and full integration of ISO 19443 and relevant standards.
Key Evidence: ISO 19443 gap assessment, training records on ISO 19443, evidence of requirements mapped to existing processes, ISO 9001 certification (prerequisite).
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
ISO 19443 is the nuclear sector's quality management standard, building on ISO 9001 with additional requirements specific to the nuclear context – including enhanced traceability, CFSI controls, graded approach application, and nuclear safety culture integration. Many companies on the F4N journey will not be certified to ISO 19443, but they need to understand its requirements and demonstrate how their current practices align with them. The F4N to ISO 19443 mapping (see Module 1 of this manual) shows exactly which F4N elements correspond to which ISO 19443 clauses. ISO 19443 certification is increasingly expected by tier-1 nuclear customers as a condition of supply.

Does the organisation have QA and QC processes in place for nuclear projects, appropriate to the safety significance of the work?

0 – None
No QA/QC processes in place for nuclear projects.
2 – Informal
Some QA/QC processes in place but not consistently applied.
7 – Formal
Strong QA/QC processes in place but occasional lapses.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive QA/QC processes integrated throughout all nuclear projects.
Key Evidence: Nuclear quality plans, inspection and test plans (ITPs), hold-point/witness-point records, QA audit schedules, QC inspection records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) are distinct but complementary. QA is about the system – the processes, procedures, and controls that prevent problems. QC is about verification – checking that the product or service meets its requirements. In nuclear, both are required, and both must be documented. Inspection and Test Plans (ITPs), hold points, witness points, and verification records are the practical tools of nuclear QA/QC. Companies that rely on final inspection without in-process controls are too late to prevent quality escapes.

Does the organisation have effective traceability and documentation systems for nuclear activities?

0 – None
No formal traceability or documentation system in place.
2 – Informal
Basic documentation and traceability systems exist but underdeveloped or inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Well-defined documentation and traceability systems in place but some areas for improvement.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive and integrated traceability and documentation systems meeting all regulatory requirements.
Key Evidence: Material traceability records (raw material to finished component), unique component identification, documentation retention policy.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Traceability in nuclear means being able to demonstrate, for every safety-related item, the complete chain from original material through all manufacturing and inspection steps to the final installed configuration. This is not just good practice – it is a regulatory expectation. When a potential safety-related issue is identified in an operating nuclear facility, the investigation starts from traceability records. Companies whose traceability is incomplete or inconsistent become a liability in a safety investigation rather than an asset.

Does the organisation have processes for managing non-conformances and deviations in nuclear operations?

0 – None
No formal process for managing non-conformances and deviations.
2 – Informal
Some processes exist but inconsistent or poorly documented.
7 – Formal
Strong processes in place but some gaps in tracking or follow-up.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive NCR and deviation management system fully integrated across all operations.
Key Evidence: NCR log with trend data, investigation and RCA records, concession/deviation request process, corrective action closure records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Every non-conformance in nuclear must be captured, assessed for safety significance, investigated to root cause, dispositioned appropriately, and formally closed. Deviation requests – where a product does not meet its specification but may be acceptable for use under specific conditions – must be reviewed and approved by competent personnel. Companies that informally resolve non-conformances, or that fail to capture and trend them, are failing to manage one of the most important quality data streams available. NCR trend data tells the story of whether a company's quality management system is working.

Does the organisation have processes for managing CFSI risks? One of the most critical nuclear supply chain requirements.

0 – None
No process for managing CFSI risks in place.
2 – Informal
Basic process for managing CFSI risks but not consistently applied or formalised.
7 – Formal
Strong processes for managing CFSI risks but occasional lapses in awareness or application.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive CFSI risk management fully embedded in all relevant processes.
Key Evidence: CFSI procedure document, training records for buyers and goods-in staff, incoming inspection records for safety-critical items, approved supplier list.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
CFSI (Counterfeit, Fraudulent and Suspect Items) is one of the most serious quality risks in the nuclear supply chain. Counterfeit fasteners, fraudulently certified materials, and suspect components have been found in nuclear facilities globally – including in safety-critical applications. The consequences can include facility shutdown, regulatory enforcement action, and in extreme cases, safety incidents. The F4N CFSI requirement is specifically designed to ensure companies have robust controls to prevent CFSI entering the supply chain – and this is one area where the SCC must not accept a weak or theoretical answer.

NSS Section: Supply Chain Readiness

In the nuclear sector, your supply chain is only as strong as its weakest compliance link. This section investigates how well the organisation understands and implements nuclear-specific procurement and supplier assurance practices.

Does the organisation understand and apply nuclear-specific procurement and supply chain requirements?

0 – None
No awareness or application of nuclear-specific procurement requirements.
2 – Informal
Some awareness but inconsistent application.
7 – Formal
Good understanding and mostly consistent application.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive application of nuclear-specific procurement and supply chain requirements.
Key Evidence: Nuclear procurement procedure, evidence of nuclear requirements applied in procurement decisions, nuclear client purchase order requirements understood.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Nuclear-specific procurement is categorically different from standard commercial purchasing. It involves understanding quality grades, certificate of conformance requirements, SQEP requirements for suppliers, traceability obligations, and flow-down of nuclear requirements. Companies that apply standard commercial procurement practices to nuclear-specific purchases risk introducing non-compliant materials or components into safety-related applications. This is one of the most common gaps found in companies new to nuclear supply chain work.

Does the organisation maintain an approved supplier list with formal qualification and audit processes for nuclear projects?

0 – None
No approved supplier list or qualification processes in place.
2 – Informal
Some suppliers approved and qualified but process informal or incomplete.
7 – Formal
Well-established ASL and qualification process; some improvement opportunities.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated supplier approval, qualification, and audit processes.
Key Evidence: Approved Supplier List (ASL) with qualification criteria, supplier qualification records, audit programme and completed reports, evidence of ongoing re-qualification.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
An Approved Supplier List (ASL) with formal qualification and audit processes is the mechanism by which a company assures itself that its suppliers are capable of meeting nuclear requirements. In nuclear, 'I've been buying from them for years' is not a sufficient basis for supplier approval – formal qualification, including assessment of quality management, SQEP, traceability, and CFSI controls, is expected. Regular re-qualification and surveillance audits ensure that supplier standards are maintained over time.

Does the organisation ensure nuclear requirements are effectively flowed down to subcontractors?

0 – None
No formal process for communicating nuclear requirements to subcontractors.
2 – Informal
Some nuclear requirements communicated but inconsistently or informally.
7 – Formal
Formal process in place to flow down nuclear requirements.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated and consistent flow-down of nuclear requirements to all subcontractors.
Key Evidence: PO terms and conditions including nuclear quality requirements, nuclear requirements in subcontract documentation, subcontractor briefing records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Nuclear requirements do not stop at the first tier of the supply chain. Every subcontractor who contributes to nuclear work must understand and meet the applicable nuclear quality, safety, and traceability requirements. Flow-down failures – where a company receives nuclear requirements from its customer but does not pass them to its own suppliers – are a systematic supply chain vulnerability. Companies must be able to demonstrate that nuclear requirements are explicitly included in subcontract documentation and that subcontractors understand their obligations.

Does the organisation perform regular inspection and surveillance of nuclear suppliers?

0 – None
No inspection or surveillance activities carried out.
2 – Informal
Some activities performed but informal or irregular.
7 – Formal
Regular inspection and surveillance carried out with documented results.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive inspection and surveillance programme fully integrated with quality management.
Key Evidence: Supplier surveillance plan, completed surveillance visit reports, evidence of findings raised and closed.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Inspection and surveillance of suppliers means physically visiting suppliers, witnessing inspections, and reviewing their quality records – not just reviewing paper submissions. In nuclear, where the consequences of supplier failures can cascade into safety incidents or project shutdowns, passive supply chain management is unacceptable. A systematic surveillance programme, with risk-based prioritisation of the most critical suppliers, demonstrates that a company takes its supply chain obligations seriously.

Does the organisation conduct independent verification or use third-party oversight for critical nuclear supply chain activities?

0 – None
No independent verification or third-party oversight used.
2 – Informal
Some independent verification activities performed but informally or occasionally.
7 – Formal
Formal independent verification processes in place for critical activities.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated independent verification programme with regular third-party oversight.
Key Evidence: Independent verification procedure, records of third-party audits on nuclear work, customer hold-point witness records.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Independent verification and third-party oversight provide an additional check on the quality and integrity of nuclear supply chain activities that is valued by both customers and regulators. Hold points and witness points – where customer or third-party inspectors must formally sign off before work proceeds – are standard tools in nuclear quality plans. Companies with mature independent verification programmes provide greater assurance to their customers than those relying entirely on self-certification.

NSS Section: Human Performance

People are the greatest asset – and risk – in any safety-critical industry. This section focuses on competence management: how the organisation trains, assesses, and supports staff in performing their roles safely and reliably.

Does the organisation have a competence management system for safety-critical roles? SQEP is the nuclear standard.

0 – None
No formal competence management system for safety-critical roles.
2 – Informal
Systems exist but not fully aligned with safety-critical work requirements.
7 – Formal
Well-established competence management systems but some areas need improvement.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive and fully integrated competence management for all safety-critical roles.
Key Evidence: SQEP records for all safety-critical roles, competence assessment framework, authorisation records, competence review schedule.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
SQEP (Suitably Qualified and Experienced Persons) is the nuclear sector's formal framework for ensuring that people performing safety-critical tasks are demonstrably competent to do so. It goes beyond general training records – it requires documented evidence that each individual has the specific qualifications, experience, and ongoing training to perform their specific role safely. Companies without a SQEP framework have a fundamental governance gap that nuclear customers will identify immediately. This is consistently one of the most significant barriers to F4N granting.

Does the organisation have clear training, authorisation, and qualification processes for nuclear staff?

0 – None
No formal training, authorisation, or qualification processes for nuclear staff.
2 – Informal
Some processes in place but not fully formalised or consistent.
7 – Formal
Training, authorisation, and qualification systems in place but require more robust tracking.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive and fully integrated training, authorisation, and qualification for all nuclear staff.
Key Evidence: Training matrix for nuclear roles, authorisation records, qualification certificates, training needs analysis, evidence only authorised staff carry out safety-critical tasks.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Training, authorisation, and qualification are the three-stage process by which nuclear organisations ensure that people are ready to perform safety-critical work. Training provides knowledge and skill. Authorisation formally confirms that a person has demonstrated competence and is permitted to perform specific tasks. Qualification provides external certification of technical competence. In nuclear, all three are required – not just training. Companies that allow non-authorised personnel to perform safety-critical tasks are operating outside the standards that nuclear customers and regulators expect.

Does the organisation utilise human performance tools such as pre-job briefings, peer checking, and STAR?

0 – None
No use of human performance tools or error prevention techniques.
2 – Informal
Some tools used but application inconsistent.
7 – Formal
Strong use of tools and techniques but room for further improvement.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated human performance tools and error prevention in all nuclear operations.
Key Evidence: Pre-job briefing records, peer check records, STAR technique training, task observation programme records, examples of error prevention applied.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Human performance tools – pre-job briefings, peer checking, STAR (Stop, Think, Act, Review), task observation – were developed specifically to reduce human error in safety-critical environments. They recognise that even well-trained, conscientious people make mistakes, and that systematic practices can significantly reduce error rates. In nuclear, these tools are not optional extras – they are standard operating practice for safety-critical work. Companies that rely purely on individual skill and attention without error-prevention tools are accepting higher error rates than necessary.

Does the organisation have a fatigue management and workload control system to ensure nuclear workers are fit for duty?

0 – None
No formal fatigue management or workload control system.
2 – Informal
Some practices in place but not fully formalised.
7 – Formal
Strong fatigue management and workload control systems but occasional lapses.
10 – Best Practice
Comprehensive and fully integrated fatigue management and workload control for all nuclear staff.
Key Evidence: Fatigue management policy, working hours records for safety-critical staff, shift rotation schedules, fitness-for-duty checks.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Fatigue is one of the most significant human performance risks in any safety-critical industry. Studies consistently show that fatigued workers make more errors, take more risks, and are less likely to notice and respond to safety concerns. In nuclear, where a single error in a safety-critical task can have severe consequences, fatigue management is a safety critical issue, not just an employment law consideration. Companies must demonstrate that they actively manage working hours, shift patterns, and workload for personnel performing safety-critical tasks.

Does the organisation monitor human performance regularly to identify areas for improvement?

0 – None
No formal performance monitoring system.
2 – Informal
Some monitoring in place but needs further integration.
7 – Formal
Comprehensive performance monitoring in place but room for more frequent reviews.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated performance monitoring with CI loops for all nuclear operations.
Key Evidence: Human performance monitoring records, trend analysis of human error events, performance improvement plans.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Human performance monitoring – tracking error rates, near miss trends, task observation findings, and authorisation compliance – provides the data needed to identify systemic human performance issues before they result in significant incidents. In nuclear, this data-driven approach to human performance management is expected by regulators and customers alike. Companies that monitor human performance only reactively (after incidents) are missing the early warning signals that a proactive monitoring programme would provide.

NSS Section: Security of Information

Protecting sensitive information is vital for safety, compliance, and national security. This section assesses whether the organisation has clear, robust systems for classifying and securing nuclear-related information.

Does the organisation have clear processes to classify and protect nuclear-related information?

0 – None
No classification or protection measures for nuclear-related information.
2 – Informal
Some measures in place but inconsistent or informal.
7 – Formal
Formal and consistent classification and protection system in place.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated classification and protection system with monitoring and audit.
Key Evidence: Information classification policy, evidence of classification applied to nuclear documents, access control records, staff training on information handling.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Nuclear information – design details, security arrangements, operational data, and commercial intelligence – is sensitive in ways that go beyond normal commercial confidentiality. Some nuclear information is classified under national security frameworks. Even unclassified nuclear information can be commercially sensitive and potentially useful to those who wish to disrupt nuclear operations. Companies in the nuclear supply chain must have clear, systematic processes for identifying, classifying, and protecting nuclear-related information.

Does the organisation have adequate cybersecurity controls for working in the nuclear supply chain?

0 – None
No cybersecurity measures specific to nuclear sector.
2 – Informal
Basic cybersecurity measures but not aligned to nuclear risks.
7 – Formal
Cybersecurity aligned with nuclear supply chain risks and regularly reviewed.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated, proactive cybersecurity programme tailored to nuclear sector.
Key Evidence: Cybersecurity policy, nuclear-relevant cyber risk assessment, staff cybersecurity training records, incident response plan.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Cyber attacks on nuclear infrastructure and supply chains are a real and growing threat. The nuclear sector has been specifically targeted by state-sponsored cyber attacks, including attacks on supply chain companies that provide software, control systems, or digital services to nuclear facilities. Companies in the nuclear supply chain must have cybersecurity controls that are specifically calibrated to the nuclear threat environment – not just generic commercial cybersecurity. Customers will assess this as part of supply chain due diligence.

Does the organisation have measures to protect sensitive nuclear documents and intellectual property?

0 – None
No measures to protect sensitive documents or IP.
2 – Informal
Some measures in place but not formalised or consistently applied.
7 – Formal
Formal protection measures for sensitive documents and IP in place.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated document and IP protection programme across all operations.
Key Evidence: Document control with access controls, NDA/confidentiality agreements, IP protection policy, physical security measures.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Sensitive nuclear documents – technical specifications, quality records, security plans, and intellectual property – must be protected from unauthorised access, unintended disclosure, and loss. Document control systems with access controls, non-disclosure agreements, and physical security measures for hard copies are the practical tools of document protection. In nuclear, the loss of controlled documents is an incident that must be reported and investigated – not just an administrative inconvenience.

Does the organisation ensure appropriate security vetting and clearance for nuclear contract personnel?

0 – None
No vetting or clearance processes in place.
2 – Informal
Some vetting conducted but not consistently or formally.
7 – Formal
Formal vetting and clearance system in place for nuclear personnel.
10 – Best Practice
Fully integrated vetting and clearance programme aligned with nuclear sector best practice.
Key Evidence: Security vetting policy, records of vetting/clearance for relevant staff, process for new starters on nuclear contracts.
Why This Matters for Nuclear Supply Chain Readiness
Security vetting and clearance for nuclear personnel ranges from basic Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS) checks to full security clearance depending on the nature of the work and the facilities involved. Companies new to nuclear supply chain work are often surprised by the extent and formality of vetting requirements. Having a clear, documented vetting process – and understanding the vetting requirements of specific customers and sites – is a prerequisite for being able to mobilise personnel on nuclear contracts efficiently.
06

Module 12: Conducting the OSV and Writing the Report

The On-Site Verification (OSV) is the pivotal event in the F4N journey. It is the moment when the SCC transitions from desk-based review to physical, evidence-based verification. A well-conducted OSV builds trust, reveals the true picture of the business, and creates the action plan that drives the company towards granting. A poorly conducted one wastes a day, produces a weak report, and fails the company. This module tells you exactly how to do it well.

12.1 OSV Preparation – Before You Arrive

Preparation is what separates an excellent OSV from a mediocre one. An underprepared SCC arrives on site with no independent view, gets led by the company narrative, and misses the gaps that matter. An over-prepared SCC arrives with a clear hypothesis about where the gaps are likely to be, specific questions ready for each category, and a plan for the day.

Step-by-Step Pre-OSV Checklist

  • Review the full self-assessment at least 48 hours before the visit. For every question where the company has scored 7 or 10, note your view of whether that score is plausible given what you know about the company. Flag every score you intend to probe.
  • Note the company's size, sector, main products, and key customers. Look at their website, LinkedIn, and any public quality certifications. Do their certifications match what they have claimed? Are they UKAS accredited?
  • Check whether the company has any prior F4N history – were they in a previous programme? What did they score then? Has the picture changed?
  • Draft your session-by-session questions. For each of the six BE categories, prepare at least three open questions based on what you have seen in the self-assessment. Do not arrive empty-handed.
  • Confirm the agenda with the company at least one week in advance. Be explicit that you need SLT present for the Strategy session at 09:30 – without directors, you cannot assess Strategy & Leadership properly.
  • Send the pre-OSV checklist and request it is completed and returned to you at least one week before the visit. Review it when it arrives. If it reveals significant gaps in evidence preparation, contact the company before the visit.
  • Plan your route and allow plenty of travel time. Arriving flustered or late undermines your authority for the day.
Pre-OSV Checklist – Documents to Request in Advance
Mission, Vision and Values statement – any format Strategic plan or equivalent (last 12 months) Organisation chart – current version Current ISO certificates (check they are UKAS accredited and in date) Most recent internal audit report Training plan / training matrix CSIP / improvement project register Near miss / incident log (last 12 months) Current KPI dashboard or management report Any nuclear-related work they have won or are tendering for

12.2 The Day of the OSV – How to Run Each Session

Every session in the OSV agenda has a different purpose and a different primary audience. The SCC must adapt their approach accordingly – more formal and governance-focused for Strategy, more observational and hands-on for the facility tour, more detailed and technical for QHSE and Process Excellence.

09:00 – Meet and Introductions

This is not a wasted fifteen minutes. Use the time over coffee to establish rapport and reduce the company's anxiety. Explain the purpose of the day clearly: you are there to help them, not catch them out. Set expectations for how the day will run – you will be moving between sessions, looking at documents, walking the site, and speaking to different people. Make clear that you will give initial feedback at 14:45, but that the formal report follows within fourteen working days.

Opening Remarks Template – What to Say at 09:00
'Today is about verification, not interrogation. I've reviewed your self-assessment and I'm here to understand the evidence behind it.' 'I'll be honest with you about my views – if I think a score needs to be adjusted up or down, I'll tell you why, and I'll tell you what you'd need to do to get to the next level.' 'The output of today is your action plan – the roadmap to granting. So the more open you are with me today, the more useful the plan will be.' 'I need your full leadership team for the Strategy session at 09:30. After that, the relevant manager for each area should be available during their session – but doesn't need to sit through the whole day.'

09:30 – Strategy & Leadership

This session is with the directors and senior management team. It is the most governance-heavy part of the day. You are assessing whether the SLT actually leads the business with intent, or whether they are passengers in their own organisation. Key things to do:

  • Ask to see the strategic plan – physically. Not a summary, not a PowerPoint. The actual document. How recent is it? Does it reference nuclear as a growth target? Is there a financial or market rationale?
  • Ask the MD or CEO to walk you through the strategy in their own words. If they cannot, the deployment score is likely too high.
  • Check whether there are cascaded objectives – ask to see one department's objectives and how they link back to the corporate strategy.
  • Look for the CSIP – is it a live document with recent entries, or a one-off spreadsheet from two years ago?
  • Ask about leadership development: 'Tell me about how you develop your leaders. Can I see an example of a development plan for someone in this room?'
  • Observe the SLT's body language and engagement. Are they aligned? Do junior managers defer entirely to the MD? Is there healthy challenge in the room? These are cultural indicators.

10:15 – Facility Tour

The facility tour is one of the most important parts of the OSV because it is the hardest to fake. Do not let a manager guide you past the best bits. Ask to see areas that are not on the promotional route. Things to look for:

  • 5S: Is the floor organised, clearly demarcated, with visual management boards? Or is it cluttered, with unlabelled containers and no visible standards?
  • SOPs: Are they displayed at workstations? Are they clearly dated and current? Ask an operator: 'How do you know what to do if something changes on this process?' Their answer will tell you whether SOPs are real or decorative.
  • Visual management: Are KPIs visible and current? Do they show real data? Ask someone: 'What does this number mean? What happened when it dropped last month?'
  • Safety: Are safety hazards identified and controlled? Are near-miss boards visible and recently updated? Is there evidence of safety culture – do operators raise concerns naturally?
  • Maintenance: Is equipment in good condition? Are maintenance records accessible? Look for oil leaks, warning lights, worn tooling – these are indicators of planned maintenance maturity.
  • People: Are people engaged and aware of visitors, or do they retreat? Can operators explain what they are doing and why quality matters?

11:00 – Design & Project Management

This session is with the Technical Director or equivalent. If the company does no design, the first four questions score 0 and are adjusted – do not spend disproportionate time on them. For those that do design, focus on:

  • The drawing register: Is it version controlled? Ask to find a specific part number and its drawing. How long does it take? Is it easy to identify the current revision?
  • FMEA: Ask to see a completed FMEA for a current or recent product. Is it a real working document or a theoretical template? Who completed it? Was there cross-functional involvement?
  • Project management: Ask them to walk you through a current project. Show me your plan. What is the current status versus target? What risks are live? Who owns them?
  • Lessons learned: 'Tell me about a project that didn't go to plan. What did you learn, and how did you change your approach as a result?'

11:45 – Process Excellence

This session is with the Operations Director or equivalent. Process Excellence is where many companies have the largest improvement opportunity – and where Lean maturity (or its absence) is most visible. Focus on:

  • VSMs: Has the company mapped their value streams? Show me. Are they current? What waste did the mapping reveal, and what actions followed?
  • KPIs: Ask to see the current KPI dashboard. Not the polished board, the real live data. What was last month's OTIF? What was the worst-performing metric and what action was taken?
  • Problem solving: 'Tell me about a significant quality problem you've had recently. Walk me through how you investigated it and what changed as a result.' Listen for structured RCA (5 Whys, 8D) versus ad-hoc firefighting.
  • 5S audit: Ask to see the last 5S audit report. What scores did each area achieve? What improvement actions were raised? Are they closed?
  • SOPs: For a process you observed on the tour, ask to see the SOP. How current is it? When was it last reviewed? Was the operator trained on it? How do you know?

12:30 – Working Lunch & Reflection

Use this time to consolidate your notes from the morning. Do not spend the lunch break in conversation about the company – you need to reflect independently. Make sure your morning scoring notes are current. Identify any areas where you are uncertain and plan your afternoon questions accordingly. Stay professional but cordial – the relationship with the company matters.

13:00 – People Excellence

This session is with HR, People Director, or a Senior Manager responsible for people. This is one of the most commonly under-evidenced categories. Focus on:

  • SQEP: 'Can you show me your skills matrix? Let's look at two or three roles together – what qualifications are required, and how do you know the people in those roles hold them?' If they cannot show you a SQEP-aligned skills matrix, the score is likely no higher than 2.
  • PDPs: Ask to see two or three Personal Development Plans (names can be redacted). Are they SMART? Are they linked to the strategic plan? When were they last reviewed?
  • Near miss and engagement: Ask for the employee engagement survey results. What did they say? What actions did the company take? If there is no survey, the morale score is likely 2.
  • Training records: For a specific person (e.g. a QA inspector), show me their full training record. What mandatory training have they completed? When is it due for renewal?

13:45 – QHSE

This session is with the Quality Manager, H&S Manager, or both. QHSE is where nuclear supply chain expectations are most demanding and where the gap between 'ISO certified' and 'genuinely excellent' is most stark. Focus on:

  • Certifications: Confirm all ISO certificates are UKAS accredited and in date. A non-UKAS certificate scores lower. Ask to see the most recent external audit report – what did the auditor find?
  • CFSI: 'Walk me through what happens when you receive a delivery of safety-critical materials. Who checks it? What do they check for? What happens if something looks suspect?' If the process only exists on paper, the score is 2.
  • Near miss culture: Ask to see the near-miss log for the last six months. How many were raised? Is the trend improving? 'Walk me through the last near miss that led to a process change.'
  • NCR process: 'Show me your last three NCRs. What were they? Who investigated them? What was the root cause? Are the actions closed?'
  • BCP: Ask to see the Business Continuity Plan. Has it been tested? Who knows where it is? What scenario was most recently exercised?

14:15 – Supply Chain & Social Values

This is the final category session. Focus on:

  • Supplier scorecard: 'Show me your approved supplier list and your supplier performance data. Who are your most critical suppliers? How do you measure and manage their performance?'
  • CFSI in procurement: Probe how CFSI risks are managed in buying decisions – not just in goods-in inspection. Do buyers know what to look for? Is the approved supplier list restricted to verified sources for safety-critical items?
  • Community: What has the company actually done in their community in the last twelve months? Not aspirations – actions. STEM ambassadors, apprenticeships, volunteering, charitable projects.
  • Modern Slavery Act: If the company is over the £36M turnover threshold, they must have a statement. Where is it? When was it published? Has it been reviewed?

14:45 – Initial Feedback Session

This is your oral summary of the day's findings. It is not the final scores – that is in the report. It is your initial honest view, delivered constructively, that sets up the action planning process. The feedback session is one of the most important skills an SCC develops. Done well, it energises the company. Done badly, it demoralises them or – worse – leads them to believe they have done better than they have.

How to Deliver Effective Initial OSV Feedback
Start with genuine positives – every company has things they do well. Name them specifically with examples: 'Your near miss reporting culture stood out – you had 23 near misses raised last month, which tells me people feel safe to report. That is a real strength.' Introduce the scoring gaps honestly but constructively: 'On SQEP – I think your self-assessment score of 7 is a little ahead of where you are. I couldn't see a SQEP matrix covering all safety-relevant roles. What I need to see to verify a 7 is...' Never leave a gap without a direction: for every area where you are adjusting the score down, explain exactly what a 7 would look like. Give them something to aim for. Be specific about priorities: identify the two or three areas that will have the biggest impact on the journey to granting. These should become the first priorities in the action plan. Close on momentum: 'Overall, you have a solid foundation. The action plan from this visit will be very actionable. I'll have the full report to you within fourteen working days. I think with focused effort on the key areas, granting is very achievable.' Never promise a granting timeline you cannot guarantee. But do not be vague either – give them a realistic view of where they stand.

12.3 Writing the OSV Report

The OSV report is the most important document you will produce in each engagement. It is the permanent record of your professional assessment. It will be read by the company, reviewed by your NucCol engagement manager, and scrutinised by the Granting Panel. It must be objective, evidence-based, professionally written, and issued within fourteen working days of the visit.

Structure of the OSV Report

A well-structured OSV report covers the following sections in order:

  • Executive Summary – a brief overview of the visit, the company's overall position, the headline findings, and the recommended priority areas for the action plan. This should be no more than one page and should give a reader who reads nothing else a clear picture of where the company is.
  • Overall Score Summary – a table of the verified scores for all 60 BE questions, grouped by category. Include the company's self-assessment score alongside the verified score for each element, so the company can see clearly where gaps exist.
  • Category Commentary – for each of the six BE categories, a narrative commentary covering: what was discussed and observed, what evidence was seen, the verified score for each element with rationale, and specific recommendations for the action plan. This is the heart of the report.
  • NSS Assessment Summary – if the NSS has been introduced, include verified NSS scores and commentary.
  • Action Plan Recommendations – a prioritised list of recommended actions, grouped by category, each with a suggested target score to achieve and indicative evidence requirements.
  • Photographs – include photographs taken during the facility tour where these support the narrative. 5S boards, KPI displays, visual management, facility condition – these add credibility and provide a baseline for comparison at pre-granting.

Writing the Category Commentary – What Good Looks Like

For each of the six categories, your commentary should follow this pattern: state what the category is assessing, describe what you saw and discussed (with specific examples), state the score you are awarding with a clear rationale that references specific evidence, and state what the company needs to do to improve to the next scoring level. Here is an example:

Example Category Commentary – Strategy & Leadership: Mission, Vision, and Values
VERIFIED SCORE: 7/10 (Self-assessment: 10/10) During the Strategy session with the MD and Operations Director, the company's MVV statement was reviewed. The values ('Integrity, Quality, People') are displayed throughout the facility on posters and are included in the employee induction pack. The Operations Director was able to articulate the values clearly. However, when asked about the MVV during the facility tour, two of the three operators spoken to could not recall the values without prompting. The MVV has not been updated since 2021 and does not specifically reference the company's ambition to enter the nuclear sector – a significant omission given the purpose of this programme. Score rationale: The MVV is well-defined and displayed (supporting a 7), but is not yet fully embedded at shopfloor level and does not reflect the current strategic direction. A score of 10 would require: MVV updated to reference nuclear ambition; consistent employee awareness at all levels evidenced by survey; MVV actively referenced in team briefings and management reviews.

Common Report Writing Mistakes to Avoid

  • Vague statements: 'The company has a reasonable approach to QHSE.' This tells the Granting Panel nothing. Be specific: name the evidence you saw, state what was present and what was absent.
  • Unjustified score changes: If you are moving a score down from the self-assessment, the reason must be clear from the evidence you describe. The company has a right to understand why.
  • Positive bias: Many SCCs are uncomfortable delivering difficult messages in writing. Resist this. A report that scores the company higher than the evidence supports may feel kind – but it stores up problems for the Granting Panel.
  • Report templates filled by rote: Do not copy and paste generic descriptions into your commentary. Every element of every report must reflect what you actually saw at that specific company on that specific day.
  • Missing photographs: Photographs are not optional decoration. They are evidence. A photo of a 5S board, a near-miss log, a skills matrix, or a facility before and after improvement tells the Granting Panel what words cannot.
  • Late reports: Fourteen working days is the deadline. Missing it without prior communication damages the company's confidence in the programme and your credibility as an SCC.

12.4 Supporting the Company Between OSV and Pre-Granting

The OSV is not the end of the SCC's active involvement – it is the beginning of the most intensive phase of the relationship. The period between the OSV and pre-granting (typically 6–18 months) is where most of the real improvement happens. The SCC's role during this period is to keep the company moving, unblock problems, challenge weak action plan entries, and ensure the portal is kept up to date.

Reviewing Action Plan Entries

Each action plan entry on the F4N portal must be reviewed by the SCC when submitted. When reviewing entries, ask:

  • Is this action specific? A good action is: 'Develop and implement a SQEP skills matrix covering all quality-critical roles by 31 October 2026, owned by Quality Manager.' A poor action is: 'Improve SQEP.'
  • Is the target score achievable from this action? If someone is scoring 0 on CFSI and their action is 'Review CFSI procedure', that will not get them to a 7 – they need to implement the procedure, train staff, and demonstrate it in practice.
  • Is the evidence uploaded sufficient? A policy document alone does not close an action. You need to see evidence of implementation – records, photographs, training logs, meeting minutes.
  • Is the deadline realistic? Overly optimistic deadlines that are missed repeatedly demoralise the company and stall progress. Coach companies to set achievable deadlines and hit them.

Dealing with Progress Stalls

Progress stalls are common and have predictable causes. Recognising them early and responding proactively is one of the most important skills an SCC can develop.

Common Stall CauseSCC Response
Internal champion left the companyContact the company immediately. Identify the new internal champion. Provide additional support to get the new person up to speed. Do not wait for the company to re-engage.
SLT disengaged from the programmeEscalate to your NucCol engagement manager early. Request a joint call with the company's MD to re-affirm commitment. F4N cannot succeed without SLT buy-in.
Company overwhelmed by day-to-day pressuresHelp them prioritise. Identify the three actions with the highest impact on granting and focus there. Agree a realistic re-engagement date.
Evidence gathering is the bottleneckProvide specific guidance on what evidence is needed for each stalled action. Offer to review draft evidence before it is uploaded to avoid wasted effort.
Company believes they are ready when they are notBe honest. A direct, evidence-based conversation at this point saves much more painful feedback at pre-granting or the Granting Panel.
Company has genuinely improved but has not documented itCoach the company on documenting their improvements. Improvement that is not documented does not count – not because it hasn't happened, but because the panel cannot see it.

Portal Discipline

The F4N portal is the record of the company's journey. It is what the Granting Panel reviews. It is the SCC's responsibility to ensure companies understand this and use the portal consistently throughout the programme – not just in the final weeks before granting. Key portal disciplines to reinforce with companies:

  • Evidence should be uploaded as actions are completed – not stockpiled for the end.
  • Action plan entries should be updated with progress notes even when not yet complete.
  • Scores should only be updated in the portal once evidence genuinely supports the revised score – not aspirationally.
  • The Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) must be populated thoughtfully – vague or defensive entries will be challenged by the panel.

12.5 Co-Creating the Action Plan - The SCC's Coaching Role

The OSV report triggers the action plan, but the SCC's role in shaping that plan is critical. A well-constructed action plan is the difference between a company that achieves granting in 14 months and one that stalls for three years. While the action plan is the company's document - they own it and must drive it - the SCC's coaching in the early stages shapes its quality fundamentally.

Prioritising the Action Plan - Not Everything is Equal

Companies looking at 30 or more action items can feel overwhelmed. One of the most valuable things an SCC can do is help the company understand which actions matter most. The priority framework below will serve most companies well:

Priority LevelWhat Belongs Here
Immediate - do these firstAny element currently at 0. Any SQEP or CFSI gap. Any QHSE element below the 85% threshold needed for granting. Any NSS element that requires cultural change (cultural change takes time - start early).
High - complete in first 6 monthsStrategy deployment and CSIP - these underpin everything else and take time to embed. People Excellence development plans and SQEP records. ISO certification upgrades where UKAS accreditation is needed for a score of 10.
Medium - complete in months 6 to 12Process Excellence improvements that require capital investment or significant reorganisation. Supply Chain improvements that depend on supplier engagement. Environmental and social values elements.
Lower priority - complete before pre-grantingDesign elements where scores are already at 7 and only incremental improvement is needed. Elements where the company already has evidence and simply needs to upload it.

Sequencing Actions for Maximum Impact
