Some actions are prerequisites for others. Coaching companies to sequence their plan correctly prevents wasted effort. For example: 'Implement a CSIP' must come before 'Link departmental objectives to the CSIP'. 'Complete SQEP skills matrix' must come before 'Close SQEP competency gaps'. Point these dependencies out early so the company does not find themselves blocked mid-programme.

Action Plan Quality - What the SCC Should Challenge
Actions that are too vague: 'Improve safety culture' is not an action. 'Deliver nuclear safety awareness training to all 45 employees by 31 March, covering ALARP, defence in depth, and personal accountability, with signed attendance records uploaded to portal' is an action. Actions with unrealistic timescales: A company targeting ISO 9001 UKAS accreditation in 3 months has not understood the process. Coach them to set timescales that reflect reality. Actions that don't change the score: An action to 'review and update our CFSI procedure' will not move a company from 0 to 7. Moving to 7 requires the procedure to exist, be implemented, staff to be trained, and evidence of it working in practice. The action must reflect all of that. Actions without named owners: Every action must have a named individual responsible for it - not a department or a vague 'management team'. Maintaining low scores without justification: A company that maintains a score of 2 on a granting-critical element without a compelling reason is setting themselves up to fail. Challenge this directly.

12.6 Worked Examples from Real F4N Verification Assessment Reports

The most effective way to learn OSV report writing is to study real reports. The following examples are drawn from actual F4N verification assessment reports and show what strong, professional SCC commentary looks like. For each example, a weaker version is shown first so you can see the contrast clearly. The stronger version is the standard you should aim for.

Example 1: Executive Summary (BE Report – Strong Version)

This is an example of how the Executive Summary should read – specific, balanced, professionally written, and giving the reader a clear picture without having to read the whole report.

Strong Executive Summary – Drawn from a Real F4N BE Report
An on-site Business Excellence verification assessment was undertaken at [Company Name] as part of the Fit For Nuclear (F4N) programme delivered by Nuclear Collaboration Ltd (NucCol). The purpose of the assessment was to review and verify the organisation's self-assessment submission across the six core Business Excellence categories: Strategy & Leadership, Design & Project Management, People Excellence, Process Excellence, QHSE, and Supply Chain & Social Values. The organisation demonstrated a well-established and capable business operating within complex and safety-critical sectors, with clear strengths identified in QHSE, Design & Project Management, operational control, digital specification management, and workforce competence. The organisation benefits from strong leadership engagement, well-established project delivery systems, and a positive approach towards safety, quality, and continuous improvement. Particular strengths were observed within the organisation's QHSE arrangements, with strong leadership involvement, structured management systems, embedded risk management processes, and good workforce competency arrangements evident throughout the assessment. Whilst many positive arrangements were observed throughout the assessment, several opportunities for further improvement were also identified. These primarily relate to greater deployment and communication of business strategy throughout the organisation, improved visual management of operational KPIs, development of more structured problem-solving and root cause analysis capability, and re-establishment of sustained 5S workplace organisation activities. Overall, the organisation demonstrated a capable and well-established business with many of the core business excellence fundamentals already in place. Continued focus on embedding lean manufacturing principles, strengthening strategic deployment, and driving further operational consistency will support the organisation's ongoing development within complex and safety-critical industries such as nuclear.
Weak Executive Summary – What to Avoid
The visit went well and the company is doing a lot of things right. There are some areas that need improvement but overall they are a good company. Strategy could be better and they need to work on 5S. QHSE is good. Recommend they work on the action plan.

Notice the difference: the strong version is specific about what was strong (QHSE, design, digital specification management), specific about what needs work (strategic deployment, 5S, RCA training), and written in a tone that is respectful and constructive. The weak version is vague, unprofessional, and gives the company no useful direction.

Example 2: Strategy & Leadership Category Commentary – Strong Version

Category commentary is where the SCC demonstrates their professional judgement. It should tell the story of what was seen, what was strong, and what needs to change – referencing specific evidence.

Strong Strategy & Leadership Commentary – Drawn from a Real F4N BE Report
The organisation has established a comprehensive set of company values, consisting of Safety, Collaboration, Future Focus, Integrity, Excellence, Dedication, and Sustainability. These values were observed during the site induction process and are also accessible via the company portal. This demonstrates that the organisation has taken steps to formally define the behaviours and cultural standards expected throughout the business. The Mission and Vision are referred to internally as 'Ambition & Purpose', with these accessible through the company portal. Whilst these are established at leadership level, it is recommended that greater emphasis is placed on embedding them into the wider business culture through increased visibility and regular communication. Displaying these statements in prominent operational areas, meeting rooms, welfare areas, and production environments would help reinforce alignment across all levels of the business. The business has a high-level strategic plan in place, supported by SWOT and PESTLE analysis, alongside several overarching business objectives covering key operational and commercial areas. This demonstrates that the organisation has considered both internal and external factors affecting future growth and sustainability. However, whilst the strategy exists at a senior level, there is currently limited evidence of this being fully cascaded throughout the wider organisation in a structured and measurable way. Strategic reviews are undertaken regularly at departmental level on a monthly basis, which provides good operational oversight. However, it is recommended that the wider business strategy is formally reviewed by the Senior Leadership Team at least annually, with outputs documented and linked to improvement actions and investment decisions.
Weak Strategy & Leadership Commentary – What to Avoid
The company has a strategy. It was reviewed at the visit. Some employees know about it but not all. The SLT needs to communicate it better. Score adjusted to 45%.

The strong version names specific evidence (SWOT and PESTLE, company portal, Ambition & Purpose), acknowledges what is positive before addressing gaps, and explains the business case for improving (alignment, accountability, engagement). The weak version is a list of observations with no narrative, no evidence, and no explanation of why the improvements matter.

Example 3: NSS Executive Summary – Strong Version

The NSS (Nuclear Sector Specific) report requires a different tone to the BE report – it is more focused on behaviours, culture, and nuclear-specific gaps. The executive summary should reflect this.

Strong NSS Executive Summary – Drawn from a Real F4N NSS Report
This report reflects the organisation's position within the Nuclear Sector Specific element of the Fit For Nuclear (F4N) programme, following successful completion of the Business Excellence assessment and achievement of F4N status. Having worked with the organisation on the Business Excellence process, there is a clear understanding of its operational capability, leadership approach, and systems maturity. The self-assessment scores submitted for the nuclear sector-specific requirements are considered to be a fair and accurate reflection of the organisation's current level of development in relation to nuclear sector expectations. The organisation demonstrates a strong operational foundation, particularly in QHSE and core process delivery. There is evidence of growing awareness across key areas such as nuclear safety principles, regulatory frameworks, and quality expectations. However, this awareness is not yet fully embedded into formal governance structures, assurance processes, or day-to-day operational behaviours at the level expected within the nuclear industry. Key development areas include the strengthening of nuclear-specific leadership and governance arrangements, alignment of quality management systems to standards such as ISO 19443, and the introduction of more structured approaches to human performance and safety-critical competence. Supply chain readiness represents the most significant gap, with a need to formalise supplier qualification, assurance processes, and the consistent flow-down of nuclear requirements. Overall, the organisation is a capable and well-managed business with a strong foundation from which to build. With focused leadership and a structured development approach, the organisation is well placed to close the identified gaps and progress towards full alignment with nuclear industry expectations.

Example 4: The 'Additional Guidance' Section – What Good Recommendations Look Like

The Additional Guidance section of the report is where the SCC provides written improvement recommendations for every element where improvement is needed. These must be specific, constructive, and written in plain English. They form the basis of the company's action plan. The following examples are drawn from a real F4N report.

ElementStrong Recommendation (from Real F4N Report)
Mission, Vision and ValuesThe organisation should continue to strengthen the deployment and visibility of its Mission, Vision, and Values across all levels of the business to ensure they become fully embedded within the organisational culture and day-to-day behaviours. This could include greater visual management throughout operational areas, integration into Town Hall briefings, departmental objectives, appraisals, and continuous improvement activities. Fully embedding these principles helps align employees to the long-term direction of the business, strengthens organisational culture, improves employee engagement, and supports more consistent decision-making across the organisation.
Strategic ReviewsA more formal and structured strategic review process led by the Senior Leadership Team should be implemented on at least an annual basis, supported by measurable business data, risk analysis, operational performance trends, and future market considerations. Outputs from these reviews should be documented and linked to improvement actions, investment decisions, and strategic objectives. A more robust strategic review process would help ensure the business strategy remains current, responsive to change, and aligned to both operational performance and long-term business goals.
Strategy DeploymentThe organisation should introduce a more structured strategy deployment framework to ensure business objectives are consistently cascaded from Senior Leadership Team level through to departments, teams, and individual employees. The use of visual deployment tools such as X-Matrices, Orbit Charts, or aligned departmental KPI dashboards would help improve visibility, accountability, and understanding of strategic priorities across the business. Strengthening strategy deployment would support improved organisational alignment, clearer ownership of objectives, and greater employee engagement in delivering business goals.
Ideas and SuggestionsThere is an opportunity to introduce a more structured and visible idea management process to ensure suggestions are formally captured, tracked, reviewed, and communicated back to employees. A simple RAG-rated system could be beneficial: Green = idea accepted and progressed; Amber = additional evaluation required; Red = not progressed, with rationale communicated. Implementing a structured feedback loop would strengthen employee engagement further by demonstrating transparency and genuine responsiveness to employee contribution.
What Makes a Good Recommendation
It names the specific action the company should take – not just 'improve this area' but how to improve it. It explains the business benefit – why this improvement matters, what it will deliver for the company. It is constructive and forward-looking – it acknowledges what is already in place before suggesting improvements. It is written in the third person ('The organisation should...') – consistent, professional tone throughout. It gives practical examples where possible – X-Matrices, RAG-rated idea systems, Town Hall briefings – not abstract concepts. It is proportionate – a major gap gets more detailed guidance than a minor one.
07

Module 13: Pre-Granting, the Granting Panel & Maintain and Sustain

Modules 12 covered the OSV and the action planning phase. This module covers the end of the F4N journey to granting and the post-granting Maintain and Sustain programme. For a new consultant, understanding these final stages in detail is essential – they are where the company's entire F4N investment is validated, and where the SCC's professional credibility is most visibly on the line.

13.1 Knowing When a Company is Ready for Pre-Granting

One of the most common mistakes new SCCs make is rushing companies to pre-granting before they are genuinely ready. The Triple 85 criteria are necessary but not sufficient – a company can technically meet the numerical thresholds while still having significant cultural or evidence gaps that the Granting Panel will identify. The SCC's professional judgement is what bridges the gap between the numbers and the reality.

Signs a Company is Genuinely Ready for Pre-Granting
The Triple 85 are met (85% overall, 85% H&S, 85% actions complete) – but these are the floor, not the ceiling. The company can explain every score in their self-assessment from memory – not by looking it up. The nuclear safety culture is visible on the shopfloor, not just in the boardroom. Operators can articulate what nuclear safety culture means to them. SQEP records are complete and current for all safety-relevant roles. CFSI controls are embedded in practice – the goods-in process, the approved supplier list, staff training – not just a procedure document. The action plan has substantive evidence uploaded, not just tick-boxes. The NSS assessment is complete with thoughtful, specific actions – not generic or defensive entries. The Benefits Statement is written, specific and evidence-based, signed by a senior leader, and uploaded to the portal. The F4N Charter is downloaded, signed by the MD or equivalent, and uploaded to the portal. All ISO certificates are UKAS accredited, in date – and the latest ISO 9001 audit report shows all NCs closed with corrective action evidence. The company has momentum and confidence – they are proud of what they have achieved and can tell the story of their improvement journey.
Signs a Company is NOT Ready for Pre-Granting Yet
The scores have been achieved arithmetically but key areas are thin on evidence. SQEP or CFSI gaps are unresolved – these are specific Granting Panel red flags. The NSS assessment has not been started or is populated superficially. The SLT is not engaged – they see F4N as the Quality Manager's project, not their own. The company's narrative about their journey is vague – they cannot articulate what has changed since the OSV. Key actions are marked as complete but the evidence uploaded is insufficient to support the claim. The Benefits Statement has not been written, is too generic, or is not signed by a senior leader. The F4N Charter has not been downloaded, signed, or uploaded. Open NCs from the ISO 9001 audit have not been closed with evidence. When you ask a member of staff about a specific improvement, they have no idea what you are referring to.

13.2 Conducting the Pre-Granting Visit

The pre-granting visit is a focused, structured review – not a repeat of the full-day OSV. Its purpose is to verify that the company genuinely meets the granting criteria, not to re-run the assessment from scratch. Allow approximately half a day. Structure the visit as follows:

  • Factory tour (30 mins): Start with a walk of the facility. You are looking for evidence that visible improvements from the action plan are real and sustained. Has the 5S improved since the OSV? Are the visual management boards more current? Is the near-miss board actively used? Take photographs to compare with your OSV photographs.
  • Action plan review (60–90 mins): Work through the action plan line by line with the company's F4N champion and relevant managers. For each completed action, confirm the evidence is uploaded, the evidence genuinely supports the claimed score, and the improvement is real in practice – not just on paper.
  • Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) review (30 mins): Review each NSS section. Challenge any entries that appear vague, defensive, or inconsistent with what you are seeing. Look specifically for: evidence that nuclear safety culture is genuinely understood (not just defined), evidence that CFSI controls are embedded, evidence that leadership is visibly accountable for nuclear safety.
  • ISO 9001 audit review (20 mins): Review the current ISO 9001 certificate – confirm it is UKAS accredited and in date. Then request and review the most recent external ISO 9001 audit report. Read through every finding the external auditor raised. For every Non-Conformance (NC) ask: Has a root cause been identified? Has a corrective action been implemented? Is the action closed with evidence? For every Opportunity for Improvement (OFI) ask: Has the company considered and acted on it? Open NCs with no evidence of closure are a granting blocker – this must be resolved before the panel submission. See Section 13.2a below for full detail.
  • Benefits Statement and F4N Charter check (10 mins): Confirm the company has completed and uploaded their signed Benefits Statement and signed F4N Charter. These are both mandatory pre-granting requirements. If either is missing, set a firm deadline before you leave. See Sections 13.2b and 13.2c below for full detail.
  • Nuclear work discussion (10 mins): Ask about nuclear-specific opportunities. Has the company won any nuclear work? Who are they targeting? This contextualises their F4N status – are they actively pursuing nuclear supply chain opportunities, or is F4N theoretical for them?
  • SCC notes and next steps (15 mins): Make detailed notes throughout the visit. These form the basis of your panel submission. If you have concerns, state them clearly to the company before leaving. Do not raise significant concerns for the first time in your panel submission.

13.2a – The ISO 9001 Audit Report: NCRs and OFIs in Detail

The ISO 9001 external audit report is one of the most valuable documents the SCC reviews at pre-granting – and one that is most frequently overlooked. An external auditor has already done a structured assessment of the company's quality management system. Their findings are an independent view that should inform and corroborate the SCC's own scoring. The SCC must read the report carefully and use it actively.

What the SCC Must Do with the ISO 9001 Audit Report
Request the most recent external audit report at the pre-granting visit – not a summary, the full report. Read every Non-Conformance (NC) raised. NCs are actual failures against the ISO 9001 standard. For each one, establish: What was the root cause? What corrective action was taken? When was it implemented? Is the NC formally closed with the certification body? Has the company uploaded evidence of closure to the F4N portal? Read every Opportunity for Improvement (OFI). OFIs are not mandatory – the standard does not require them to be acted on – but in the context of F4N, the SCC should probe whether the company has considered them and whether any are relevant to their F4N improvement journey. If any NCs are open or closed without credible corrective action evidence, this is a scoring implication for the QHSE category and may be a granting blocker. If the most recent audit is more than 12 months old, probe why. Has the company's ISO surveillance audit been missed? A missed surveillance audit may mean the certificate is technically invalid – check the certificate expiry date carefully.
ISO Audit Finding TypeWhat It Means & SCC Response
Non-Conformance (NC) – MajorA fundamental failure against ISO 9001. The certification body will not issue a certificate (or may suspend an existing one) until a Major NC is closed. If a company has an open Major NC, their ISO 9001 certificate may be at risk. Treat this as a significant granting blocker and escalate.
Non-Conformance (NC) – MinorA specific lapse against ISO 9001. Must be closed within a defined timescale agreed with the certification body. For granting purposes, the SCC must see: the root cause identified, a corrective action implemented, evidence of the fix, and formal closure confirmation from the certification body.
Opportunity for Improvement (OFI)A recommendation from the auditor – not a requirement. The company is not obliged to act on OFIs. However, the SCC should review each OFI and consider whether it is relevant to the F4N action plan. If an OFI relates directly to a BE category where the company is borderline on score, the SCC should encourage the company to address it before granting.
ObservationA lesser finding noted by the auditor – similar to an OFI. Review for relevance to F4N scoring.

For the panel submission, the SCC must be able to state clearly: 'The company's most recent ISO 9001 audit (date) raised [X] minor NCs. All have been closed with corrective action evidence uploaded to the F4N portal. [Y] OFIs were noted. The company has addressed [Z] of these as part of their F4N action plan.' This demonstrates to the Granting Panel that the SCC has done a thorough pre-granting review.

13.2b – The Benefits Statement: What It Is and What the SCC Must Check

The Benefits Statement is a mandatory pre-granting document that must be completed and uploaded to the F4N portal by the company before they can be moved to pre-granting status. It is the company's own account of how the F4N programme has helped them improve – written in their words, on their headed paper, and signed by a senior member of their leadership team.

What a Good Benefits Statement Should Include

Many companies produce thin or generic Benefits Statements that add little value. The SCC should coach companies to produce a statement that is specific, evidence-based, and genuinely reflective of their journey. A strong Benefits Statement typically covers:

  • Specific operational improvements with measurable outcomes – 'Our OTIF improved from 72% to 94% over the programme period', 'We reduced our defect rate by 40%', 'Near miss reporting increased from 3 per month to 22 per month, reflecting a genuine cultural shift.'
  • Strategic improvements – 'We now have a documented five-year strategic plan with nuclear sector as a target growth market, cascaded to departmental objectives for the first time.'
  • People and culture improvements – 'We implemented a SQEP framework covering all 14 safety-relevant roles. All staff have completed nuclear safety awareness training. Employee engagement survey scores improved by 18 points.'
  • Commercial outcomes – 'Since starting F4N we have won [£X] in nuclear contracts / been shortlisted for [programme] / been placed on [tier-1]'s approved supplier list.'
  • The company's view of the programme itself – 'The F4N programme gave us a structured framework to improve our business in ways we would not have done independently. The SCC relationship was invaluable in keeping us focused and on track.'
SCC Checklist: Reviewing the Benefits Statement Before Pre-Granting
Is the statement on company headed paper? – Required. Is it signed by a senior leader (MD, Director, or equivalent)? – Required. Does it include specific, measurable improvements? – It should. Generic statements ('F4N has been really helpful') add little value. Coach the company to be specific. Does it reference the nuclear sector or nuclear ambitions? – It should, given the purpose of the programme. Has it been uploaded to the portal? – Check the portal before the visit. If it is not uploaded, set a deadline during the visit. Would you be proud to present this to the Granting Panel as evidence of the programme's impact? – If not, ask the company to revise it.

If the company has not yet written their Benefits Statement, use the pre-granting visit as an opportunity to coach them on what to include. A well-written Benefits Statement is also a powerful commercial document for the company – it articulates their improvement journey in a way that is compelling to nuclear customers and can be shared in tender responses.

13.2c – The F4N Charter: What It Is and How Companies Complete It

The F4N Charter is a formal document that the company downloads from the portal, reviews, signs, and uploads as a pre-granting requirement. It represents the company's commitment to the F4N standards, values, and ongoing nuclear readiness expectations. Without a signed and uploaded F4N Charter, the company cannot proceed to the Granting Panel.

The F4N Charter Process – Step by Step

  • The company navigates to the pre-granting section of their dashboard on the F4N portal.
  • They click 'Download the BE Charter' to download the F4N Charter document.
  • They review the Charter – the SCC should encourage the company's MD or senior director to read it personally, not just hand it to the quality manager to sign.
  • The Charter is printed and signed by the appropriate senior leader.
  • The signed Charter is scanned or photographed.
  • The company uploads the signed Charter via the 'Upload BE Charter' link on their dashboard.
  • They click Choose File, attach the signed Charter document, and click Save.
What the F4N Charter Commits the Company To
Upholding the standards and values of the F4N programme. Continuing to demonstrate nuclear readiness and business excellence. Maintaining transparency and honest engagement with NucCol and their SCC. Actively participating in the Maintain and Sustain programme post-granting. Representing the F4N brand and logo responsibly in marketing and tendering.

The Charter signature should come from the most senior person in the organisation – ideally the MD or CEO. If a quality manager signs the Charter while the MD has minimal involvement in F4N, this is itself a signal about the depth of SLT commitment to the programme. The SCC should note this if it occurs.

SCC Pre-Granting Document Checklist – Complete Reference
✓ ISO 9001 certificate – UKAS accredited and in date ✓ ISO 9001 latest external audit report – all NCs closed with evidence, OFIs reviewed ✓ ISO 14001 certificate (if applicable) – UKAS accredited and in date ✓ ISO 45001 certificate (if applicable) – UKAS accredited and in date ✓ Benefits Statement – on headed paper, signed by senior leader, uploaded to portal ✓ F4N Charter – downloaded, signed by MD/Director, scanned and uploaded to portal ✓ Sector-specific Impact Statement – submitted on portal by company ✓ CSIP (Continuous Sustainable Improvement Plan) – uploaded to portal ✓ Action plan evidence – all completed actions have supporting evidence uploaded ✓ NSS Assessment – all sections scored, actions completed and approved by SCC ✓ Photographs – facility, 5S, visual management, KPI boards, near-miss boards ✓ H&S documentation – near miss log, incident record, toolbox talk records

When to Delay Pre-Granting

The SCC has both the authority and the professional responsibility to delay pre-granting if the company is not ready. If during the pre-granting visit you identify concerns about evidence quality, SQEP gaps, CFSI practice, or nuclear safety culture maturity, you must address these with the company directly and agree a remediation plan before proceeding. Delaying pre-granting is not a failure – it is the correct professional response to insufficient readiness. It protects the integrity of F4N and ultimately serves the company's long-term interests.

13.3 Building the Granting Panel Submission

The granting panel submission is your formal recommendation that the company is ready to receive F4N Granted status. It is the most consequential document you will produce. It must be thorough, accurate, and honest. The Granting Panel will probe every element of it.

What the Panel Submission Must Include

Submission ElementWhat Is Required
Business Excellence SummaryA written summary of the company's position across all six BE categories – strengths, gaps resolved, and any remaining areas for continued improvement post-granting.
Verified ScoresThe final verified scores for all 60 BE questions, reflecting the evidence seen at OSV and pre-granting. Any scores that have moved since the OSV should be noted with a rationale.
Section CommentaryNarrative commentary for each category covering: what improved, what evidence exists, and the SCC's professional view of the company's readiness in that area.
Action Plan EvidenceConfirmation that 85%+ of the action plan is complete with evidence uploaded to the portal. Outstanding actions must be noted with a completion timeline.
Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS)Completed and populated NSS checklist with scores, actions, and evidence. The SCC should add their own commentary to each NSS section.
PhotographsA selection of photographs from the OSV and pre-granting visit evidencing physical improvements – 5S, visual management, KPI boards, facility improvements, near-miss boards.
ISO Certificates & Audit ReportCopies of all current ISO certificates (9001, 14001, 45001 where applicable) – confirm each is UKAS accredited and in date. The most recent ISO 9001 external audit report must be included, with a clear SCC commentary confirming all NCs are closed with evidence and all OFIs have been reviewed. This demonstrates the SCC has done a thorough pre-granting review, not just accepted the company's word that everything is fine.
H&S DocumentationEvidence of safety culture – near miss log (last 12 months with trend data), incident record, toolbox talk records, safety committee minutes. The near miss rate trend is one of the most reliable cultural indicators – a rising rate (more reports) is positive.
Signed Benefits StatementWritten by the company on headed paper, signed by a senior leader (MD or Director), describing specifically how F4N has improved their business. Must include measurable outcomes. Must be uploaded to the portal. The SCC should review and, if necessary, coach the company to make it specific and evidence-based before accepting it for the panel submission.
Signed F4N CharterDownloaded from the portal, reviewed, printed, signed by the MD or most senior leader, scanned, and uploaded to the portal. Represents the company's formal commitment to F4N standards, values, and ongoing nuclear readiness. The seniority of the signatory matters – it should be the MD or equivalent, not delegated to the quality manager.
SCC RecommendationYour explicit, written recommendation that the company should (or, if concerns remain, should not yet) be awarded F4N Granted status. State your professional view clearly.

What the Granting Panel Assesses

The Granting Panel is not simply checking that the numbers have been reached. It is assessing the quality and credibility of the SCC's submission and making a judgement about whether the company genuinely deserves F4N Granted status. Specifically, the panel considers:

  • Has the company fully addressed business excellence expectations across all six categories?
  • Has a demonstrable shift in culture, leadership, and continuous improvement occurred – not just process documentation?
  • Is nuclear safety culture genuinely embedded, or is it a checklist exercise?
  • Does the evidence support the scores, or is the submission inflated?
  • Is the SCC's commentary credible and specific, or is it generic?

What Could Delay Granting Approval

The panel may delay granting – and will provide clear feedback to the SCC – in any of the following circumstances:

  • Evidence is weak, missing, or not uploaded to the portal
  • Action plan entries are vague, defensive, or lack measurable outcomes (e.g., 'we already do this' type entries)
  • The safety culture is not demonstrably embedded – particularly if the NSS checklist entries are superficial
  • SQEP or CFSI gaps remain unresolved
  • The company has not shown credible traction on nuclear-specific requirements
  • The SCC's own commentary lacks specificity or does not address areas the panel considers important

When granting is delayed, the SCC works with the company to address the panel's feedback and resubmits when the concerns have been resolved. This is not a failure – it is the system working correctly.

What Happens When Granting is Approved

  • The company receives formal F4N Granted status and the F4N Certificate.
  • It is listed on the F4N Nuclear Supplier Directory (subject to the company's permission).
  • It may be promoted to Tier 1 vendors and key stakeholders in the nuclear industry by NucCol.
  • The company can use the F4N branding and logo in marketing and tendering.
  • They move into the Maintain & Sustain annual subscription (£3,000 per year).
  • The SCC transitions their role from improvement coach to ongoing review partner.

13.4 Maintain and Sustain – The Post-Granting Relationship

Granting is not the end of the F4N journey – it is the beginning of the ongoing commitment to nuclear readiness. The Maintain & Sustain (M&S) programme is an annual subscription (£3,000) that retains the company's F4N Granted status, provides continued SCC support, and drives ongoing improvement. Without an active M&S subscription, F4N Granted status cannot be retained after the first year.

The SCC's Role in M&S

Under M&S, the SCC conducts two review visits per year – typically six months apart. These are not full reassessments. They are structured conversations with evidence review, focused on whether the company is continuing to improve and sustain the standards they achieved at granting. The SCC should arrive at each M&S visit having reviewed the company's portal for any updates since the previous review, noting what has changed and what questions arise from those changes.

Running an Effective M&S Review Visit – Step by Step

The M&S review meeting lasts approximately 1.5 to 2 hours. The SCC chairs the meeting. The following structure, drawn from the NucCol Maintain and Sustain Meeting Agenda, should be followed:

Agenda ItemDuration & What the SCC Should Do
1. Welcome & Introductions5 mins. Remind the company of the purpose of the meeting and the M&S programme. Recap what was agreed at the last review. Set a positive, forward-looking tone.
2. M&S Programme Overview10 mins. For first-year companies especially, recap what M&S includes and what is expected: no reassessment, continued portal updates, twice-yearly reviews, evidence of ongoing improvement.
3. Company Progress Update15 mins. Ask about: new projects or contracts won (especially nuclear), new capabilities, changes to organisation or senior personnel, strategic developments. Listen for signals of growth momentum or stagnation.
4. Action Plan Review20 mins. This is the core of the meeting. Work through the outstanding and recently completed actions. Challenge actions that are marked complete without credible evidence. Identify and unblock anything that is stalled. Agree new actions where the company has regressed or new improvement areas have emerged.
5. Continuous Improvement Discussion15 mins. Review CI activity: Kaizen events, improvement projects, KPI trends, Lean activity. Check near miss reporting rates – is the culture sustaining? Review employee engagement initiatives.
6. H&S and Quality Culture Review10 mins. Review H&S performance data – incident rate, near miss rate, audit findings. Check for any changes to certifications. Ask about any quality events or customer complaints since the last review.
7. Strategy and Leadership Reflection10 mins. How is the strategy being communicated and cascaded? Is the SLT still visible and engaged? Has there been any leadership change? How is the company developing its future leaders?
8. Open Discussion & Feedback10 mins. Invite the company to share their reflections on the programme. Share any relevant learnings from other F4N companies (anonymised). Offer NucCol support, events, or resources relevant to their current situation.
9. Next Steps5 mins. Agree specific actions from the meeting with named owners and deadlines. Set the date for the next M&S review. Confirm any portal update commitments.

When M&S Companies Stop Improving

The most common M&S challenge is a company that achieved granting with strong momentum, and then – once the pressure of the granting process is removed – settles into complacency. Standards drift. The portal is not updated. CI activity slows. When this happens, the SCC must be direct. M&S is not just a subscription payment – it is a commitment to ongoing nuclear readiness. If a company is not sustaining the standards that earned them their F4N status, it is the SCC's professional responsibility to say so clearly, document it in the visit record, and agree a recovery plan.

Signs of M&S Drift – and What to Do
Portal not updated since last review → Coach on portal discipline. Agree specific update deadlines before you leave the meeting. Near miss reporting rate has dropped → Probe whether this reflects genuine improvement or under-reporting. Ask to see recent near miss logs. Key certified staff have left and not been replaced with equally qualified people → Flag this as a SQEP gap. Agree an action to address the competence gap. ISO certificate expired or downgraded (e.g. lost UKAS accreditation) → This is a significant QHSE regression. Agree an urgent action plan and escalate to NucCol if unresolved at next review. SLT has changed and new leaders are not engaged with F4N → Arrange a re-engagement conversation directly with the new MD or equivalent. The SCC should not assume the company's commitment automatically transfers to new leadership. Company says 'we're doing fine' but cannot evidence it → A company that is genuinely sustaining excellence can demonstrate it. If they cannot show you, it is not happening. Be honest.

13.5 The SCC's Professional Standards Throughout

Across every stage of the F4N journey – from the first OSV to a tenth year of M&S reviews – the SCC is a professional representative of NucCol and of the F4N programme. The quality and integrity of the programme depends entirely on the quality and integrity of its SCCs. The following professional standards are non-negotiable.

StandardWhat It Means in Practice
ObjectivityEvery score you award must reflect the evidence you have seen – not what the company wants, not what would make the conversation easier, not what you think they deserve for effort. The panel will challenge you on your scores.
ConfidentialityEverything you see, hear, and read at a client company is strictly confidential. Never discuss one company's performance, scores, or commercial situation with another company. Never share client information with third parties without explicit NucCol authorisation.
HonestyIf a company is not ready for pre-granting, tell them clearly – do not delay the conversation because it is uncomfortable. If a score needs to go down, put it down. Long-term, the companies that benefit most from F4N are those whose SCCs were honest with them throughout.
TimelinessOSV reports within 14 working days. M&S visit records within five working days. Action plan feedback within five working days of submission. Responsiveness to company queries within two working days. These are professional commitments, not aspirations.
Nuclear Safety FirstIn any situation where nuclear safety – culture, CFSI, SQEP, quality – is at stake, the SCC must never compromise. A company whose CFSI controls are inadequate does not get a pass because everything else is good. A company whose safety culture assessment is superficial does not get to the panel on the strength of their BE scores alone.
EscalationIf you are uncertain about a situation – a company in distress, a potential ethics concern, a company whose SLT is pressuring you to inflate scores, a safety issue – escalate to your NucCol engagement manager immediately. Do not try to resolve it unilaterally.
Continuous DevelopmentStay current. Attend NucCol briefings and SCC development sessions. Read ONR guidance updates. Follow nuclear industry news. Your credibility with clients depends on being knowledgeable about the sector you are preparing them for.

Module 14: The Nuclear Sector – Context for the SCC

This final module provides the nuclear sector context that every SCC needs to have credible conversations with their clients, understand the standards they are preparing companies for, and demonstrate the specialist knowledge that distinguishes F4N from generic supplier development programmes. A client who believes their SCC understands the nuclear sector will engage more deeply, trust their guidance more readily, and be more motivated to achieve the standards required.

14.1 The UK Nuclear Landscape – What the Work Actually Is

The UK nuclear sector encompasses several distinct segments, each with different technical requirements, regulatory frameworks, commercial structures, and supply chain characteristics. SCCs must understand all of them, because the companies on the F4N programme may be targeting any or all of these markets.

SegmentProgrammes & Key Facts
New BuildHinkley Point C (EDF/CGN) – UK's first new nuclear plant in decades, under construction in Somerset. Sizewell C (EDF/Great British Nuclear) – planned for Suffolk. These are multi-decade, multi-billion pound programmes with extensive UK supply chain requirements. STEP (Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production) – UKAEA fusion programme at West Burton, Nottinghamshire – a long-term R&D investment.
Small Modular Reactors (SMRs)Rolls-Royce SMR – UK's most advanced SMR programme, targeting 470MWe factory-built reactors. GE-Hitachi BWRX-300 – selected for Wylfa, Anglesey. X-energy – compact high-temperature gas-cooled reactor. Westinghouse AP300 – scaled-down version of the AP1000. SMRs represent a major near-term opportunity for UK manufacturers – many components can be manufactured in the UK at scale.
Defence NuclearThe Dreadnought-class nuclear-powered, nuclear-armed submarine programme – the UK's most strategically significant defence project. Delivered by Rolls-Royce (reactor), BAE Systems (boat), and a broad supply chain. The programme will run until the 2060s and represents decades of sustained supply chain demand. Security requirements for defence nuclear are exceptionally high.
DecommissioningNuclear Decommissioning Authority (NDA) – responsible for the UK's 17 nuclear legacy sites. Sellafield Ltd – the UK's largest and most complex decommissioning site, employing approximately 11,000 people and with a programme lasting until the 2120s. Decommissioning requires a very different skill set from new build – specialist dismantling, waste handling, and environmental remediation.
ResearchUKAEA – UK Atomic Energy Authority, responsible for the STEP fusion programme and the Culham Centre for Fusion Energy. National Nuclear Laboratory (NNL) – provides technical and scientific services to the nuclear sector. These organisations are not large employers of manufacturers but are important for innovation and skills development.

14.2 The Nuclear Regulatory Framework – What SCCs Must Know

The UK nuclear sector is one of the most tightly regulated industries in the world. Understanding the regulatory framework is essential context for SCCs – it explains why the NSS assessment questions exist, why safety culture is so important, and why ISO 19443 has the specific requirements it does.

The Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR)

The ONR is the UK's independent nuclear regulator, established under the Energy Act 2013. It regulates nuclear safety, nuclear security, transport of radioactive materials, and safeguards. The ONR operates under a permissioning regime – nuclear site licensees must obtain ONR permission before undertaking certain activities. The ONR can – and does – shut down nuclear operations when it has safety concerns. For the supply chain, the key ONR implications are: the Safety Case must be maintained and supported by the quality of components and services supplied; supplier qualification is a regulatory expectation; and safety culture extends throughout the supply chain, not just within the licensed site.

Key Legislation

  • Nuclear Installations Act 1965 – the primary legislation governing the licensing and regulation of nuclear installations in the UK.
  • Energy Act 2013 – established the ONR as an independent statutory body.
  • Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 – applies to all nuclear workplaces, supplemented by nuclear-specific regulations.
  • Nuclear Industries Security Regulations 2003 – governs physical and cyber security of nuclear material and facilities.
  • Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 – governs exposure to ionising radiation in the workplace.

14.3 Why Nuclear is Different – The Principles Every SCC Must Be Able to Explain

SCCs are frequently asked by company directors: 'Why does nuclear demand all of this? We already have ISO 9001.' The following explanations should be second nature to every SCC.

Defence in Depth

Nuclear safety relies on multiple independent layers of protection. Each layer – physical barriers, engineered systems, operational procedures, human behaviours, and quality of supplied components – is designed to prevent hazards from becoming accidents. The critical principle is that no single layer can be relied upon alone. If your component or service is part of one of those layers, its failure must not be able to cause an accident on its own. This means every link in the supply chain must meet its quality requirements independently – you cannot rely on the next person in the chain to catch your mistakes.

ALARP – As Low As Reasonably Practicable

Nuclear regulation does not require zero risk – it requires that risks are reduced to ALARP. This means demonstrating that proportionate, cost-justified steps have been taken to reduce risks, and that the residual risk is tolerable. For suppliers, ALARP means: identifying risks in your processes, investing in controls that are proportionate to those risks, and being able to demonstrate the rationale for your risk management decisions. A company that manages risk only to minimum legal compliance is not applying ALARP thinking.

The Safety Case

Every nuclear facility operates under a formal safety case – a comprehensive, documented, and argued case that the facility is safe to operate. The safety case specifies the quality requirements for every component, system, and activity that contributes to safety. When a supplier provides a component for a nuclear facility, they are contributing to the safety case – even if they do not know it. A quality failure in a supplied component can invalidate part of the safety case, potentially shutting down the facility until the issue is resolved. This is why nuclear customers are so demanding about quality – the consequences of getting it wrong extend far beyond a warranty claim.

The Graded Approach

Not every item in a nuclear facility is safety-critical. The graded approach means that quality controls, inspections, documentation, and oversight are proportionate to the safety significance of the item. A safety-critical item (e.g., a reactor pressure vessel component) demands much higher levels of quality assurance than a non-safety-related item (e.g., office furniture in the visitors' centre). Understanding the graded approach allows suppliers to direct their resources to the areas where they matter most – and demonstrates to customers that the supplier understands the nuclear environment. The F4N QHSE category's question on quality plans specifically tests whether companies understand how to apply this principle.

14.4 Key Standards – What SCCs Must Know and Why

StandardWhat It Is & Why It Matters to F4N
ISO 9001:2015The foundation quality management system standard. A prerequisite for nuclear supply chain participation – no tier-1 customer will engage with a supplier that does not hold ISO 9001. The SCC should confirm UKAS accreditation (not all certifications are equal). The most recent external audit report is a key document at OSV and pre-granting.
ISO 19443:2018The nuclear-specific QMS standard that builds on ISO 9001 with additional requirements unique to the nuclear sector: enhanced traceability, CFSI controls, graded approach application, nuclear safety culture integration, and specific qualification requirements for suppliers. F4N preparation maps directly to ISO 19443 clauses – companies that complete F4N are substantially closer to ISO 19443 readiness. Increasingly required by tier-1 customers as a condition of supply.
ISO 45001:2018The Occupational Health and Safety Management System standard, replacing OHSAS 18001. UKAS-accredited ISO 45001 certification is the score-10 standard for the QHSE 'Policy and Strategy' element. Companies working towards ISO 45001 score 7; those certified by a UKAS body score 10.
ISO 14001:2015The Environmental Management System standard. Relevant to both the QHSE category and the Supply Chain & Social Values category (environmental sustainability). As with ISO 45001, UKAS-accredited certification is required for a score of 10.
ISO 22301:2019The Business Continuity Management System standard. Relevant to the QHSE element on Business Continuity & Major Incident Planning. Companies with a tested BCP aligned to this standard demonstrate higher maturity.
SQEPSuitably Qualified and Experienced Person – not a formal standard but a well-established concept in UK nuclear, embedded in ONR guidance, the Quality Management Framework, and nuclear procurement requirements. Every person performing safety-relevant work must be demonstrably SQEP – meaning their qualifications and experience are documented, verified, and appropriate for the specific task. The F4N People Excellence 'Skills and Competence' element and the NSS Human Performance section are both rooted in the SQEP concept.
NQA-1 / RCC-M / ASMEInternational nuclear quality assurance standards for components. NQA-1 is the US standard; RCC-M is the French standard (used extensively at HPC/Sizewell); ASME covers pressure vessels and piping. Companies supplying components to these standards will need to achieve these as well as F4N – but F4N provides the business foundation on which these more technical standards are built.

14.5 The F4N to ISO 19443 Mapping

One question SCCs are frequently asked is: 'How does F4N relate to ISO 19443?' The answer is that they complement each other. F4N builds the business maturity and culture; ISO 19443 certifies it. The following mapping, drawn from NucCol's own documentation, shows how F4N categories align with ISO 19443 clauses.

14.6 Common Questions from Client Companies – How to Answer Them

New SCCs benefit from knowing how to respond to the most common questions and objections raised by company directors during the F4N journey. The following table covers the most frequent ones.

Question or ObjectionHow the SCC Should Respond
'We already have ISO 9001 – why do we need F4N?'ISO 9001 is the foundation, but it is sector-agnostic. It tells a nuclear customer you have a quality system – but not that you understand nuclear safety culture, CFSI, SQEP, or the graded approach. F4N is what demonstrates nuclear readiness specifically. Many nuclear tier-1 customers now require F4N or ISO 19443 in addition to ISO 9001.
'This is taking too long – can we shortcut the process?'The programme takes 12–18 months because genuine business improvement takes time. Shortcuts create weak action plans, thin evidence, and panel submissions that get delayed. Companies that rush the process rarely achieve granting on the first submission. The companies that invest the time consistently get more value from the programme – and win more nuclear work as a result.
'We scored ourselves a 7 – why are you giving us a 2?'Walk through the evidence together. A 7 requires a formal, working system with evidence that it is being followed consistently. What I saw was an informal process that depends on one individual's knowledge. I'm not saying your intent isn't there – I'm saying the evidence doesn't yet support a 7. Here's specifically what you'd need to evidence to get there.
'The Managing Director is too busy to be involved in this.'F4N requires SLT commitment. Not just endorsement – active involvement. The Strategy session at the OSV requires the directors. The Granting Panel expects to see evidence of SLT leadership throughout the journey. Without MD-level engagement, F4N will not deliver its full value – and the Granting Panel will see through a submission where the leadership layer is absent. This is a conversation you need to have with the MD directly.
'We've won nuclear work already – do we still need to do all of this?'Winning nuclear work is a great start and it will inform some of your action plan. But F4N is about demonstrating the business-wide readiness that tier-1 customers and Rolls-Royce, EDF, and Sellafield expect from a strategic supply chain partner – not just a one-off order. F4N Granted status is what gets you onto preferred supplier lists and gives you a competitive advantage in procurement decisions.
'Can we get F4N status without completing all the actions?'No – the Triple 85 criteria exist for good reason. A company that has completed only 60% of its action plan has not yet made the improvements that nuclear readiness requires. Granting is not a reward for effort – it is a standard. Our job is to help you reach it.

14.7 Staying Current – Continuing Professional Development for SCCs

The nuclear sector moves quickly. New programmes are announced, standards are updated, regulatory guidance evolves, and the expectations of tier-1 customers change. An SCC who is not continuously learning will find their credibility with clients eroding. The following are the key sources of current knowledge every SCC should be monitoring:

  • NucCol SCC Briefings – attend all NucCol briefing sessions for SCCs. These cover programme updates, scoring guidance changes, and sector developments.
  • ONR News and Publications – the ONR publishes regular news, inspection findings, and guidance updates at onr.org.uk. Follow these to stay current on regulatory expectations.
  • Nuclear Industry Association (NIA) – the NIA represents the nuclear industry and publishes regular updates on sector developments, policy, and supply chain opportunities.
  • World Nuclear News (world-nuclear-news.org) – daily news covering global nuclear sector developments including UK new build, SMRs, and decommissioning progress.
  • ISO Standards Updates – monitor ISO 9001, ISO 19443, ISO 45001, and ISO 14001 for revision notifications. Clients may ask about forthcoming changes.
  • NucCol Events and Webinars – attend NucCol sector roundtables, supply chain events, and webinars. These provide valuable market intelligence and networking opportunities to share with clients.
  • Peer Learning – connect with other SCCs in the NucCol network. Shared learnings from other engagements (appropriately anonymised) are one of the most valuable professional development resources available.

Module 15: Nuclear Awareness – The Industry, the Regulator, and the Standards

This module draws on NucCol's Nuclear Awareness programme content to give SCCs a deeper understanding of the nuclear sector context they need to be credible advisers. A consultant who can speak knowledgeably about the ONR, the regulatory licence conditions, TAG 77 supply chain requirements, and the global nuclear landscape will earn significantly more trust from their client companies than one who cannot. This module is not a comprehensive nuclear physics course – it is the sector knowledge that is directly relevant to the F4N consultant role.

15.1 The Origins and Credibility of F4N

The F4N assessment framework was not created in isolation. It was developed with direct input from major industry standards and regulatory expectations to ensure it reflects exactly what the nuclear market requires. Every SCC should be able to explain this credibility to clients who ask 'why should we trust this programme?'

What F4N is Built On
INPO 14-005 – Traits of a Healthy Nuclear Safety Culture (Institute of Nuclear Power Operations) WANO Principles – International nuclear safety norms (World Association of Nuclear Operators) ONR TAG 77 – Supply chain governance and assurance requirements in the UK ONR TAG 49 – Additional ONR technical assessment guidance applicable to the supply chain NIA and Buyer Guidance – Practical expectations from EDF, Rolls-Royce SMR, NDA, and Sellafield Sellafield Contract Quality Requirements (SLM 4.06) Hinkley Point C Supplier Quality Requirements Manual Nuclear Institute Good Practice Guide to Supply Chain Quality Requirements ASME NQA-1 – American Society of Mechanical Engineers nuclear quality assurance checklist EFQM and ISO 9001/45001/14001 – Embedded business excellence and compliance models

This means F4N carries genuine credibility with tier-1 nuclear customers. When you tell a company that achieving F4N Granted status will be recognised by EDF, Rolls-Royce SMR, Sellafield, and NDA, you are not making a marketing claim – you are describing a programme built on the very standards those organisations apply in their own procurement.

15.2 The Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) – In Depth

What the ONR Is

The ONR independently regulates nuclear safety and security at 37 nuclear licensed sites across the UK. It was set up as a non-statutory agency of the Health and Safety Executive on 1st April 2011, formally launched on 1st April 2014, with its form and function defined in the Energy Act 2013. It operates on a technology-neutral basis and is non-prescriptive in its regulatory approach – unlike some international equivalents such as the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), which is more prescriptive.

The ONR's Mission and Three Key Outcomes

The ONR's mission is 'to provide efficient and effective regulation of the nuclear industry, holding it to account on behalf of the public.' To achieve this, it works towards three key outcomes:

  • All of its stakeholders value the ONR's work
  • A nuclear industry that has a culture of continuous improvement and sustained excellence in operations
  • A nuclear industry that controls its hazards effectively

How the ONR Works – Four Key Activities

ONR ActivityWhat It Involves
PermissioningAssessing licensees' safety cases, on a sample basis according to potential consequences, to ensure hazards have been understood and are properly controlled.
Compliance InspectionsChecking that licensees comply with licence conditions through planned inspections, on a sample basis according to information derived from safety cases and operational intelligence.
EnforcementThe full spectrum of enforcement activities, from provision of advice through to prosecution, in accordance with the Enforcement Policy Statement and the Regulators' Compliance Code.
InfluencingUsing influence to gain improvements in areas that are difficult to regulate directly – particularly safety culture, leadership, and vision.

The 36 Licence Conditions

The ONR regulates through 36 Site Licence Conditions (SLCs) applied to each nuclear licensed site. These range from SLC 1 (interpretation) through to SLC 36 (organisational capability). Each condition places specific obligations on the licensee. Critically for the supply chain, the licensee is responsible for ensuring that its supply chain meets the standards required to support the safety case – which is the direct reason why nuclear procurement requirements are so demanding.

ONR Principles and Guides

ONR Document SetWhat It Covers
Safety Assessment Principles (SAPs)Eleven areas from fundamental principles and leadership/management for safety through to radiation protection, fault analysis, accident management, and decommissioning. The SAPs define what a nuclear facility must demonstrate to be licensed.
Security Assessment Principles (SyAPs)Covering fundamental principles, security delivery principles, key security plan principles, and regulatory assessment of security plans. Relevant to the NSS Security of Information section.
Technical Assessment Guides (TAGs)108 nuclear safety TAGs covering specific technical areas from radiation shielding (NS-TAST-GD-002) through to ageing and degradation management (NS-TAST-GD-109). 43 civil nuclear security TAGs. 2 safeguards TAGs.

TAG 77 – Supply Chain Management Arrangements (Most Relevant to F4N)

ONR Technical Assessment Guide 77 (TAG 77) covers supply chain management arrangements and is the single most important ONR document for understanding the expectations that flow down to nuclear supply chain companies. It maps directly to the F4N Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) themes. TAG 77 covers the following supply chain management elements:

TAG 77 ClauseSupply Chain Requirement – and F4N Connection
5.2.1 Supply Chain StrategyThe licensee must have a coherent strategy for managing its supply chain. F4N: Strategy & Leadership (nuclear strategy deployment)
5.2.2 Intelligent CustomerThe licensee must understand what it is buying and be able to assure it. F4N: Supply Chain & Social Values (supplier qualification, capability assessment)
5.2.3 SpecificationRequirements must be clearly specified and flowed down. F4N: Design & Project Management (specification control, flow-down)
5.2.4 Supply Chain Organisation & Technical CapabilitySuppliers must have the technical capability and organisational structure to deliver. F4N: People Excellence (SQEP), Process Excellence
5.2.5 Supply Chain Management SystemsQuality management systems, quality plans, and records. F4N: QHSE (quality plans, ISO 9001/19443)
5.2.5.1 Quality PlansSpecific quality plans for safety-related work. F4N: QHSE (quality plans element)
5.2.5.2 RecordsTraceability and documentation of safety-related activities. F4N: QHSE (traceability & NCR)
5.2.6 Deviations from Specified RequirementsNon-conformance management and formal deviation/concession process. F4N: QHSE (NCR and CFSI)
5.2.7 Supply Chain Oversight and AssuranceInspection, surveillance, and independent verification. F4N: NSS Supply Chain Readiness
5.2.7.1 OversightOngoing monitoring of supplier performance. F4N: Supply Chain & Social Values (supplier KPIs)
5.2.7.2 AssuranceFormal assurance activities including audits and witness points. F4N: NSS Independent Verification
5.2.8 CFSICounterfeit, Fraudulent and Suspect Items – prevent CFSI from entering safety-critical supply chain. F4N: QHSE and NSS Quality & Compliance
5.2.9 Supply Chain Operational Experience (OPEX)Capture and share operational experience feedback from supply chain. F4N: NSS – continuous learning
SCC Key Point: TAG 77 and the F4N Checklist
The F4N Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) (NSS assessment) was built specifically to align with TAG 77's supply chain requirements. When you explain to a company why the NSS questions exist, you can reference TAG 77 directly – it is the ONR's own expectation that these standards are met throughout the supply chain. A company that scores well on the F4N NSS assessment is demonstrating that it meets the supply chain management expectations that ONR places on nuclear site licensees. This is why the NSS assessment is taken seriously by tier-1 customers – it is not an arbitrary add-on to F4N, it is aligned to the regulatory framework they themselves operate under.

15.3 The WANO Safety Culture Traits – What Every SCC Must Know

The World Association of Nuclear Operators (WANO) defines the internationally recognised traits of a healthy nuclear safety culture. These ten traits are what F4N's Nuclear Safety Culture assessment is measuring – every SCC must be able to explain them confidently to client companies. They originate from INPO 14-005 (Traits of a Healthy Nuclear Safety Culture) and WANO's own principles.

WANO TraitWhat It Means in Practice for a Supplier
Personal Accountability (PA)Everyone is personally responsible for nuclear safety – not just the safety team. Every operator, buyer, engineer, and manager owns safety in their domain. Companies must demonstrate this goes beyond a policy into individual behaviour.
Questioning Attitude (QA)People question assumptions and flag concerns without fear. A healthy nuclear supply chain company has people at every level who will stop and ask 'is this right?' when something seems off. The absence of questions is a warning sign.
Safety Communications (CO)Safety information flows clearly and openly in all directions – from leadership down and from shopfloor up. Companies must demonstrate genuine two-way safety communication, not just top-down briefings.
Leadership Accountability (LA)Leaders visibly demonstrate their commitment to safety through actions, not just words. Gemba walks, safety tours, personally leading toolbox talks, and stopping work for safety concerns are the evidence.
Decision-Making (DM)Safety is explicitly factored into every decision, including commercial and schedule decisions. A company that sacrifices quality to hit a delivery target is failing this trait.
Respectful Work Environment (WE)A workplace where people are treated with respect and feel valued. Intimidation, blame culture, and marginalisation of those who raise concerns are incompatible with nuclear safety culture.
Continuous Learning (CL)The organisation systematically learns from events, near misses, and external lessons. This is not just a nice-to-have – in nuclear, learning from experience is a regulatory expectation (TAG 77, 5.2.9 OPEX).
Problem Identification and Resolution (PI)Problems are identified early, investigated properly, and resolved at their root cause. A company with low near-miss reporting rates is not safer – it is under-reporting.
Environment for Raising Concerns (RC)Employees feel genuinely safe to raise concerns about safety, quality, and compliance without fear of blame or retaliation. This is the just culture principle in practice.
Work Processes (WP)Work is planned, controlled, and executed to approved procedures. Improvisation in safety-related work is not acceptable. Standards are followed because they are understood and valued, not just mandated.
How to Use WANO Traits in F4N Assessments
When assessing the NSS Safety Culture section, use the WANO traits as your mental checklist. Probe for evidence of each trait in discussions and observations. When a company says 'we have a strong safety culture', ask them to demonstrate which specific traits they can evidence. This moves the conversation from assertion to evidence. Near-miss reporting rates are your most reliable leading indicator of safety culture maturity. If a company reports fewer than one near miss per employee per year, probe their reporting culture. Look for examples of people at non-management levels exercising a Questioning Attitude – stopping work, raising concerns, challenging assumptions. If this only happens at management level, the culture is not yet embedded.

15.4 Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) and Market Readiness – What SCCs Should Know

TRL and Market Component Readiness Level (MCRL) frameworks are used extensively in nuclear procurement – particularly in new build, SMR, and decommissioning programmes. SCCs should understand this context because client companies will often ask where they sit in relation to these frameworks, and because some F4N companies will be developing new technologies or capabilities specifically for nuclear.

LevelTRL Definition
TRL 1 – Basic PrinciplesThe basic properties, hypothesis, or structure has been established.
TRL 2 – Invention and ResearchA practical application is invented or investigation of challenge, acquisition of new knowledge, or correction of previous knowledge is undertaken.
TRL 3 – Proof of ConceptDemonstration, in principle, that the invention has the potential to work – preliminary desktop demonstration or trial.
TRL 4 – Bench ScaleThe technology is starting to be developed in a laboratory or research facility.
TRL 5 – Pilot ScaleTesting at small to medium scale to demonstrate specific aspects of the design.
TRL 6 – Large ScaleTesting at or near full scale – design not yet finalised.
TRL 7 – Inactive CommissioningFactory or desk-based testing at near-final design stage. Tested using inactive simulants.
TRL 8 – Active CommissioningActive commissioning with the intended marketplace or on the target platform.
TRL 9 – OperationsThe technology and capability is now operationally used in an active facility or applied commercially.

The Market Readiness Level (MRL or MCRL) framework maps alongside TRL and describes a company's readiness to enter and win work in a specific market – moving from 'understanding market and potential fit' through 'finding a preparation and capability match' to 'qualification, down-selection, and winning/execution'. F4N sits in the readiness zone – it prepares companies for the qualification and down-selection stage where nuclear prime contractors and Tier 1s select their supply chain partners.

15.5 The Nuclear Safety Culture Triangle – Radiological, Industrial, and Environmental Safety

Nuclear safety is not a single concept – it encompasses three distinct but interconnected safety domains. SCCs should understand these and be able to explain them to companies new to the sector.

Safety DomainWhat It Means for the Supply Chain
Radiological SafetyProtection of workers and the public from ionising radiation. Radiological safety requires understanding of shielding, containment, and contamination control. For supply chain companies, this primarily means understanding the radiological environment their products or services will operate in, and ensuring their processes do not introduce contamination or compromise radiological barriers.
Industrial SafetyConventional workplace safety – machinery, working at height, COSHH, electrical safety, manual handling. Nuclear sites apply these standards with exceptional rigour because of the heightened consequence environment. Supply chain companies must have equivalent industrial safety standards (ISO 45001 as the benchmark) to be trusted on nuclear sites.
Environmental SafetyPrevention of radioactive and non-radioactive contamination of the wider environment. Environmental management systems (ISO 14001) and waste management competence are increasingly important supply chain requirements, both for regulatory compliance and for the nuclear sector's net-zero commitments.

15.6 The Global Nuclear Landscape – Context for Market-Facing Conversations

Companies preparing for F4N are often doing so because they want to win nuclear contracts – sometimes in the UK, sometimes internationally. SCCs should have a working knowledge of the global nuclear landscape to have credible conversations about market opportunities.

Region/CountryNuclear Context
United KingdomNew build at HPC and SZC. SMR programme with Rolls-Royce. STEP fusion. Dreadnought defence programme. Extensive decommissioning at NDA sites. ONR regulation. Target market for F4N companies.
FranceWorld's most nuclear-intensive electricity system (~70% nuclear share). EDF operates 56 reactors. RCC-M quality standard. F4N companies supplying HPC/SZC will likely encounter RCC-M requirements.
United StatesLargest nuclear fleet globally. NRC regulation. ASME standards. AP1000 new build at Vogtle. Advanced reactor programme (TerraPower, X-energy, NuScale). NQA-1 quality standard. Export opportunity for UK suppliers.
Eastern EuropeSignificant nuclear expansion – Poland, Czech Republic, Romania, Bulgaria all planning new build. UK government support for UK supply chain engagement in these markets.
CanadaSMR-focused new build programme. Darlington, Bruce, and Pickering fleet. OPG and Bruce Power buyers. Export opportunity for F4N companies with proven UK track record.
Middle EastSaudi Arabia, UAE nuclear programmes. UK government export focus. F4N Granted status increasingly recognised as a quality signal in international nuclear procurement.
