Module 16: Using the F4N Portal – The SCC's Complete Guide

The F4N portal is the operational backbone of the programme. Every company record, self-assessment result, action plan entry, OSV report, pre-granting submission, and granting decision lives on the portal. As an SCC, you will use it at every stage of every engagement. This module tells you exactly how to use the portal for each of your key tasks – from reviewing a self-assessment through to completing a granting recommendation.

16.1 Portal Overview – What the SCC Can See and Do

The portal provides SCCs with a dashboard view of all their assigned companies, their current stage in the programme, and any actions requiring their attention. The SCC's view includes:

  • A list of all companies in their portfolio with current programme stage indicators
  • An 'Actions to Take' queue – all items requiring SCC attention (self-assessment referrals, action plan submissions awaiting review, pre-granting items, visit bookings)
  • Access to each company's full record – assessments, scores, action plans, documents, visit history, staff comments, and timeline
  • Programme-level reports – workflow report, current workload, completed workload, engagement report, process improvement report, and programme impacts report
  • The ability to export portal data
Key SCC Portal Principle
Everything that matters in a company's F4N journey must be recorded on the portal – not in emails, not in personal files, not in notebooks. The portal is the official record of the programme. It is what the Granting Panel reviews. It is what is used if there is ever a dispute about what happened during a company's journey. If it is not on the portal, it did not happen – at least as far as NucCol is concerned. Your first responsibility at every stage is to ensure the portal is up to date before you move to the next activity.

16.2 Reviewing a Self-Assessment

When a company submits their self-assessment, it is referred to the SCC for review. The portal notifies you by email. Here is how to review it:

From the Dashboard

  • Under the 'Actions to Take' menu, click the Type button.
  • Select 'Self Assessment referred'.
  • Find the related company action and click the Review button.
  • Click the 'View self assessment' button to review the responses.
  • To accept: click the Accept button, enter a reason for acceptance in the text box, click Accept.
  • To reject (if the assessment is clearly incomplete or inaccurate): click Reject, enter a reason, click Reject.

From the Menu

  • Click the menu button and select the relevant programme.
  • Click Self Assessment > Referral.
  • Click View self assessment, then Accept or Reject as above.
What to Look For When Reviewing the Self-Assessment
Are all 60 BE questions answered? Has the company skipped any? Are the scores plausible? Note any score of 7 or 10 on areas where the company is unlikely to have strong evidence – these are your OSV probe points. Has more than one person contributed? The self-assessment should not be completed by a single individual. If answers appear one-dimensional, probe this at the OSV. Is there a sector-specific context that makes some answers immediately questionable (e.g., a 10-person company claiming best practice ISO 19443 alignment)? Make your notes before you accept – once accepted, you move to OSV booking.

16.3 Booking a Verification Assessment (OSV)

From the Dashboard

  • Under the 'Actions to Take' menu, click the Type button.
  • Select 'Pending onsite verification visit'.
  • Find the related company action and click the Arrange button.
  • Enter the assessment date.
  • Update the assessor if required (defaults to you as the assigned SCC).
  • Update the company's contact details if required.
  • Click the Arrange button to confirm.

Changing or Cancelling an OSV

  • From the menu, select the programme > Verification > Arranged/In progress.
  • To cancel: click the Cancel button and confirm by clicking OK.
  • To rebook: click the Rebook button, enter the new date, click Rebook OSA to confirm.

16.4a Recording, Completing and Closing a Company Visit on the Portal

Every SCC interaction with a company – OSV, interim review, pre-granting visit, M&S review, telephone call resulting in agreed actions – should be recorded on the portal. This is not bureaucracy; it is your professional audit trail. If a question is ever raised about what happened during an engagement, the portal record is what NucCol and the Granting Panel will refer to.

Recording a Visit – Step by Step

  • From the selected company record, select the Visits tab in the sub-menu.
  • Click the Record visit button.
  • Select the company from the company dropdown menu.
  • Select which assessment the visit relates to from the Assessment dropdown (BE, NSS, M&S).
  • Enter the date of the meeting.
  • Select the reason for the meeting from the dropdown (OSV, pre-granting visit, interim review, M&S review, telephone review, etc.).
  • Update the Visited by section if required (defaults to your name as the assigned SCC).
  • Update the Supported by section if another NucCol team member attended.
  • Click Save.

Completing and Closing a Visit

  • From the company record, select the Visits tab.
  • Locate the visit you wish to complete.
  • Click the Complete/Close visit button.
  • Add any relevant notes about the visit outcomes, key observations, agreed actions, and next steps in the notes field.
  • Click Save to close the visit record.
What to Record in the Visit Notes
A brief summary of what was covered during the visit or call. Any scores you discussed adjusting and the rationale. Specific action plan items reviewed and your assessment of the evidence. Any concerns you raised with the company and their response. Agreed next steps with dates – what the company will do, by when. Any escalation items you flagged to NucCol. If a call rather than a site visit: confirm what was agreed in writing to the company within 24 hours.

Providing Feedback on an Action Plan

Every time a company submits an updated action plan, the SCC receives a notification and is expected to provide feedback within 10 working days. This feedback is one of the most important touchpoints in the engagement – it either drives the company forward or allows them to drift. Poor feedback ('good progress, keep going') is almost as unhelpful as no feedback.

Submitting Action Plan Feedback – Step by Step

  • You will receive an email notification when a company submits their action plan.
  • From your dashboard, under 'Actions to Take', click the Type button and select 'Action plan submitted'.
  • Locate the company and click the Review button.
  • Click 'Changes overview' – this shows only what has changed since the last submission. Review these changes first.
  • Click 'Action plan' to view the full plan if needed.
  • Click 'View previously submitted action plans' to check the history and track progress over time.
  • In the feedback text box, enter your detailed written feedback. See guidance on writing effective feedback below.
  • Update the Predicted granting date if this has changed.
  • Click the Send feedback button.
Writing Feedback That Actually Drives Progress
Acknowledge what has been completed well first. Specific praise for genuine progress motivates companies and reinforces good practice. For each completed action: state explicitly whether the evidence uploaded is sufficient to support the claimed score, or whether more is needed. If more is needed, describe exactly what. For incomplete actions: identify the highest-priority items and state why they matter most. Do not list all outstanding items equally – prioritise. Be direct about concerns without being discouraging. 'The CFSI procedure has been uploaded but there is no evidence of staff training or implementation in practice – this needs to be addressed before pre-granting' is direct and helpful. Update the predicted granting date honestly. If progress is slower than expected, adjust it. An unrealistic granting date creates false expectations. Close with next steps – what should the company focus on before the next submission? One or two priorities, not a long list.

Setting Reminders and Managing Your Workflow

Use the portal's reminder functionality to stay on top of your portfolio. Set a reminder when a company has not submitted a plan update for more than four weeks. Set a reminder when a key deadline is approaching. The Engagement Report available in your SCC portal view shows the recency of interactions with each company – use it as a weekly check to identify any company that has gone quiet and needs a proactive contact from you.

16.4 Reviewing a Draft Verification Assessment Report

After you submit your OSV report to the portal, the company is notified by email and must review and accept it before proceeding to the action plan. The company can either accept the report or send comments for discussion with the SCC.

Company ActionWhat It Means for the SCC
Company accepts the reportThe draft becomes the verified assessment. The company can now create their action plan. The SCC should ensure the company understands the action plan guidance document before they start.
Company sends commentsThe company has questions or concerns about the report. The SCC should review the comments and contact the company to discuss. If the comments reveal a misunderstanding, clarify it. If they reveal a genuine error in the report, correct it. The company cannot progress to action planning until they accept the report.
Important: Companies cannot progress to the action plan without accepting the OSV report.
If a company is slow to accept the report, contact them proactively. If a company has substantive objections to the report's scores, discuss these directly. If your scoring is correct and evidence-based, explain your rationale clearly – the scores should stand. Do not adjust scores simply because a company is unhappy. Adjust scores only where you are persuaded by new evidence or where you accept you made an error.

16.5 Reviewing an Action Plan

Companies are expected to review and update their action plan on a monthly basis and submit it for SCC review via their dashboard. The SCC aims to provide feedback within 10 working days of each submission.

From the Dashboard

  • Under 'Actions to Take', click Type and select 'Action plan submitted'.
  • Find the related company and click the Review button.
  • Click 'Changes overview' to review what has changed since the last submission.
  • Click 'Action plan' to view the full submitted plan.
  • Click 'View previously submitted action plans' to review the history.
  • Enter your feedback to the company in the text box.
  • Update the Predicted granting date if this has changed.
  • Click the Send feedback button.
Writing Effective Action Plan Feedback
Be specific. 'Good progress on SQEP' is less useful than 'Your SQEP skills matrix is looking much stronger – I can see 18 roles now have documented competency records. The two remaining gaps (QA Inspector and Goods-In Controller) are the priority before pre-granting.' Challenge every action marked complete. For each completed action, confirm in your feedback whether the evidence uploaded is sufficient or whether more is needed. Identify the highest-priority next actions. Tell the company what to focus on next – do not leave them guessing. Note the predicted granting date. Keeping this realistic motivates the company and sets appropriate expectations. If an action has been incomplete for more than two submission cycles without progress, note this explicitly and propose a conversation to unblock it.

16.6 How the Action Plan Works – What the Company Sees

Understanding how the action plan works from the company's perspective helps the SCC guide them more effectively. Here is what the company experiences:

  • After accepting the OSV report, the company clicks 'Create action plan' on their dashboard.
  • For each question that did not score 10, the company sees two options: improve the score (by selecting a higher-level statement and committing to the actions needed to achieve it), or maintain the current score (with a written reason).
  • For each improvement action, the company must record: the specific action to be undertaken, the action owner, and the completion target date.
  • When an action is 100% complete, the company marks it complete and uploads supporting evidence. The score on the portal automatically recalculates.
  • The company submits the updated plan to the SCC for review. During SCC review, the plan is locked and cannot be edited by the company.
  • Once the SCC provides feedback, the plan is re-opened for the company to update.
Common Action Plan Mistakes – and How the SCC Should Challenge Them
Vague actions: 'Improve SQEP' is not an action. A good action is specific, measurable, and time-bound. Require specificity before accepting. Defensive statements: 'We already do this' entered as the reason for maintaining a low score is not acceptable if the score is below granting threshold. Challenge this directly. Insufficient target scores: If the target score the company has selected will not be sufficient to reach the Triple 85, the portal will show a warning. The SCC must ensure the company addresses this – not ignore it. Evidence uploaded that does not match the action: A policy document uploaded as evidence that a process has been implemented does not close the action. The SCC must review evidence and flag insufficient uploads before accepting actions as complete. Too many actions in parallel: Companies that try to progress all actions simultaneously often stall on all of them. Coach them to focus on high-impact priority actions first.

16.7 Moving a Company into Pre-Granting

Pre-granting can only be initiated by the SCC via the submission and review of an action plan. The SCC must be satisfied that the company genuinely meets the Triple 85 criteria before initiating pre-granting status on the portal.

Pre-Conditions That Must Be Met Before Initiating Pre-Granting

  • 85%+ overall Business Excellence score
  • 85%+ QHSE (Health & Safety) score
  • 85%+ of action plan completed with evidence
  • A sector-specific impact statement submitted on the portal by the company
  • A sector-specific pre-granting meeting must have been completed
  • Note: The Triple 85 rule can be overridden by a NucCol admin after prior agreement – this is an exception, not the norm
  • Note: Companies who have never been granted BE (or were granted on the original F4N programme) must be pre-granted on both their BE and sector specific assessments

From the Dashboard – Initiating Pre-Granting

  • Under 'Actions to Take', click Type and select 'Action plan submitted'.
  • Find the related company action and click the Review button.
  • Click 'Changes overview' to review the specific changes since the last submission.
  • Click 'Action plan' to view the submitted action plan.
  • Enter plan feedback in the text box.
  • Click 'Send and advance to pre-granting' – this moves the company to pre-granting status.

From the Menu

  • Menu > Programme > Action Plan > Reviewing.
  • Locate the company and click 'Give feedback'.
  • Review the changes overview and action plan.
  • Enter feedback and click 'Send and advance to pre-granting'.

16.8 Completing the Granting Recommendation Form

Once the pre-granting visit has been completed and the SCC is satisfied the company meets all granting criteria, the SCC completes the granting recommendation form on the portal. This is the formal submission to the Granting Panel.

From the Menu

  • Menu > Programme > Pre-granting > Awaiting recommendation.
  • Locate the company you wish to recommend for granting.
  • Click 'Recommend for F4' button.
  • Complete all the required fields in the recommendation form.
  • Confirm that all required granting criteria are met.
  • Confirm that the company has submitted an impact statement.
  • Confirm that the company has submitted a benefits statement.
  • Click the 'Recommend for F4' button to submit.
Granting Recommendation Checklist – Before You Submit
All required portal documents uploaded: ISO certificates, benefits statement, F4N Charter, CSIP, impact statement Triple 85 all met – overall 85%+, QHSE 85%+, action plan 85%+ Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) populated with thoughtful, specific actions and commentary Pre-granting visit completed and recorded on portal Photographs uploaded (facility tour, 5S, visual management, KPI boards) Your written commentary covers all six BE categories with specific evidence references You have personally satisfied yourself that this company is genuinely nuclear-ready

16.9 Recording and Completing Company Visits on the Portal

Every SCC visit to a company – OSV, pre-granting, interim progress review, or M&S review – must be recorded on the portal. This is part of the official company record.

Booking a Company Visit

  • From the company record, select the Visits tab in the sub-menu.
  • Click 'Record visit' button.
  • Select the company from the company dropdown menu.
  • Select which assessment the visit relates to from the Assessment dropdown.
  • Enter the date of the meeting.
  • Select the reason for the meeting (OSV, pre-granting, interim review, M&S review, etc.).
  • Update the 'Visited by' section if required (defaults to your name).
  • Update the 'Supported by' section if another NucCol team member attended.
  • Click Save.

16.10 Viewing Company Records and Reports

The portal holds a comprehensive record of each company's journey. SCCs should know how to navigate these records efficiently.

Portal RecordWhere to Find It and What It Shows
Assessment scores and historyCompany record > Assessments tab. Select which assessment to view. You can switch between assessments to compare – useful for tracking improvement over time.
Benefits statementCompany record > Current assessments menu > Benefits Statement link under pre-granting section.
F4N CharterCompany record > Current assessments menu > F4N Charter link under pre-granting section.
CSIPCompany record > Current assessments menu > CSIP link under pre-granting section. Note: only the last updated CSIP is visible.
UK Subsidy Control declarationCompany record > Current assessments menu > Eligibility Statement link.
Uploaded company documentsCompany record > Documents tab.
Staff comments and correspondence logCompany record > Staff comments tab. Add comments by selecting a comment type, entering the text, and clicking Add comment.
Company timelineCompany record > Progress button on top banner. Select the journey to view. Click blue link text to see specific reports.
Previous granting recommendations and decisionsCompany record > Current assessments menu > Previous Decisions link.

16.11 Portal Reports Available to SCCs

ReportWhat It Shows
Workflow reportYour current queue of actions requiring attention across all companies.
Current workload reportAll companies currently active in your portfolio and their programme stage.
Completed workload reportCompanies that have completed their F4N journey with you.
Engagement reportFrequency and recency of SCC interactions with companies – useful for identifying companies that have not been contacted recently.
Process improvement reportProgramme-level data on improvements across the portfolio.
Programme impacts reportThe commercial and operational impacts reported by F4N companies – jobs created, contracts won, investment secured.

16.12 Other Key Portal Functions

Enabling/Starting a Sector Specific Assessment

The NSS assessment does not start automatically. The SCC must enable it on the portal when the time is right – typically when the company is approaching the Triple 85 threshold on their BE assessment (around 3–4 months before expected granting). From the menu, navigate to the company record and use the 'Enable sector specific assessment' function.

Updating a Company's Assigned SCC

If a company needs to be transferred to a different SCC (e.g., due to capacity changes or specialist needs), this is done via the 'Update/change company's Industrial Advisor' function from the company record. This should only be done with NucCol management agreement.

Setting and Managing Company Reminders

The portal allows SCCs to set reminder flags on company records. Use these to prompt action when: a company has not submitted a plan update for more than four weeks; a key deadline is approaching; or follow-up is needed after a visit or call. Email reminders can be turned on or off from the company record.

De-Granting and Extending Granted Status

In exceptional circumstances, F4N Granted status can be revoked (de-granting) if a company no longer meets the required standards. This is a serious action handled by NucCol management – if an SCC has concerns about a company's post-granting standards, the correct action is to raise these through the M&S review process and escalate to NucCol if they cannot be resolved. Status extensions can also be applied where there is a legitimate reason for a company to need additional time beyond their expiry date.

16.13 Company Portal Guidance – Helping Companies Use Their Portal Effectively

Part of the SCC's role is ensuring companies use their portal correctly. The following reference covers the most common company-side questions the SCC will be asked.

Company QuestionHow to Guide Them
How do I switch between Business Excellence and Sector Specific dashboards?From the dashboard, click the Sector button from the top banner and select the dashboard view from the dropdown. Importantly: they must ensure they have selected the correct dashboard view before completing assessments or submitting action plans.
How do I view my F4N journey progress?Click the Progress button on the top banner, select which Fit For journey to view, and click any blue link text to see that specific part of the journey.
How do I upload evidence for a completed action?When updating progress on an action, click the 'Update progress' button for the specific action, then use the upload function to attach evidence files before marking the action as complete.
How do I submit the F4N Charter and Benefits Statement?In the pre-granting section of the dashboard. Download and print the Charter, sign it, scan/photograph it, and upload via the Upload BE Charter link. For the Benefits Statement, write it on headed paper, have it signed by a senior leader, and upload via the Upload benefits statement link.
How do I submit a CSIP?Pre-Granting button > Upload CSIP link. Click Choose File, attach the CSIP document, click Save.
How do I change my company details?Account button > Edit company details. Review all five sections, make changes, ensure all sections are complete, click Save changes to company.
How do I add a new user to our portal account?Send the new user's name and email address to their SCC, who will arrange this with NucCol. The new user will receive a confirmation email with a request to create a password.
How do I view my Fit For certificates?When F4N Granted status is awarded, a Certificates link appears on the top banner. Click it to view programme name, start date, granting date, and expiry date.
How do I withdraw from the programme?Contact their SCC directly. The SCC handles withdrawal requests with NucCol.

Module 17: F4N in Practice – Case Studies, Terminology & SCC Reference

This final module brings together three important resources for the new SCC: real-world F4N case studies that demonstrate what the programme delivers for companies; a terminology and roles clarification guide to prevent confusion with older Nuclear AMRC naming conventions; and a consolidated reference section covering items from the portal guidance that apply specifically to how SCCs advise companies on their action plans.

17.1 F4N Case Studies – Real Impact from Real Companies

As a new SCC, you will regularly need to make the case for F4N to sceptical company directors. The most powerful way to do this is with real evidence from companies that have been through the programme. The following case studies are drawn from F4N's company portfolio and demonstrate the breadth of impact the programme delivers – operational, commercial, and cultural.

Case Study 1: Graham Hart

CategoryWhat Changed
Delivery performanceAchieved 100% on-time, in-full (OTIF) delivery rates – enabled by in-house graphical planning and real-time project tracking systems developed during the F4N journey.
Lean and SQEPLean training and SQEP-based shopfloor work instructions introduced. Reduced lead times, better forecasting, and stronger delivery discipline.
Supply chain alignmentStrategic realignment of supply chain to nuclear standards – suppliers themselves uplifted as part of the company's F4N commitment.
Market reachF4N Granted status respected internationally. Initial response from potential customers is curiosity, which turns to respect when they see the F4N logo – including in France and Saudi Arabia.
Graham Hart – Direct Quotes
'F4N gave us the framework to turn vision into action.' 'Paid big rewards overall, not just in the nuclear sector.' 'People now believe in the change. It's not just talk.'

Case Study 2: KGD

CategoryWhat Changed
KPI and management systemsNew KPI tracking and job review systems implemented. Helped monitor cost vs quality and drive operational efficiency.
Quality certificationsFormalised systems, upgraded welding capability, gained ISO 14001, ISO 18001, and ISO 3834 certifications – boosting credibility with customers.
People and leadershipHealth & Safety, leadership, and strategy training. The whole team became more engaged with company development.
Commercial confidenceRenewed confidence when approaching new companies. The F4N journey helped KGD define and strengthen their value proposition.
KGD – Direct Quotes
'The assessment helped us pinpoint where the biggest gains were waiting.' 'Renewed confidence – we're now approaching new companies we wouldn't have targeted before.' 'One-stop shop approach offers customers real benefits in cost and quality.'

Case Study 3: Lion Engineering

CategoryWhat Changed
Culture and strategySignificant culture change. Strategic planning now fully documented. Helped diversify into aerospace, defence, and nuclear.
Customer engagementShopfloor engagement with customers during audits. Improved customer confidence and quality perception significantly.
Infrastructure investmentSite upgrades including new machinery and staff facilities. New qualifications achieved across the team.
Nuclear contract winsHelp land nuclear contracts. Full body of documentation that nuclear expects now in place – de-risked nuclear bidding and quoting.
Lion Engineering – Direct Quotes
'It wasn't just about certification – F4N brought people along the journey.' 'Working with the programme opened doors for projects, funding, and training.' 'We now have the full body of documentation nuclear expects.' 'We quote with confidence.'
Using Case Studies with New Clients
Use case studies early in the engagement – ideally at the first meeting – to demonstrate that F4N delivers real business value, not just a badge. Match the case study to the client. If they are a precision machining company, use a machining case study. If they are concerned about culture, use Lion Engineering. If they want commercial impact, use Graham Hart's export story. Always emphasise the whole-business nature of the improvement – not just the quality certificate, but the delivery performance, the team engagement, and the commercial doors it opened. The ROI data (£2.1 billion new contracts, 100% recommendation rate) is powerful for board-level conversations. Use it alongside the qualitative company stories for maximum credibility.

17.2 Terminology Clarification – Old vs New

F4N has evolved over more than a decade, first under Nuclear AMRC and now under NucCol. During that evolution, terminology has changed. New SCCs will encounter older documents, presentations, and client companies who use the legacy terms. The following table clarifies the correct current terminology so there is no confusion in client communications or formal documents.

Old Term (Nuclear AMRC era)Current NucCol TermNotes
Industrial Advisor (IA)Supply Chain Consultant (SCC) or Senior Supply Chain Consultant (SSCC)The IA role under Nuclear AMRC is now the SCC/SSCC role under NucCol. Same function, updated title. Some source documents still use IA – always use SCC in formal communications.
Nuclear ChecklistNuclear Sector Specific (NSS) AssessmentThe Nuclear Checklist was the original name for the sector-specific layer of F4N. Under NucCol it is called the Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment. The NSS tab on the portal is the same tool, updated and expanded.
F4 / Fit4NuclearF4N / Fit For NuclearBoth are used informally. F4N is the preferred abbreviation in formal documents. 'Fit4Nuclear' (with the '4') is sometimes used in legacy materials.
BE Checklist / Business Excellence ChecklistBusiness Excellence (BE) AssessmentThe 60-question assessment covering the six categories. BE is the standard abbreviation.
Triple BarIOSH Managing Safely / Nuclear Safety Culture training'Triple Bar' was a Nuclear AMRC training programme branding. The training itself (nuclear safety culture, safety management) is still relevant – the programme name has changed.
F4N portal / NucCol portalF4N portal (accessed via NucCol)The portal is the same – now branded as the NucCol F4N portal. Companies and SCCs use it in the same way.
NAMRC / Nuclear AMRCNucCol / Nuclear Collaboration LtdThe organisation delivering F4N has changed from Nuclear AMRC (University of Sheffield) to NucCol (independent). NucCol was established in 2024 by the Nuclear AMRC leadership team.
Important: How to Handle Legacy Terminology with Clients
If a company refers to the 'Nuclear Checklist', understand they mean the Nuclear Sector Specific (NSS) Assessment – correct them politely and use the current term going forward. If a company refers to their 'Industrial Advisor', they mean their SCC. In your communications, always refer to yourself as their Supply Chain Consultant. Legacy documents in a company's portal may still use old terminology. This does not invalidate them – but it is worth noting in the OSV report or action plan feedback when you are updating scores or actions.

17.3 Impact Statements – What They Are and Why They Matter

One element of the pre-granting process that new SCCs sometimes overlook is the Impact Statement. This is a separate requirement from the Benefits Statement and must be submitted by the company before they can be moved into pre-granting status on the portal.

What an Impact Statement Is

The Impact Statement captures positive impacts that the Fit For programme has had on the company's operations. It is required by NucCol's funders to demonstrate the programme's economic and operational value. It is submitted by the company on the portal – not by the SCC. The company completes a structured form covering the positive operational and commercial impacts they have experienced.

How Companies Submit an Impact Statement

  • From the company dashboard, select the 'Impact Statements' link on the top banner.
  • Click the 'New impact statement' button.
  • Complete all fields with information about positive impacts the F4N programme has had on the organisation.
  • Click Submit to send the form to NucCol.
SCC Role on Impact Statements
The SCC must ensure the company has submitted an impact statement before initiating pre-granting on the portal – it is a pre-condition that is checked during the granting recommendation process. Coach companies to write their impact statement when they are approaching the Triple 85 – not at the last minute under pressure. Well-written impact statements with specific metrics and outcomes are more valuable to NucCol and more useful for the company's own commercial narrative. Encourage companies to include: specific contracts won or new markets entered, measurable operational improvements (OTIF, defect rates, near miss reporting rates), staff engagement or retention improvements, and any commercial recognition or industry visibility gained. Companies can submit more than one impact statement – encourage them to record impacts as they occur throughout the programme, not just at the end.

17.4 The Fourth Granting Criterion – Sector Specific Assessment

The Triple 85 criteria are widely known and referenced throughout this manual. However, the full granting criteria include a fourth requirement that is sometimes overlooked:

Complete F4N Granting Criteria – All Four Requirements
1. 85% overall Business Excellence score (or 78–80% if design is out of scope via the Design Factor). 2. 85% Business Excellence score in QHSE/Health & Safety – must be evidenced during the pre-granting visit. 3. 85% overall Business Excellence action plan completion – must be evidenced during the pre-granting visit. 4. A completed Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment (NSS) with corrective actions completed and approved by the Supply Chain Consultant.

The fourth criterion is critical and is specifically required by the Action Plan Guidance. It means the NSS assessment cannot simply be partially complete or have open, unapproved actions at the time of granting. The SCC must have reviewed and approved all NSS corrective actions before the company can proceed to the Granting Panel. This reinforces why the NSS assessment should be introduced 3–4 months before expected granting – it needs time for genuine actions to be taken and evidence gathered.

17.5 Custom Actions – A Powerful but Underused Tool

The F4N portal allows both SCCs and companies to add custom actions to the action plan – actions that are not tied to any of the 60 BE questions or NSS questions. These appear at the bottom of the action plan after the initial plan has been reviewed by the SCC. Custom actions are an important tool that new SCCs sometimes underuse.

When to Use Custom Actions

  • When the OSV report identifies a significant gap that does not map neatly to a single BE question. For example: 'Develop a comprehensive nuclear market entry strategy for Hinkley Point C supply chain opportunities' – this cuts across Strategy, Supply Chain, and NSS but may not be fully captured in any single question action.
  • When a company needs to take a specific action to address a nuclear customer requirement that has emerged during the programme. For example: 'Complete RCC-M awareness training for key engineering staff in preparation for the HPC Tier 2 qualification process.'
  • When an action plan needs a specific nuclear sector development action that the SCC wants to track formally. For example: 'Attend NucCol nuclear supply chain event and document three new potential customer contacts.'

How Companies Create Custom Actions

  • From the action plan, click the 'Add new custom action' button at the bottom of the plan.
  • Enter the description of the action required.
  • Enter the action owner.
  • Enter a completion target date.
  • Leave the percentage completion blank if no progress has been made yet.
  • Click 'Add custom action' to save.

How Companies Update Custom Actions

  • Click the 'Update progress' button against the selected custom action.
  • Enter progress made in the progress update box.
  • Update the completion percentage.
  • Add evidence attachments using the 'Add new document' button or by dragging files.
  • Click 'Update action button' to save.
SCC Guidance on Custom Actions
Use custom actions strategically – do not use them to pad the action plan with low-value tasks, but do use them when a genuine additional action is needed that the standard question set does not capture. Custom actions are visible to the SCC and count towards overall action plan completion. Ensure companies know this. If a company changes a custom action's description after it has been created, they must use the 'Update action description' button (not the progress update box). The SCC should brief companies on this to prevent frustration. Custom actions can be removed from the plan if they are no longer relevant – the company can do this via the 'Remove' button on the update screen. Confirm with the SCC before removing.

17.6 Action Plan Export and Reporting

Both companies and SCCs can export the action plan to Excel for offline analysis and reporting. This is a useful feature for companies who want to share their action plan progress with their board, and for SCCs who want to review a company's full plan history offline before a visit.

How Companies Export the Action Plan to Excel

  • From the company dashboard, select the 'Update action plan' link.
  • Click the 'Export to Excel' button at the top right of the screen.
  • The Excel file will download, containing all actions, owners, completion dates, and percentage progress.

Encourage companies to export their action plan before each SCC review visit – it gives both parties a portable reference document for the meeting that does not require portal access.

17.7 Key Contacts and Escalation Paths for SCCs

Every SCC should know who to contact at NucCol when they need support, guidance, or escalation. The following escalation paths apply to common situations the SCC will encounter.

SituationWho to Contact / What to Do
Uncertain about how to score an elementContact your NucCol engagement manager for guidance. Do not guess on important scores – a wrong score can create problems at the Granting Panel.
Company's SLT is disengaged and not respondingEscalate to your NucCol engagement manager early. A joint call or letter from NucCol leadership may be needed.
Company is experiencing financial difficultyReport to NucCol immediately. Financial instability can affect the company's ability to complete the programme and may affect their place on the Nuclear Supplier Database.
You believe a score has been inflated by pressure from the companyReport to your NucCol engagement manager immediately. Your professional integrity and the credibility of the F4N mark depend on your independence. NucCol will support you.
A company you have granted is behaving in a way that brings F4N into disreputeReport to NucCol immediately. De-granting procedures exist for this situation.
You need to transfer a company to another SCCAgree with your NucCol engagement manager first. Do not transfer a company unilaterally.
General portal issues or technical problemsContact NucCol support – your engagement manager can provide the current support contact.
A nuclear safety concern arises during a company visitIf you observe a genuine nuclear safety concern at a site you are visiting, your professional duty is to raise it with the site management immediately and report it to NucCol. This is not an F4N matter but a professional and ethical obligation.

17.8 F4N Glossary – Complete Reference

TermDefinition
ALARPAs Low As Reasonably Practicable. The standard to which risks must be reduced in the nuclear sector.
ASLApproved Supplier List. A managed list of suppliers who have been formally qualified to supply to a company.
BEBusiness Excellence. The 60-question, 6-category core F4N self-assessment.
BCPBusiness Continuity Plan. A documented plan for maintaining operations during a major disruption.
CFSICounterfeit, Fraudulent and Suspect Items. Items misrepresented as to identity, authenticity, or performance.
CSIPContinuous Sustainable Improvement Plan. The company's live improvement register, linked to F4N actions.
DFMDesign for Manufacture. Designing products with manufacturability in mind from the outset.
FMEAFailure Mode and Effects Analysis. A systematic tool for identifying and mitigating design and process failure modes.
GDAGeneric Design Assessment. ONR's technical assessment process for new nuclear facility designs.
IAIndustrial Advisor. The old Nuclear AMRC term for what is now called the Supply Chain Consultant (SCC).
INPOInstitute of Nuclear Power Operations. US nuclear industry organisation that published the INPO 14-005 safety culture traits framework.
ISO 19443Nuclear-specific Quality Management System standard built on ISO 9001.
M&SMaintain & Sustain. The annual subscription programme that retains F4N Granted status post-granting. Fee: £3,000/year.
MCRLManufacturing/Market Component Readiness Level. Framework describing a company's readiness to enter a specific market.
MVVMission, Vision, Values. The strategic foundation of an organisation.
NDANuclear Decommissioning Authority. Responsible for the UK's 17 nuclear legacy sites.
NIANuclear Industry Association. The trade body representing the UK civil nuclear industry.
NNLNational Nuclear Laboratory. Provides technical and scientific services to the UK nuclear sector.
NSSNuclear Sector Specific. The nuclear-focused assessment layer within F4N, formerly called the Nuclear Checklist.
NucColNuclear Collaboration Ltd. The organisation delivering F4N, successor to Nuclear AMRC. Established 2024.
ONROffice for Nuclear Regulation. The UK's independent nuclear regulator. Established 2011/2014.
OPEXOperational Experience Feedback. The nuclear sector practice of capturing and sharing lessons from incidents and near misses (TAG 77 clause 5.2.9).
OSVOn-Site Verification. The full-day consultant visit to verify the self-assessment.
PDPPersonal Development Plan. An individual's documented development record linked to strategic objectives.
RCARoot Cause Analysis. A structured technique for identifying the true underlying cause of a problem.
SAPSafety Assessment Principles. ONR's principles for assessing nuclear safety cases.
SCC/SSCCSupply Chain Consultant / Senior Supply Chain Consultant. The F4N consultant roles under NucCol.
SLCSite Licence Condition. One of the 36 conditions applied by the ONR to nuclear licensed sites.
SLTSenior Leadership Team. The directors and C-suite of the company being assessed.
SQEPSuitably Qualified and Experienced Person. The nuclear sector's framework for competency in safety-relevant roles.
SyAPSecurity Assessment Principles. ONR's principles for assessing nuclear security.
TAGTechnical Assessment Guide. ONR's technical guidance documents – 108 nuclear safety TAGs, 43 security TAGs.
TRLTechnology Readiness Level. A 9-level scale describing the maturity of a technology.
UKAEAUK Atomic Energy Authority. Responsible for the STEP fusion programme.
VSMValue Stream Map. A Lean tool mapping the flow of materials and information through a process.
WANOWorld Association of Nuclear Operators. International organisation that publishes the nuclear safety culture principles.

Module 18: Knowledge Checks – Self-Assessment and Trainer Questions

The following knowledge checks cover the key content across all 17 training modules. They can be used in three ways: as self-assessment questions for a new SCC working through the manual independently; as discussion questions for a trainer or engagement manager to use in a structured induction programme; or as preparation questions before a new SCC's first shadowing visit or solo OSV.

There are no trick questions. Every answer can be found in this manual. The purpose is to confirm understanding of the core concepts and flag any areas for further reading before moving into live delivery.

Module 1 and 2: F4N Fundamentals and the Journey

QuestionAnswer Guidance
What does F4N stand for, and who delivers it?Fit For Nuclear. Delivered by NucCol (Nuclear Collaboration Ltd), established in 2024 as the successor to Nuclear AMRC.
Name three specific commercial impacts that F4N has delivered.Any three from: £2.1 billion new contracts won by F4N companies; 3,049 jobs created or safeguarded; £43 million additional investment; 100% of surveyed companies would recommend it.
What are the 8 stages of the F4N journey in order?Capability Questionnaire (NCQ); BE and NSS Self-Assessment; On-Site Verification (OSV); Improvement Plan and Execution; Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment; Pre-Granting; Granting Panel; Maintain and Sustain.
What is the Triple 85 and what is the fourth granting criterion?85% overall BE score, 85% QHSE score, 85% action plan completion. The fourth criterion is a completed NSS assessment with all corrective actions approved by the SCC.
When should the NSS assessment be introduced, and why not earlier?Approximately 3–4 months before expected granting, when the company is approaching Triple 85 on BE. Introducing it too early can overwhelm the company, lead to vague actions, and dilute strategic focus.
What must a company submit on the portal before they can enter pre-granting status?Impact statement, signed Benefits Statement, signed F4N Charter, ISO certificates, latest ISO 9001 audit report with all NCs closed, CSIP, completed action plan with evidence, NSS assessment with SCC-approved actions.

Module 3: The Scoring System

QuestionAnswer Guidance
What do the four scores represent?0 = nothing in place; 2 = informal/inconsistent; 7 = formal, documented, working system (granting readiness threshold); 10 = best practice, typically requiring UKAS-accredited certification.
A company shows you their QHSE policy. What score does having a policy alone support?A score of 2. A policy alone is informal/documented intent but not a deployed working system. Deployment and evidence of it working scores 7+.
What UKAS-accredited certifications are needed for a score of 10 on the QHSE Policy and Strategy element?ISO 9001, ISO 14001, and ISO 45001 – all certified by a UKAS-accredited certification body.
Why is 7 the granting readiness threshold rather than 10?Because 7 represents a formal, working approach with evidence – genuine operational readiness. A score of 10 (best practice/certified) is the improvement goal post-granting, not a prerequisite for it.

Modules 4–9: Business Excellence Categories

QuestionAnswer Guidance
How many questions are in the BE assessment and how many categories?60 questions across 6 categories, 10 questions per category.
Name the 6 BE categories.Strategy & Leadership; Design & Project Management; People Excellence; Process Excellence; QHSE; Supply Chain & Social Values.
A company scores itself 7 on SQEP but cannot produce a skills matrix. What should the SCC do?Adjust the score down to 2. A 7 on SQEP requires a defined framework covering all safety-relevant roles with documented qualification and experience requirements and verified evidence that post-holders meet them. A skills matrix is the primary evidence vehicle for this.
What is CFSI and why does it matter in nuclear?Counterfeit, Fraudulent and Suspect Items – items misrepresented as to identity, authenticity, or performance. In nuclear, a non-conforming component in a safety-critical application can be catastrophic. CFSI controls prevent unverified or counterfeit items entering the supply chain.
A company has near-miss reporting rates of two per month across 50 employees. What does this tell you about their safety culture?It is a warning sign of under-reporting, not evidence of good safety. Companies with healthy safety cultures typically report significantly more near misses – a high near-miss rate is a positive cultural indicator, not a concern.
What is the Design Factor and when does it apply?An adjustment to the overall granting threshold for companies whose ISO 9001 scope does not include design. The first four Design & PM questions may score 0 for legitimate scope reasons. The threshold adjusts to 78–80% overall rather than 85%.

Modules 10–11: Nuclear Sector Specific Assessment

QuestionAnswer Guidance
Name the seven NSS sections.Nuclear Industry Fundamentals; Nuclear Safety Culture; Leadership and Governance; Quality and Compliance (ISO 19443); Supply Chain Readiness; Human Performance; Security of Information.
What is ALARP and why is it relevant to the supply chain?As Low As Reasonably Practicable. The standard to which nuclear risks must be reduced. For suppliers, it means demonstrating that proportionate, cost-justified steps have been taken to reduce risks in their processes. Supplying to a nuclear facility means your components and services must support, not undermine, the ALARP demonstration.
Name four of the ten WANO nuclear safety culture traits.Any four from: Personal Accountability; Questioning Attitude; Safety Communications; Leadership Accountability; Decision-Making; Respectful Work Environment; Continuous Learning; Problem Identification and Resolution; Environment for Raising Concerns; Work Processes.
What is ONR TAG 77 and why does it matter to F4N?ONR Technical Assessment Guide 77 covers supply chain management arrangements. The F4N NSS assessment was built to align with TAG 77's requirements, meaning a company that scores well on the NSS assessment is demonstrating compliance with the ONR's own expectations for supply chain management.
What is the difference between a Major NC and an OFI in an ISO 9001 audit?A Major NC is a fundamental failure against the standard and must be closed before certification can continue or be renewed. An OFI (Opportunity for Improvement) is a recommendation from the auditor – not a requirement. The company is not obliged to act on OFIs, but SCCs should review them for relevance to F4N scoring.

Modules 12–13: OSV, Pre-Granting and the Panel

QuestionAnswer Guidance
What are the three types of evidence the SCC uses during the OSV?Documentary (written records, policies, certificates), Observational (what you see on the shopfloor – cannot be faked), Demonstrative (live demonstrations of systems and processes).
Why is observational evidence the most reliable?Because it cannot be prepared specifically for the visit. A clean shopfloor, live KPI boards, and staff who can explain the near-miss process reflect the actual culture of the organisation – not a managed impression.
Within what timeframe must the OSV report be issued?Within 14 working days of the visit.
What should the SCC do if they identify concerns during the pre-granting visit that make them uncomfortable recommending the company?Raise concerns directly with the company before leaving. Agree a remediation plan. Delay pre-granting until concerns are resolved. Do not proceed to a panel recommendation if you cannot honestly stand behind the submission.
What is the Benefits Statement, who writes it, and what must it include?Written by the company on headed paper, signed by a senior leader (MD or Director). It must describe specifically how F4N has improved the business with measurable outcomes – operational improvements, commercial results, cultural changes. Generic statements are not acceptable.
Name three things the Granting Panel may consider as grounds for delaying granting.Any three from: weak or missing evidence; vague/defensive action plan entries; safety culture not demonstrably embedded; SQEP or CFSI gaps unresolved; NSS assessment superficially completed; SCC commentary lacking specificity.

Modules 14–15: Nuclear Sector and Awareness

QuestionAnswer Guidance
Name four nuclear programmes that UK manufacturers can target through F4N.Any four from: Hinkley Point C; Sizewell C; Rolls-Royce SMR; STEP fusion; GE-Hitachi BWRX-300; Dreadnought-class submarine programme; NDA decommissioning programmes; Sellafield.
What is the Safety Case and why does it matter to suppliers?A formal, documented, argued case that a nuclear facility is safe to operate. Every component and service in the supply chain must be able to support the Safety Case. A quality failure in a supplied component can invalidate part of the Safety Case, potentially shutting down the facility.
What are the 36 Licence Conditions?Site Licence Conditions (SLCs) applied by the ONR to each nuclear licensed site, from interpretation (SLC 1) to organisational capability (SLC 36). They place specific obligations on licensees and cascade quality and safety requirements throughout the supply chain.
What is the Graded Approach?The principle that controls, inspections, documentation, and oversight are proportionate to the safety significance of the item or activity. Not everything in a nuclear facility is safety-critical – the Graded Approach ensures effort is directed where it matters most.

Module 16: The F4N Portal

QuestionAnswer Guidance
How does the SCC initiate pre-granting status on the portal?By reviewing the company's submitted action plan and clicking 'Send and advance to pre-granting' – but only after confirming all pre-conditions are met (Triple 85 criteria, impact statement submitted, pre-granting meeting completed).
Within how many working days should the SCC provide action plan feedback?10 working days.
What must happen before a company can progress to creating their action plan?They must accept the draft OSV report on the portal. They cannot proceed to the action plan until the report is formally accepted.
A company wants to add an action to their plan that relates to a specific nuclear customer requirement not covered by any BE question. What portal function do they use?Custom actions – available at the bottom of the action plan after initial creation. The company can add, update, and evidence custom actions in the same way as standard BE actions.
What is the Engagement Report and when should the SCC use it?A portal report showing the recency of SCC interactions with each company. SCCs should review it weekly to identify companies that have not been contacted recently and may need a proactive touchpoint.

Website Features
☢️ NuclearReady Profile
Shows/hides the NuclearReady Profile tab for every member on nuccol.co.uk/members.html
🤖 Frankie Link (Members Sidebar)
Shows/hides the Frankie chat link in every member's sidebar on nuccol.co.uk/members.html. OFF by default while testing — turn on when ready to go live.
⚛️ Nuclear Engineering Mode (Frankie Chat)
Lets Frankie's chat pull from the 61k-chunk reactor design-document library (real DCD/FSAR/PCSR/GDA text) when a question actually looks nuclear-engineering-flavoured — instead of just the F4N-compliance knowledge base. OFF by default — this content was deliberately kept out of default chat for the member soft launch; turn on only once you're ready for it to affect every member's chat.

This is site-wide — takes effect for all members immediately, not just this browser.
